articles.title: The cash an owner can actually claim
articles.short_title: The cash an owner can actually claim
questions: Why can a profitable business have little cash that its owner can safely withdraw?
How much reinvestment and operating working capital does the business need?
Which daily cash, customer, stock and supplier measures should trigger action?
How do owner pay, borrowing, growth and succession affect transferable earning power?
articles.workbook_name: Project 1 - MSME Owner Earnings and Operations.xlsx

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

An owner opens the mobile banking app and sees KSh 1.2 million. How much of it can they take home?

The tempting answer is “the cash balance.” The careful answer begins with a different question: what does that cash have to do before it belongs to the owner? Payroll is due. A customer has paid in advance for goods the business has not delivered. A tax instalment is scheduled. A loan repayment falls next week. The business needs stock before the next sales cycle. The account balance is real, but it has several claimants.

That is why this series treats “owner earnings” as a way of thinking about earning power, not as a synonym for cash, profit, or a dividend. Buffett’s 1986 shareholder letter described owner earnings as reported earnings plus certain non-cash charges, less the average capital expenditure needed to maintain long-term competitive position and unit volume, and less additional working capital needed for the same purpose. He also warned that the maintenance-capital estimate can be difficult [1]. That caveat belongs in the formula, not in a footnote.

sections.heading: Four questions, four answers
sections.text:
Start by separating four measures:

1. Cash generated in the period asks what entered and left the bank accounts for one stated period.
2. Accounting profit matches recognized income and expenses under the business’s accounting basis. It can differ from cash because customers may owe money, stock may remain unsold, or invoices may be unpaid.
3. Owner earnings estimates how much the business can earn over time after reinvestment needed to keep the operation competitive and at the same level of activity.
4. Cash that can prudently be distributed asks what can leave the business after upcoming obligations, debt principal, restrictions, and a sensible operating reserve.

They may happen to be close in a stable, simple business. They often diverge in a growing or seasonal one. A fast-growing shop may report a profit while cash is tied up in new inventory and unpaid invoices. A business may also show cash because it drew a loan. That cash came with a matching liability. It is not sales revenue.

A useful starting bridge for an owner-managed business is:

> Reported profit after a market-level payment for the owner’s work  
> + relevant non-cash charges, if they have not already been included in the starting cash measure  
> − estimated maintenance and replacement investment  
> − additional working capital needed for the activity being sustained  
> = an owner-earnings estimate

Then run a separate liquidity bridge:

> Cash available before distribution  
> − due payroll, supplier and tax payments  
> − scheduled loan principal and other required cash commitments  
> − required or chosen operating reserve  
> = cash the owner could consider distributing

If the same expense appears in both bridges, check for double-counting. For instance, do not begin with net income, subtract an expense again, and call that conservatism. State the treatment once.

sections.heading: A small example
sections.text:
Imagine a repair shop with one owner who also manages the staff and works at the counter. For this fictional year, after recording a reasonable wage for that work, the books show KSh 800,000 of profit. Depreciation is KSh 150,000. The business has bought replacement tools, but it also opened a second service bay. The accounts do not identify which shillings of equipment spending merely kept the first bay running and which created extra capacity.

A model might show a maintenance range of KSh 120,000–250,000, with a central working assumption of KSh 180,000. If maintaining the existing volume also ties up an extra KSh 100,000 in parts and customer credit, the central estimate is:

KSh 800,000 + 150,000 − 180,000 − 100,000 = KSh 670,000

That is an estimate of owner earnings under those assumptions. It is not a precise audited line. The book’s cash could still be lower because old invoices remain unpaid, a loan principal payment is due, or a tax payment differs from the tax expense recognized during the year. Nor should the owner automatically withdraw KSh 670,000. First reconcile the actual bank movement and list obligations due before the next reliable receipts.

The owner’s labour matters too. If the owner worked full-time but recorded no salary, the apparent profit includes pay for a job. A buyer would need someone to do that work. For valuation, estimate the cost of competent replacement labour and subtract it before treating the remaining profit as a return on ownership. For a sole proprietor deciding what to transfer to a personal account, salary and owner draw may be booked differently. The economic question is still: did the business earn a return after paying for the work that keeps it open?

sections.heading: What the research adds
sections.text:
Working-capital decisions can shape both profit and available cash. Deloof studied 1,009 large Belgian non-financial firms and found associations between profitability and the time firms held receivables and inventory [2]. García-Teruel and Martínez-Solano examined 8,872 Spanish SMEs and reported that shortening collection periods and inventory holding periods was associated with higher profitability in their sample [3]. Those are useful reasons to measure the cash cycle. They are not a target that every Kenyan shop should hit. A wholesaler who cuts stock below what reliable service requires may lose customers. A small supplier who shortens payment terms may lose a large buyer.

For a lender or a buyer, the entity also matters. A loan in the owner’s personal name, a company overdraft, a director’s guarantee, and a supplier balance may all affect risk, but they are not the same liability. The Business Credit series already demonstrates why a lender’s legal borrower and the business whose cash flow is being assessed must be joined carefully. The cash is only available to the party that owns the account and is free to use it under its contracts. Merton’s structural credit model is a useful reminder that equity and debt are different claims on the same business assets [4]. It is not a substitute for the owner’s dated cash schedule: the model needs asset value and risk inputs that most small businesses do not observe reliably.

sections.heading: A five-minute owner check
Rebuild the year before asking what can be drawn
sections.text:
Take the last twelve months and put the business cash story in one schedule. Reconcile sales to invoices, till receipts, mobile payments and merchant settlements. A KSh 2 million sale recorded on credit is not KSh 2 million in the bank. Reconcile purchases and payroll to invoices, payslips and payment runs. A bill received after year end may belong to the period even if it has not been paid. The point is to know which timing differences explain cash, not to force cash to equal profit.

Use a repeatable order:

1. Choose one legal entity and period. If the shop, warehouse and vehicle are owned by different companies or relatives, identify intercompany rent, loans, guarantees and assets before combining cash.
2. Tie opening and closing cash to statements. Include bank, mobile money and till cash separately. Remove restricted deposits and amounts held for tax or customers.
3. Tie revenue and costs to records. Identify VAT or other indirect tax, refunds, discounts, bad debt, stock adjustments and personal spending.
4. Reconcile operating cash. Add back noncash charges once, then reflect actual changes in receivables, stock, supplier balances and other operating items.
5. Classify investment. List cash asset additions and disposals; distinguish maintenance, compliance, replacement and growth using asset-level evidence.
6. Separate financing. Draws are receipts from financing; principal repayments are cash outflows. Interest treatment depends on the starting point and valuation question.
7. Normalize owner work and one-offs. Replace below-market or above-market compensation with supportable costs for necessary work.
8. State working-capital assumptions. Determine whether balances reflect normal trading, seasonality, overdue suppliers or one-time catch-up.
9. Calculate separate answers for earning power and liquidity. Owner earnings is not the same as cash available this week.

This is more demanding than “profit plus depreciation,” but it reveals missing books. If the owner cannot reconcile deposits to sales, improve transaction capture before building a more complicated valuation.

sections.heading: A detailed fictional cash bridge
sections.text:
Suppose a workshop reports KSh 1.8 million net income after paying the proprietor KSh 900,000 for management and repair work. Depreciation is KSh 240,000. Receivables rise from KSh 800,000 to KSh 1.05 million, inventory from KSh 1.20 million to KSh 1.45 million, and trade payables from KSh 700,000 to KSh 830,000. On these simplified balances, incremental net working capital consumes KSh 370,000: 250,000 more receivables plus 250,000 more stock less 130,000 more payables. Cash from operations before other accruals is roughly KSh 1.67 million.

The shop spends KSh 680,000 on equipment. The asset list shows KSh 380,000 replaces two lifts and a diagnostic unit supporting current service; KSh 300,000 fits out a second bay. A simple historical cash figure after all capex is KSh 990,000. Yet that is not normalized earning power: actual capex includes growth, while future maintenance may not equal this year’s replacement spend.

For an owner-earnings view, the KSh 1.8 million profit already includes KSh 900,000 compensation. A qualified replacement manager and mechanic would cost KSh 1.2 million. Adjust down by only the KSh 300,000 shortfall; do not subtract the full replacement wage again. Using KSh 380,000 maintenance and KSh 370,000 additional working capital, normalized owner earnings are KSh 990,000, calculated as KSh 1.8 million profit + KSh 240,000 depreciation − KSh 380,000 maintenance − KSh 370,000 additional working capital − KSh 300,000 replacement-pay gap. The KSh 1.29 million figure is the intermediate estimate before the replacement-pay adjustment; it is not the final normalized owner-earnings figure. This bridge also happens to equal the KSh 990,000 historical cash-after-total-capex proxy because this example's KSh 300,000 growth-bay outlay and KSh 300,000 replacement-pay adjustment offset numerically. That coincidence will not generally hold. The KSh 300,000 growth bay remains a separate investment decision, not maintenance; test its expected incremental return separately and do not deduct it again from the no-growth owner-earnings estimate.

The distribution question uses actual dates. If the bank has KSh 1.2 million, upcoming payroll is KSh 250,000, critical suppliers KSh 260,000, rent and utilities KSh 80,000, taxes KSh 90,000, loan principal KSh 100,000, and a prepaid order requires KSh 130,000 to complete, those uses total KSh 910,000. With a KSh 150,000 reserve floor, only KSh 140,000 is provisionally above the listed needs. If a disputed KSh 200,000 customer receipt was mistakenly counted, even that headroom disappears. A business can earn KSh 1.29 million over a normalized year and still have little safe cash for an immediate draw.

Every line must be tested. Check maintenance with the technician and quotations; replacement cost with the actual job description; working capital across several seasons; and the forecast with dated receipts. Keep the bridge auditable enough that a lender, partner or buyer can challenge it.

sections.heading: Reconcile annual cash to the bank statement
sections.text:
For each month, use the identity: opening unrestricted cash plus operating, financing and asset-sale receipts, less operating payments, capex, financing payments and owner distributions equals closing unrestricted cash. Tie the result to bank and mobile-money reconciliations after transfers between accounts are removed. If it does not tie, list the difference and investigate instead of hiding it in “other.”

A facility draw is financing, not sales cash; principal repayment is not an operating expense. Reconcile tax payable, tax expense and tax paid rather than subtracting the same tax twice. Customer deposits are receipts with delivery or refund obligations. Supplier credit can increase cash temporarily but is not sustainable working capital if it reflects overdue balances. The cash schedule should show each item on its due date.

Separate cash control from profit measurement. A bank reconciliation shows that cash exists, not that profit recurs. A stocktake checks quantity, not saleability. An invoice confirms a ledger entry, not collection. A monthly close should test both the existence and economic quality of the asset or income.

sections.heading: Use a monthly owner review
sections.text:
A monthly review can fit on one page: reported profit; profit-to-cash bridge; maintenance estimate and range; incremental working-capital use or release; market replacement pay; scheduled debt; reserve requirement; and distributions already taken. Beside each figure, record source and owner. Mark it tied, estimated or unresolved. If an unresolved line changes a drawing, loan or hiring decision, resolve it before acting.

Compare the forecast with actual dates and amounts. If collections repeatedly arrive ten days late, use observed timing instead of the sales team's best-case promise. If a repair was larger because replacement had been deferred, update the asset plan. If the owner withdrew money for a personal emergency, record the draw separately and restore the agreed reserve process. This prevents a one-off event from being misreported as ordinary performance.

The practical sequence is: close the books, reconcile cash, estimate sustainable earnings, protect the reserve, then approve a transfer. Use the earnings estimate to assess durable returns, the cash plan for today's payment decision, and a valuation method only after ownership and financing claims are reconciled.

sections.heading: Three ways the bridge can mislead
sections.text:
The first is double counting. If the starting figure is net income, tax expense and interest expense have already affected it. If the analysis adds back interest to estimate enterprise cash flow, debt service still belongs in the later financing bridge. If it starts from cash flow after interest and then subtracts interest again, it understates cash. Write the basis at the top of the schedule: equity earnings after interest, operating cash before financing, or cash available for distribution. Every add-back should have a clear reason and a matching treatment elsewhere.

The second is treating all noncash expense as disposable cash. Depreciation is not a current payment, but the assets that depreciate wear out. Adding back depreciation without a replacement estimate turns an income statement convention into a claim that equipment is free. Amortization may relate to software, licenses or acquired customer relationships with different replacement economics. Add back only where appropriate to the chosen measure, and then explicitly fund the renewal or replacement need.

The third is interpreting working-capital release as recurring earnings. A business that collects old receivables or reduces stock may generate cash this year. It cannot repeat the same release indefinitely. If the normalized closing balance is lower than the opening balance because the firm liquidated excess stock, separate that one-time release from the annual owner-earnings estimate. If supplier balances rose because invoices were unpaid, do not treat that as permanent free financing.

sections.heading: Adapt the claim to the business
sections.text:
A bakery’s cash bridge should include flour and packaging bought before daily sales, equipment replacement, waste and retailer settlement timing. A professional services firm may have little physical inventory but can carry large receivables, unbilled work, software subscriptions and key-person exposure. A farm can have substantial seasonal inventory and biological production cycles; profit and cash receipt dates can fall in different periods. A small property developer may receive deposits that are tied to units still to be completed. The same four questions apply, but the working-capital and maintenance lines are different.

For a service business, the replacement-capital question may be software, cybersecurity, employee training, regulatory licenses and customer acquisition needed to keep retention stable. For a vehicle operator, it includes tyres, engines, permits and downtime. For a retailer, it includes shelving and point-of-sale systems as well as stock availability. This is why an analyst should ask the people who operate the assets what spending preserves current service before setting the owner-earnings line.

The owner can start with three columns: reported, adjusted and unresolved. Put source values in reported. Put only evidenced corrections in adjusted. Put estimates and missing records in unresolved with a low/base/high range when possible. This keeps the reader from mistaking a plausible assumption for an audited fact. The best bridge is not the one with the fewest open items; it is the one that tells management which unresolved item could change the decision.

sections.heading: Decide whether a draw is repeatable
sections.text:
A draw can be funded by four different things: current operating cash, accumulated cash from prior good years, new borrowing, or selling an asset. Only the first may indicate current earning capacity, and even then the business must fund obligations and replacement needs. The owner should label each source. A special distribution funded from an old cash reserve might be entirely reasonable, but it should not become a monthly expectation that forces the company to borrow later.

Before a regular owner draw, compare the proposed annual amount with normalized owner earnings over several periods and with downside liquidity. If owner earnings vary sharply by season, set a lower regular amount and make a later year-end distribution only after the peak cash need has passed. If the business is expanding, decide whether the growth return exceeds the owner’s alternative use of cash. If the business is not earning enough after replacement labor and maintenance, a large transfer can turn an accounting profit into a weaker business.

The decision note can be short: “The business earned an estimated KSh X after replacement labor and maintenance under the base case; the low case is KSh Y. The next 13 weeks remain above reserve only if customer A pays by date D. We approve a draw of KSh Z today and will revisit after the cash is received.” That sentence states the estimate, condition, amount and review point. It is much more useful than saying the bank balance looks healthy.

sections.heading: Turn the bridge into a monthly decision
sections.text:
The annual owner-earnings bridge is useful only if the owner can reproduce it from the books and the bank. Build the same bridge monthly, then roll it forward over twelve months. For each month, show cash collected from customers, cash paid to suppliers and employees, tax paid, routine capital spending, principal and interest, and owner withdrawals. Reconcile the ending cash to the bank statement. This gives the owner two answers: what the business earned over a representative period and whether that earning has actually arrived as spendable cash.

Suppose a distributor reports KSh 900,000 of monthly accounting profit. Its owner performs purchasing and collections work worth KSh 160,000 a month at a realistic replacement cost. The business has KSh 140,000 of routine equipment and vehicle renewal, and receivables and stock have absorbed KSh 240,000 more cash than the prior month. Before debt principal, tax timing and reserve decisions, the month has not produced KSh 900,000 of owner cash. The example is not a universal formula or margin benchmark; it shows why each adjustment needs its own line and evidence.

The sequence matters. Deduct a replacement wage before treating owner labour as an add-back. Deduct normal maintenance investment after examining the actual assets and their service condition. Show working-capital movements as a cash timing item, not a permanent annual charge: a build-up consumes cash, while a release can temporarily inflate it. Then show taxes, interest and principal according to the purpose of the measure. A lender's cash-flow definition may use a different sequence from a shareholder's residual cash measure.

The monthly close should make timing visible. A December profit supported by invoices collected in February is profit, but it does not fund a December supplier payment unless credit is available. Keep the income statement, cash-flow movement and balance-sheet roll-forward side by side. The business owner can then distinguish an earnings problem from a collections problem and a temporary seasonal draw from a recurring structural deficit. Research on working capital and SME performance emphasizes that its cash requirements and its effect on performance are linked, but the relationship is not a one-direction rule that says less working capital is always better [2, 3].

sections.heading: Use a short forecast to test whether the cash is safe to take
sections.text:
A distribution decision should begin with a rolling 13-week cash forecast. Start with reconciled opening bank cash and show weekly collections by named customer or customer group, payroll, critical suppliers, tax, rent, debt service, capex and owner withdrawals. The base case should use expected payment dates grounded in collection history, not invoice due dates alone. A downside case can move the largest collections later, reduce sales where orders are not yet secured, and include known repairs or tax obligations.

The lowest projected weekly balance is more decision-useful than the year-end balance. If the forecast falls below the operating floor, owner withdrawals should wait or be funded through a documented financing plan. Set the floor from obligations and recovery time: payroll and statutory payments, the cash needed to continue essential deliveries, the likely delay before emergency funding, and the cost of restarting after a stock-out or service interruption. Do not copy a rule such as “three months of expenses” without checking seasonality and the actual commitments.

The forecast should be refreshed every week. At the review, compare forecast against actual cash and explain the three biggest differences. If collections repeatedly arrive later than forecast, change the assumptions and collection process. If a supplier asks for a deposit earlier than expected, confirm the purchase and delivery before moving the date. The forecast is an operating tool; it should change as evidence changes.

sections.heading: Keep a distribution ledger
sections.text:
A distribution ledger records date, amount, purpose, approving person, forecast headroom, remaining reserves and any tax or legal treatment. Separate wages for work, repayment of a documented shareholder loan, dividends or profit distributions, and personal expenses paid by the business. These categories have different accounting, tax, governance and solvency implications. The ledger prevents a strong month from obscuring repeated owner draws that were never compared with reinvestment needs.

At quarter-end, compare total distributions with normalized earnings and actual free cash over a rolling period. If cash paid out is persistently greater than cash produced after maintenance and normal working capital, the difference must come from borrowing, asset sales, a working-capital release, or delayed obligations. Name the source. This is the practical meaning of the owner-earnings question: not merely what could be withdrawn in theory, but what can be taken without weakening the operation that produces next year's earnings.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Project 1 workbook opens with the owner-earnings bridge and 13-week forecast, then links to maintenance, monthly working capital, receivable and payable ageing, inventory ABC, unit economics, debt and growth screening, a weekly action log and transaction checklist. The Article Case tab now reproduces the workshop example above: KSh990,000 normalized owner earnings, KSh140,000 provisional headroom after listed dated uses and the reserve floor, and negative KSh60,000 headroom if a disputed KSh200,000 receipt was counted. The separate Owner Earnings tab is a larger editable scenario: it starts with KSh48m revenue and KSh3.2m reported net income; after replacing KSh3m owner compensation with KSh2.2m market labour, adding KSh0.9m D&A and deducting KSh1.2m maintenance and KSh1.5m incremental working capital, owner earnings are KSh2.2m. After KSh0.6m scheduled principal and a KSh0.4m reserve top-up, that model shows KSh1.2m indicative residual cash. Both cases are fictional; do not combine their inputs. Evidence Vectors records them separately and gives their workbook locators. The earlier African Markets and Business Credit workbook informed the dated cash and facility workflow; this model connects that workflow to owner labour, maintenance needs and sustainable distributions.

sections.text:

articles.title: Maintenance capital and working capital
questions: Why can a profitable business have little cash that its owner can safely withdraw?
How much reinvestment and operating working capital does the business need?
Which daily cash, customer, stock and supplier measures should trigger action?
How do owner pay, borrowing, growth and succession affect transferable earning power?
articles.workbook_name: Project 1 - MSME Owner Earnings and Operations.xlsx

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

A business can look cash-rich because it has stopped replacing equipment. It can also look cash-poor because it is building the next stage of capacity. If we call all capital spending “maintenance,” we can understate what a growing business might earn. If we call all spending “growth,” we can overstate what an owner can safely take out.

The accounts usually tell us how much the business spent, but not how much it had to spend to keep its existing competitive position. The 1986 Berkshire letter defines owner earnings by subtracting the average capitalized expenditure needed to maintain long-term competitive position and unit volume, plus extra working capital required to sustain that position and volume [1]. The definition contains two separate judgments: fixed investment and working capital. Neither should be replaced automatically by depreciation or a percentage of sales.

sections.heading: Why depreciation does not settle the question
sections.text:
Depreciation spreads an accounting cost over an estimated useful life. It is not necessarily the money the business must spend this year to remain productive. A delivery van may be depreciated over five years, but a sudden shortage of parts may make replacement cost rise. Software can become commercially obsolete before its accounting life ends. Conversely, an old building may keep serving the same customers with modest maintenance even as accounting depreciation continues.

The gap is not proof that management is manipulating results. It is a reason to inspect the assets and the operating task they perform. A business owner can ask:

 Which equipment, systems, licenses or premises are essential to deliver today’s saleable output?
 What repairs, upgrades and replacements have been made over several years?
 Has capacity, location, service quality or product range expanded?
 Are there overdue replacements or deferred maintenance?
 Does the business plan rely on a capacity level that the current assets cannot sustain?

A useful operating history includes several years of capital spending, depreciation, disposals, capacity additions, service failures and, where possible, physical asset condition. Use cash paid for property and equipment from the cash flow statement, then reconcile it to additions in the fixed-asset note. The two can differ due to unpaid purchases, leases, acquisitions, disposals, foreign exchange, or construction timing.

Economic depreciation research makes a related point: the loss in an asset’s productive value may not follow a simple straight-line path [2]. A standard depreciation schedule can be an accounting convention rather than a map of replacement economics. It is evidence; it is not the owner-earnings answer.

sections.heading: A practical range, not a magic ratio
sections.text:
Suppose a small milling business reports KSh 1.5 million in depreciation and spent KSh 2.4 million on equipment during the year. It replaced one motor, installed a larger mill, and added a delivery vehicle. The filing or accounts may not allocate the KSh 2.4 million between upkeep and expansion.

A defensible draft might state:

 Observed fact: total equipment cash spending was KSh 2.4 million for the year, based on bank records and invoices.
 Observed fact: the new mill raised rated capacity; the motor replaced a failed unit; the vehicle added a delivery route.
 Analyst estimate: maintenance and replacement are provisionally KSh 0.8–1.3 million, pending multi-year repair and replacement records.
 Unresolved: no reliable evidence yet separates routine maintenance from the costs of keeping output at its former level.

Then show the owner-earnings range under both ends of the estimate. If earnings move materially, the uncertainty is material and belongs in the conclusion. Do not choose the number that makes the company look cheapest.

The same rule applies to listed companies. A public filing may show total additions to property, plant and equipment, but the report rarely gives a clean “maintenance capex” subtotal. Management may discuss growth projects or capacity plans, but that guidance is still a forecast and may not cover all replacement needs. The article should say “maintenance capex is not separately disclosed” and give a range only when the evidence supports one.

sections.heading: Working capital is investment too
sections.text:
Working capital is the cash committed to receivables, inventory and other operating balances, net of supplier credit and operating liabilities. It is part of the operating system. A shop that adds inventory to reduce stock-outs may tie up cash while improving customer service. A distributor that gives a retailer another month to pay is financing that customer. A growing manufacturer may need to buy raw materials before collecting from its buyer.

The basic cash-conversion-cycle estimate is:

Days sales outstanding + days inventory outstanding − days payable outstanding

For a period with suitable average balances:

 DSO = average trade receivables ÷ credit sales × days in period
 DIO = average inventory ÷ cost of goods sold × days in period
 DPO = average trade payables ÷ purchases (or a disclosed cost proxy) × days in period

The denominator choice matters. Cost of sales is not always the same as purchases. An ending balance is not the same as an average balance. Seasonal businesses can make a year-end snapshot misleading. Write down the numerator, denominator, dates and source before interpreting the ratio.

Peer-reviewed studies find links between working-capital management and firm performance, including work on large Belgian firms and a large sample of Spanish SMEs [3], [4]. Later research on UK SMEs examines how cash flow changes the relation between net working capital and performance [5]. The message is not “push CCC as low as possible.” It is “measure how much cash the operating model absorbs and what the business receives in return.” Extending payable days may protect cash this month while damaging supply reliability next quarter. Cutting stock may improve reported working capital but cost sales if lead times are long.

sections.heading: Growth and maintenance can coexist
sections.text:
Classifying an asset purchase as “growth” does not make it optional forever. A new delivery vehicle can add a route today and become part of ordinary fleet replacement later. Conversely, an asset labeled “replacement” may also add capacity or lower cost. This is why an analyst should describe what changed in the operating system rather than relying on management’s label alone.

For an owner deciding what to distribute, combine the question with the next year’s operating plan. Required maintenance spend may arrive in lumps. A motor replacement every four years does not mean the business can ignore it for three years and then be surprised by the invoice. A reserve can smooth known replacement cycles, but it should be tied to a list of assets, estimated timing, and cost range.

sections.heading: What the workbook should make visible
sections.text:
A future model should show, for each asset group, opening carrying value, cash additions, disposals, depreciation, and closing value. A separate analyst schedule should identify the basis for maintenance low/base/high cases. Working-capital inputs should show actual balances, period dates, and the formula used. The owner-earnings output should respond to both maintenance and working-capital assumptions. It should not quietly insert a universal capex-to-depreciation ratio.

The next article turns the same cash-cycle logic into a weekly operating routine: what to forecast, how to see a shortfall early, and how to avoid rules that sound precise but do not fit the business.

sections.heading: Build the estimate from the asset’s job
sections.text:
A practical asset review begins with the job each item performs. The motor in a mill may be essential to the current output. A second mill may add capacity. A backup generator may protect the business from outages even if its use is low in a normal month. A point-of-sale system may reduce theft and processing time. The model needs to know what would happen to current sales and service if the asset failed or was not upgraded.

Imagine a cold-room business with one compressor installed six years ago. Its accounting depreciation is KSh 180,000 this year. The maintenance log records routine service and refrigerant work, while a major replacement is estimated to cost between KSh 700,000 and KSh 950,000 within the next two years. A second cold room, costing KSh 1.8 million, was installed to serve a new customer. The company spent KSh 2.5 million total this year, but the numbers do not map one-for-one to maintenance and expansion. A sensible worksheet would list the compressor and new cold room separately, link invoices and service records, state replacement timing, and show the effect of the plausible replacement range on owner earnings.

If the compressor has a documented eight-year service life and the current replacement estimate is KSh 800,000, a simple reserve planning estimate might spread that cost over the remaining period. That is a planning convention, not proof that annual cash spending will be KSh 100,000. The unit could fail sooner, the replacement price could change, or maintenance could extend its life. The owner should preserve both the expected timing and the risk range. Economic replacement investment and the accounting charge can differ because asset efficiency and age do not necessarily move in a straight line [2].

sections.heading: The working-capital bridge depends on the scale
sections.text:
Suppose a wholesaler normally sells 1,000 cases a month and needs KSh 2 million of stock to support that volume. It begins a new contract requiring another 300 cases every month. If supplier credit and customer terms remain unchanged, the extra sales may require a one-time build in stock and receivables. That incremental amount funds growth. By contrast, a higher receivables balance caused by slower customer payment can increase required working capital even when monthly sales are flat.

For owner earnings at the existing volume, ask what working capital is needed to preserve service, not what happened to the entire balance this year. For an actual historical cash bridge, show the full change in operating balances. Then distinguish the portion associated with growth, payment timing, acquisition, currency or an unusual event. This prevents a growing business from being penalized as if all growth capital were a permanent maintenance charge, and it prevents a stagnating business from claiming that overdue invoices are harmless.

sections.heading: Questions for the next owner review
sections.text:
1. What is the date, condition, and role of each material asset?
2. Which repairs or replacements happened over the last three to five years?
3. What open purchase order, lease, or supplier commitment is not yet in cash capex?
4. What additional inventory or credit is required to maintain current sales volume?
5. Which working-capital changes are growth-related, seasonal, overdue, or recoverable?
6. If this assumption is wrong, how does it change cash, debt needs, and the owner-earnings range?

These questions should be answered by invoices, asset logs, monthly balances, contracts and operations records. If the answer depends only on a generic capex ratio, the analysis is not yet grounded in the business.

sections.heading: Estimate maintenance spending from the work the assets do
sections.text:
A useful maintenance estimate starts with an asset register that connects each asset to a required operating task. Include the asset ID, type, purchase date, installed cost, current condition, useful life, service capacity, repair history, replacement lead time and next planned work. Record whether the business owns it, leases it, or relies on a supplier’s equipment. A refrigerated van may be essential to preserve current customer service even if it is leased. A repair contract may already cover part of the cash cost. The register makes those facts visible before the owner chooses an estimate.

Classify spending into four work categories:

 Routine upkeep: repairs, service and consumables that keep equipment in safe working order.
 Replacement: spending that renews exhausted or obsolete capacity already required for current sales.
 Compliance: upgrades required by safety, environmental, tax, industry or customer rules to keep trading.
 Expansion or improvement: spending that adds capacity, opens a new location or materially changes the service.

A single invoice can contain more than one category. For a mixed project, record the component and its share, with the basis. A KSh 900,000 refrigeration upgrade might replace compressors worth KSh 500,000 and add a new cold room worth KSh 400,000. If invoices or contractor schedules establish that split, the model can allocate it. If not, carry a low/high allocation and state what document would narrow the range. Compliance spending may not increase output, but the business cannot sustain legal operations without it; include it in the cost of maintaining the existing ability to trade.

Use three independent lenses to estimate the range:

Asset-by-asset replacement plan. Estimate next-year repair and replacement dates and current supplier quotes. This is the most practical short-run cash budget. It can be lumpy, so a single year might not represent long-run earning power.

Multi-year normalized spending. Compare actual capital additions, repair bills, disposal proceeds and capacity changes across a full replacement cycle. Exclude clearly evidenced new capacity from the no-growth case. Include replacement spending even when it is irregular. This method helps smooth lumpy equipment years, but acquisitions, currency movements and inflation need separate treatment.

Capacity and service test. Ask what assets are necessary to produce current units at the promised quality, delivery time and compliance level. A company may have very old assets and low current capex because maintenance has been deferred. A low-spend history is not proof that current operations can continue without investment. Record breakdowns, lost orders, service delays and customer specifications as well as accounting amounts.

Compare the three results instead of averaging them automatically. A current supplier quote may exceed historical spend because replacement cost has risen. A capacity study may identify a major system that accounting depreciation understates. Show the low, base and high estimates with the item, evidence, owner and confidence. The base case is an assumption, not a fact. Change it when service records or new quotes arrive.

sections.heading: Reconcile the working-capital investment at the same activity level
sections.text:
For a repeatable analysis, split working capital into balance, cash change, days measure and reason. A useful table contains opening and closing receivables, inventory, operating payables, accrued operating costs and customer advances. The operating working-capital balance can be written as:

Trade receivables + inventory + other operating assets − trade payables − operating accruals − customer advances

The cash investment for a period is usually the increase in that balance, after separately checking noncash movements and acquisition effects. An increase uses cash. A release provides cash. A one-time release from collecting old invoices should not be counted as a recurring annual owner-earnings boost.

Separate current activity from growth. If unit sales grow 20%, the company may need more stock and receivables even with unchanged collection days. Model the cash required to support that growth in the growth case. If receivable days rise while revenue stays flat, that is a collection or customer-credit issue. If payable days rise because a supplier renegotiated and remains current, that is an agreed source of operating funding. If invoices pass their due dates with no agreement, report arrears and supplier concentration separately. Do not give a struggling company an artificial owner-earnings benefit because it stopped paying its suppliers on time.

Seasonality changes the right comparison. A fruit packer may buy, harvest and pay labour before receiving export cash. The year-end inventory balance can be close to zero just after shipment even though the peak seasonal funding need was large. A school supplier may collect deposits months before delivery and then carry an obligation to provide goods later. Use monthly or weekly balances around the busy period and align them to customer and supplier terms. Year-end snapshots answer what was on the balance sheet that day; they do not reveal the peak cash required to complete a normal trading cycle.

A working-capital assessment should finish with a funding decision. If an order increases contribution but adds a receivable and stock requirement, calculate the peak amount and days financed. Then compare customer deposits, supplier terms, a revolving facility and the owner’s own cash. The facility needs to remain available until collection occurs. Do not use a six-month asset loan as though it were automatically the right instrument for a 45-day invoice gap.

sections.heading: A practical range that keeps the decision usable
sections.text:
Suppose a mill uses a motor, grinder and delivery vehicle for its current output. Its three-year normalized replacement schedule points to KSh 800,000 of annual upkeep. New supplier quotes show KSh 1.1 million at current prices. A larger mill costs KSh 1.8 million, of which KSh 700,000 replaces the current grinder and KSh 1.1 million adds a second line. The analyst might present maintenance of KSh 0.8–1.1 million, cite the three-year invoices and quotes, and classify the second line as growth. The total capex plan remains KSh 2.9 million. This lets an owner see that the base business needs replacement capital even though only a portion of the expansion improves volume.

If no asset condition report or purchase history is available, the result is a temporary range that can guide records collection, not a confident historical valuation. The next step is concrete: inspect the equipment, ask the supplier for written replacement terms, pull three years of invoices and tie each purchase to an asset ID and operating purpose. Then update the model. This produces a stronger business decision than substituting depreciation, total capex or a generic percentage for evidence.

sections.heading: Reconcile the asset register before estimating replacement cost
sections.text:
A practical fixed-asset review begins with an inventory of what the business actually uses. Assign an asset ID, location, custodian, purchase date, original cost, current condition, downtime history, remaining useful life, repair history, replacement lead time, and whether the asset is owned, financed or leased. For a vehicle, add mileage, fuel consumption, tyre history and route capacity. For a cold room, add temperature failures, energy use, compressor service and spoilage events. The register should reconcile to the general ledger and a physical inspection; a book value alone does not confirm that an asset exists or still works.

Then link each asset to capacity. How many production hours, customer orders or deliveries depend on it? What is the fallback if it fails? An inexpensive point-of-sale system can be more critical than a costly spare machine if it controls every checkout. Rank replacement needs by business interruption and cash cost, not only replacement price. List a realistic replacement date and lead time, then spread the expected cost over the period the asset supports. This produces an annual planning reserve, while the payment schedule remains lumpy in the cash forecast.

A useful three-estimate method is: (1) recent maintenance and repair spend, excluding one-off accident or expansion costs; (2) a unit-level replacement plan based on supplier quotations and expected timing; and (3) a capacity-and-condition review by the person operating the asset. Compare the estimates. If the business has unusually low repairs but old equipment, deferred work may explain why historical capex understates the future need. If annual capex is high because the firm is adding capacity, do not label all of it maintenance. Preserve a low, base and high case with a reason for each.

Close the estimate with a cash bridge: opening asset cost plus additions minus disposals equals closing gross cost; opening accumulated depreciation plus depreciation less disposals equals closing accumulated depreciation; and opening net book value plus additions less depreciation and disposals reconciles to closing net book value. This does not calculate economic maintenance capex by itself, but it reveals where the filing or ledger fails to reconcile. For owner decisions, the next question is whether cash available after that replacement plan still covers working capital and scheduled debt.

sections.heading: Use a maintenance calendar, not just an annual budget
sections.text:
Turn the asset estimate into a rolling 24-month calendar. List the expected replacement or overhaul month, quotation date, lead time, down-payment terms, shutdown days, and whether the work can be staged. Add a confidence flag: contracted, quoted, engineering estimate or placeholder. A KSh 600,000 replacement due in three months is not equivalent to KSh 600,000 evenly spread over a year if suppliers require a deposit now. The timing belongs in the 13-week and annual cash forecasts; the long-run estimate belongs in the owner-earnings bridge.

Revisit this calendar after downtime, a safety incident, a change in production mix, or a new supplier quote. The maintenance manager can propose the work, the finance lead can test funding, and the owner can approve the timing. A written deferral should state the operational risk and the next review date so a temporary cash squeeze does not silently become a permanent underinvestment policy.

sections.heading: Review the estimate after the operating plan changes
sections.text:
A maintenance estimate is attached to a business plan, not frozen at last year's spending. Revisit it after a large customer is added or lost, equipment utilization changes, a product standard changes, a site is expanded, or a supplier discontinues parts. If volume rises materially, some working capital and maintenance needs may rise even when the business has not opened a new location. “Same assets” does not always mean “same cash requirement.”

A practical quarterly review asks the operations lead to explain every material difference between budget and actual: was a repair delayed, did an asset fail, did a replacement price change, was a project partly growth and partly renewal, did a new customer change stock or credit terms? Keep the original estimate beside the revised one. That creates a record of whether management systematically underestimates or overestimates the cost of preserving operations.

A cash estimate should include timing. If a replacement motor costs KSh 1.2 million and the supplier needs 50% on order with a 12-week lead time, the business needs a cash date as well as an annual amount. A reserve can be built over time, but it is still an earmark against future use. Show whether the company has cash, an approved facility or merely an intention to save later. Likewise, a working-capital release cannot be counted twice: once as cash already collected and again as a future source of financing.

sections.heading: A compact decision note for each proposed release
sections.text:
Before reducing stock, delaying a repair, renegotiating supplier timing or extending customer credit, write a short note with six fields: the current problem, the cash amount and date, the operational mechanism, the affected customer or supplier, the downside if the assumption is wrong, and the person who will check the outcome. This makes the cash effect comparable with the service effect.

For example, an owner may plan to cut safety stock by KSh 300,000. The decision note should name the SKUs, lead-time variability, recent stock-outs, substitute availability and expected order fill rate. If three fast-moving parts account for most downtime, reduce the slow tail first and leave the critical items protected. For a customer credit extension, estimate the incremental receivable from sales volume multiplied by the additional collection days, then compare it with contribution margin and the funding cost. Do not treat gross sales as cash benefit.

The evidence on working capital and performance helps frame the question but cannot decide it for a specific firm. Deloof and García-Teruel and Martínez-Solano study firm-level relationships in particular samples, while Afrifa examines cash flow and UK SME performance [3–5]. Differences in industry, financing access, customer power and operating cycle matter. The correct practical conclusion is to measure the company's own cash conversion and service outcomes over time, then test whether a change improves total economics.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Project 1 workbook has a Maintenance register that annualizes five illustrative replacement costs over their planning lives: KSh600,000 for a compressor over 24 months, KSh2.1m for a van over 36 months, KSh850,000 for a generator over 30 months, KSh480,000 for POS/network equipment over 24 months, and KSh300,000 for fittings over 48 months. The resulting annual reserve is KSh1.655m. Its separate three-month Working Capital example moves from KSh2.0m net working capital in October 2026 to KSh2.2m in November and KSh2.9m in December; the modeled cash cycle lengthens from about 31.0 to 41.0 days. Receivables, Inventory and Payables make due dates, stock age and supplier criticality visible. The Evidence Vectors sheet labels all these rows as fictional, records their example periods/as-of dates and points to the source cells; source and retrieval dates are not applicable because no real ledgers or asset records support them. These are not a low/base/high estimate for a real company; replace them with inspection, invoice, sales and contract evidence before using the cash result.

articles.title: The daily MSME operating toolkit
questions: Why can a profitable business have little cash that its owner can safely withdraw?
How much reinvestment and operating working capital does the business need?
Which daily cash, customer, stock and supplier measures should trigger action?
How do owner pay, borrowing, growth and succession affect transferable earning power?

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

A cash forecast is most useful before there is a crisis. For a small business, the working version does not need to predict the whole year with false confidence. It needs to answer a simpler question: if the expected customers pay when promised, and the bills on the calendar are paid when due, when does the bank balance become uncomfortable?

A rolling 13-week cash forecast gives an owner a practical weekly view. Each week begins with the prior week’s closing cash. The business adds dated receipts and subtracts dated payments. The closing number becomes next week’s opening number. Repeat weekly and update actuals as they arrive.

Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments

This forecast is about timing. It does not say the business is profitable. A loan advance appears as a financing receipt and its repayments appear later as financing payments. It should never be mixed into customer collections. For each forecast line, record the source: invoice, purchase order, payroll calendar, rent clause, loan agreement, or an explicitly marked estimate.

sections.heading: Four jobs for the weekly routine
1. See the cash trough
sections.text:
List confirmed customer receipts by expected bank date, not invoice date. Separate confirmed orders from hoped-for new sales. For customers who regularly pay late, show an expected date that reflects the observed pattern, and keep the contractual due date beside it. A receipt becomes less dependable if delivery, acceptance, or a missing document can delay payment.

Payments should have the same specificity: payroll date, rent date, tax payment, supplier payment terms, loan instalment, delivery fuel, and committed stock purchases. Avoid a single “other costs” line so large that it hides an action.

The owner can compare the forecast low point with a minimum cash floor. That floor is not a universal number of weeks. It reflects payroll, cash volatility, supplier alternatives, customer concentration, seasonality and access to committed facilities. A facility counts as available only if the agreement is signed, the draw conditions can be met, and it is not already used.

sections.heading: 2. Learn where contribution comes from
sections.text:
Sales are not all equally useful. Contribution margin estimates what remains from a sale after variable costs that move with that sale. For a product line:

Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit

Break-even units = fixed costs over the period ÷ contribution per unit

Include variable costs that belong to the sale: product cost, payment processing, delivery, commissions, consumables, and relevant returns or spoilage. If labor is fixed within a period but varies with output at a higher level, explain that boundary. The equation is a decision aid, not a substitute for checking capacity and cash timing.

A fictional bakery sells a loaf for KSh 100. Flour, packaging, and incremental fuel total KSh 62 per loaf. Contribution is KSh 38 before fixed costs. If weekly fixed costs are KSh 76,000, the simple break-even volume is 2,000 loaves a week. But if the oven can produce only 1,600, then the break-even result is physically impossible under the current setup. If supermarkets pay 45 days after delivery, a profitable order can also create a cash shortage.

sections.heading: 3. Watch the invoice and stock clocks
sections.text:
DSO, DIO and DPO can help describe the timing of money through a business. Compute them consistently and compare the business with itself over time before comparing it with others. For a seasonal shop, use weekly or monthly detail to explain why a year-end number moved.

An ageing list is often more actionable than a single average. For receivables, show invoice number, customer, amount, original due date, days overdue, dispute status, promised payment date, and the person responsible for follow-up. For inventory, show SKU, quantity, last movement, reorder lead time, open purchase order, expiry or damage exposure, and annual usage value.

ABC analysis can rank stock by usage value. It does not mean that every “C” item should be removed. A low-value spare part can prevent a costly machine stoppage. A reorder point can start with expected demand during supplier lead time plus safety stock. The safety stock depends on demand variability, supplier reliability, and the service level the business chooses. There is no safe universal rule that every MSME should carry three times its average stock or write off an item after an arbitrary number of days.

sections.heading: 4. End each review with decisions
sections.text:
A weekly meeting should leave a small action log. For example: “Call customer A about invoice 184, due last Friday; confirm whether the delivery note is accepted by Tuesday; owner: Sam; expected receipt date: 4 October.” Or: “Hold the optional equipment order; check the repair quote and next two weeks’ receipts by Thursday.”

Separate facts from assumptions. “Invoice issued” is a fact. “The customer will pay on Friday” is an estimate unless the customer confirms it. The owner should compare forecasts with actuals each week, not to punish a forecast that was wrong, but to learn which customer or payment type is repeatedly mis-timed.

Research on SMEs supports treating cash and working capital as connected operating choices. García-Teruel and Martínez-Solano found relationships between shorter collection/inventory periods and profitability in their Spanish SME panel [1]. Afrifa’s study of UK SMEs found that incorporating cash flow changed the modeled relationship between working capital and performance [2]. These findings motivate monitoring; neither supplies an ideal DSO or cash reserve for a Nairobi wholesaler. Deloof studies a separate Belgian-firm sample, while Nicolas examines short-term financial constraints and SME investment through the working-capital channel [3], [4]. Different settings and research questions are a reason to use this literature as context for measurement, not as a universal operating threshold.

sections.heading: Do not confuse a ratio with a policy
sections.text:
A widely repeated LTV:CAC ratio, a gross-margin target, or a stock-holding rule can be useful in a narrow setting only when the terms are defined and the business economics fit. “Customer acquisition cost” might exclude owner time, failed trials, or sales commissions. “Lifetime value” might assume customers stay much longer than they do. A healthy ratio on a spreadsheet cannot rescue a business that pays for inventory months before customers pay.

Likewise, shortening payables can harm the business if a key supplier stops offering credit. Delaying tax, payroll or a secured loan is not a harmless cash-management tactic. The forecast should show the consequences and the contract terms, not simply call every delayed payment “working-capital optimization.”

sections.heading: Turn the 13-week view into a weekly operating ritual
sections.text:
A cash forecast works when the people closest to each event update it. Finance owns the ledger; sales owns customer commitments; procurement owns supplier dates; operations owns stock and delivery; the owner resolves trade-offs. Ask each person to bring evidence: remittance advice, signed purchase order, supplier statement, payroll schedule, tax deadline or loan notice. A forecast entry should carry an amount, date, source and confidence status. This is often more valuable than adding more rows or formulas.

Use a rolling window. At the end of each week, archive the prior forecast, enter actual cash, move the horizon forward by one week and add newly known events in week 13. Never overwrite last week’s expected date because it was missed; retain the variance. This gives the owner a short record of forecast accuracy. If a customer is normally 10 days late, after several observed delays the forecast can use a later date and the credit policy can change. If one storm created a unique delay, keep it in the downside case instead of making every customer appear permanently unreliable.

Separate confirmed from conditional receipts. A cleared mobile-money settlement is confirmed. A customer promise by phone is conditional. An unsigned order is pipeline and belongs in a sales forecast, not a cash forecast. If management wants to include pipeline as a scenario, show probability and the week cash would realistically arrive after delivery, invoice and terms. Do not let the current sales target masquerade as a bank deposit.

Create two cash lines: unrestricted cash and restricted or committed cash. The latter can include tax collected for remittance, customer deposits due for fulfillment, security deposits, lender reserve accounts and grant funding with restrictions. The business may have the funds in its account but not have the right or practical ability to spend them on payroll. Likewise, show a committed overdraft separately from cash and record draw conditions, borrowing base, renewal date and required clean-down.

A useful weekly meeting ends with named actions, not a spreadsheet tour. Identify the next low-cash week, the three receipts or payments most likely to move it, what evidence will arrive before the next review, and who will respond. If the lowest projected balance remains above the reserve floor, the meeting can focus on margin and stock quality. If it falls below the floor, the owner decides now whether to collect, reduce orders, defer optional capex, negotiate a payment schedule or draw committed funding. The decision and expected cash impact are recorded, then tested against actuals next week.

sections.heading: Measure burn without inventing runway
sections.text:
For a young or loss-making firm, define operating burn from recurring operating cash after customer collections and ordinary supplier payments. Report gross cash operating outflow separately if it helps show the cost base. Exclude financing proceeds from the operating measure. Identify one-off restructuring, asset purchase and growth expansion separately so a temporary buildout is not mislabeled as normal burn. Also show debt principal, tax, capex and owner withdrawals because these consume cash even if they are not in a chosen operating-burn definition.

A runway quotient is useful only when net cash burn is positive and reasonably stable. If a company has KSh 3 million unrestricted cash and burns KSh 500,000 monthly, a simple six-month quotient is an initial signal. But if KSh 2 million of supplier payments fall in month two or a seasonal collection arrives in month three, the dated cash forecast gives a different answer. If net burn is zero or positive, do not display infinite runway. Say that the quotient is not meaningful in that period, then show the minimum projected cash and major upcoming obligations.

Separate operating cash, expansion cash and one-off cash needs. A new branch may make the forecast negative even though mature units generate cash. Conversely, positive gross margin may not cover central staffing or old debt. Show how many weeks of runway remain if growth hiring is paused, then compare it with the fully funded plan. This reveals whether a financing round is buying expansion or merely covering recurring losses. For lender review, also calculate CFADS under the contract’s definition and debt-service dates. Do not include an unsigned equity round as a committed receipt.

sections.heading: Unit economics need both contribution and cash
sections.text:
For each product, route or service, start with collected or collectible net revenue after discounts, refunds and indirect taxes where relevant. Subtract costs that change with delivery: stock, packaging, payment fee, delivery, commissions, spoilage, customer support and variable labor. The remainder is contribution. Add fixed costs at the level where the decision is made: route, store, branch or the whole company. Keep shared costs transparent rather than assigning all head-office expense to a new unit.

Consider an order sold for KSh 3,000 net. Direct product cost is KSh 1,600, packing KSh 120, payment costs KSh 60, delivery KSh 250 and expected returns or damage KSh 70. Contribution is KSh 900. If the channel spends KSh 180 per first order to acquire a new customer, initial contribution after acquisition is KSh 720 before fixed cost. If repeat orders arrive without the same acquisition cost, cohort contribution can improve. But if the customer does not repeat or pays after 45 days while suppliers require payment in 14, acquisition payback may be cash-negative. Show repeat frequency, retention and collection dates, not only lifetime-value estimates.

Calculate volume break-even as fixed cash cost divided by contribution per unit. Then calculate cash break-even by adding debt service, maintenance investment and any required tax or reserve. For example, fixed monthly operating cost of KSh 240,000, maintenance of KSh 40,000 and debt service of KSh 50,000 divided by KSh 800 contribution per delivery requires 413 deliveries per month. That threshold moves if price, discounts, delivery density or variable input costs change. Run an adverse case with lower average basket and fewer stops per route before assuming scale solves it.

When a unit has positive contribution but negative allocated profit, ask whether the contribution covers avoidable costs and whether it helps support shared capacity. When contribution is negative, additional sales generally deepen losses unless there is a clearly timed learning or launch investment with a stop rule. A new unit should have an investment gate: minimum contribution, utilization, service quality and cash payback date. Review those conditions after launch rather than letting the forecast continue unchanged.

sections.heading: Make AR aging a collection plan
sections.text:
An invoice ledger should include customer, invoice ID, work or goods delivered, invoice amount, balance, invoice date, due date, dispute status, evidence of acceptance, last contact, promised payment date, collector and credit limit. Aging is based on days past the agreed due date, not days since invoice if terms allow 30 days. Divide balances into current, 1–30, 31–60, 61–90 and over 90 days, and put disputed or not-yet-accepted balances in their own categories.

A simple DSO is average trade receivables divided by credit sales for the matched period, multiplied by period days. If a retailer also makes cash sales, total revenue will understate DSO by inflating the denominator. If sales are seasonal, compare like periods and show opening and closing balances. DSO is an average and can hide one buyer with a large late amount, so show the top five customers, concentration and overdue balances relative to weekly payroll and critical supplier needs.

The collection ladder can be proportionate: confirm delivery and invoice receipt before the due date; send a statement on the due date; ask for a specific remittance date after a miss; agree a partial payment plan if the customer is viable; stop new exposure at the credit limit; escalate to the owner or insurer; and use formal collection remedies when appropriate. A discount should have an approval limit and be compared with financing cost, bad-debt probability, margin and customer precedent. Record whether the payment actually cleared.

sections.heading: Stock control that protects service and cash
sections.text:
For each SKU, record quantity, unit cost, last sale, units sold per week, lead time, open orders, expiry or obsolescence, gross margin and supplier minimum. ABC analysis sorts by annual consumption value, but a high-value category should not automatically receive all managerial attention. A low-cost item that stops a repair or an essential service may deserve a minimum safety stock. Pair annual consumption value with criticality, uncertainty, substitution and lead time.

Turnover is cost of goods sold divided by average inventory; DIO is average inventory divided by matched-period cost of goods sold times period days. Calculate by category and compare similar seasons. Add ageing buckets and stockout days. An item that has not sold for 60 days may be normal for a seasonal product or a serious warning for fresh food; no universal dead-stock day applies. Estimate carrying costs from actual storage, insurance, spoilage, financing and markdown experience. The 20–30% holding-cost figure in the supplied notes remains an unverified lead, not a default assumption.

A reorder point can be estimated from average daily usage times supplier lead days plus safety stock for demand and lead-time variation. Validate with actual purchase-to-receipt dates. If lead time is uncertain, keep a low/base/high estimate and establish an emergency alternative. Before marking down or returning inventory, compare expected net recovery with carrying cost, expiry risk, supplier credit and the effect on customer availability. A markdown that releases cash but loses more contribution than it saves may be the wrong move.

sections.heading: AP aging must distinguish agreement from distress
sections.text:
For each supplier, record the contracted term, invoice date, due date, amount, dispute, amount paid, next delivery, alternative source and business criticality. Split current, 1–30 days overdue, 31–60, 61–90 and over 90. Reconcile ledger totals to supplier statements. An unresolved difference can indicate missing invoices, credit notes, goods received not invoiced or a genuine dispute. DPO should use credit purchases and an average payable balance for the same period; it does not certify that payments were made on terms.

Prioritize suppliers by operational dependence, lead time, quality, substitution and exposure, not simply largest balance. A written extension can be a negotiated financing source. Silence and missed due dates are not consent. If a critical supplier moves to cash-on-delivery, update the forecast immediately and estimate the stock or sales affected. When asking for relief, provide a credible payment calendar and update the supplier before each date. The business may preserve a relationship by being precise even if it cannot pay the full amount immediately.

sections.heading: Turn action choices into comparable scenarios
sections.text:
Put collection, discount, return, markdown, reorder pause, supplier plan and facility draw in the same scenario table. For each, show cash released and date, margin impact, future service risk, relationship effect, legal or contract implications, and accountable person. If a KSh 300,000 invoice can be collected 35 days earlier for a 2% discount, the discount costs KSh 6,000. At 18% annual financing cost, the simple carrying cost avoided is about KSh 3,107 before default risk and administrative effort. The discount is not justified by financing alone, but may make sense if default risk or payroll impact is substantial. State the true reason.

For stock, compare markdown proceeds with expected future net sale proceeds and carrying cost. For supplier settlement, compare a prompt-payment discount with borrowing cost and operational continuity. For a return, include restocking fees and future stockout risk. After each action, reconcile actual cash and contribution. A dashboard that never compares expected and actual impact is a reporting page, not an operating tool.

Start the weekly system with six measures: next cash trough, contribution per order, aged receivables, aged inventory, overdue critical payables and confirmed borrowing headroom. Add a metric only when a decision owner and response are clear. This keeps the operating process usable by a small team and directs attention to the cash or margin problem that can still be changed.

sections.heading: A weekly operating meeting that connects the numbers to action
sections.text:
A small firm does not need a complicated dashboard to make better decisions. It needs a short meeting with the people who can change collections, purchasing, production and customer service. Keep one page and review the same measures each week: opening cash, lowest forecast cash, collections due and collected, overdue receivables, stock-outs, slow stock, supplier commitments, payroll and statutory payments, completed orders, gross margin and work not yet invoiced.

For each measure, show current value, recent direction, owner, next action and deadline. Avoid a red-yellow-green score with no underlying amount or customer. “Collections are behind” is not an action. “KSh 420,000 from three invoices is six days past the agreed date; Amina will call the customer finance lead by Tuesday and confirm the payment reference” is. If the customer disputes delivery, assign someone to provide proof of delivery and resolve the dispute; do not continue sending generic reminders.

The meeting should last 30 to 45 minutes. Begin with the cash forecast and critical obligations. Review exceptions rather than reading every line aloud. Agree which orders to accept, defer or renegotiate based on contribution after direct costs, collection risk and capacity. End by writing decisions into an action log. The next meeting opens by checking whether each action happened and whether it changed the underlying measure.

sections.heading: Worked example: a wholesaler with rising sales and falling cash
sections.text:
Imagine a small building-supplies wholesaler whose monthly sales rise from KSh 4.0 million to KSh 4.8 million. The owner celebrates 20% growth, but the bank balance falls. A practical review finds that average customer collection has lengthened from 30 to 45 days, stock has grown by KSh 450,000 because the team bought several slow-moving lines, and suppliers have been paid promptly despite agreed 30-day terms. The company may be earning a positive gross margin while financing customers and holding stock before the cash arrives.

Start with a 13-week forecast. List the ten largest receivables by invoice and expected date, not a single assumed collection ratio. Split stock into committed fast movers, seasonal items and lines with no movement. Call customers about disputed invoices and confirm delivery documents. For new credit sales, require a limit and a named approver. For slow items, decide whether to return, discount, bundle or stop replenishment. Speak to suppliers before changing payment timing; agreed terms are a relationship and contract constraint, not free financing.

Then compare two actions. A blanket credit freeze may preserve cash but lose reliable customers and sales. Continuing current terms may preserve volume but worsen the cash gap. A narrower policy could retain terms for customers with reliable payment history while requiring a deposit or shorter terms for new and overdue accounts. Measure both the cash effect and the contribution lost or protected. Working-capital evidence in SMEs links liquidity needs, financing constraints and investment decisions, so management should evaluate the effect on operations instead of treating a lower balance as automatically superior [1, 2, 4].

sections.heading: Use triggers as questions, not universal rules
sections.text:
A trigger is a prompt to investigate. For instance, if one customer becomes a large share of overdue receivables, review concentration, dispute history and the cash effect of losing that customer. If gross margin falls, test purchase prices, discounting, product mix, waste, returns and theft before concluding that sales staff need to sell more. If stock cover rises, inspect the item-level age and supplier lead time before stopping all purchases.

Set the trigger from the business's own history, contract terms, service promise and tolerance for a missed obligation. Record the baseline, the threshold, the action it triggers and who can override it. An override should have a reason and an expiry date. This lets the owner learn whether the trigger is useful without mistaking a convenient number for an industry law.

sections.heading: Keep a simple control trail
sections.text:
Every significant number on the dashboard should lead to a source: ledger, bank statement, invoice, delivery record, stock count or signed supplier term. Mark estimates separately from actuals and record when they were last checked. Limit who can create a supplier, approve a payment or change a customer's credit limit. Where a small team cannot separate duties, use a second-person review and monthly bank reconciliation as compensating controls.

A practical toolkit is not a miniature listed-company reporting pack. It is a repeatable routine that gives the owner enough warning to act while there is still time to negotiate, collect, slow a purchase or arrange financing. The weekly meeting should produce fewer surprises over time, not simply more charts.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Project 1 workbook puts the 13-week cash forecast, low-cash point, net burn and indicative runway together on Cash13W. In its fictional route case, KSh6.0m opening cash reaches a KSh5.58m low under Base but falls to a KSh3.49m deficit under the combined downside receipts and supplier schedule. That is a warning to change the forecast or financing plan, not a claim about a real business. Receivables and Payables calculate outstanding balances and ageing from due dates; Inventory calculates stock value, ABC share, days since sale and a lead-time reorder review; Unit Economics calculates contribution and break-even; Action Log records an owner, deadline, cash or margin effect and outcome. Evidence Vectors maps the 13 forecast periods and the invoice/SKU schedules to their cells and marks the case as fictional; the forecast has explicit week starts, while the other scenario dates are tied to their own schedules and as-of date. Replace sample ledgers with dated customer, stock and supplier records.
