articles.title: Owner pay, reserves, growth and debt
articles.short_title: Owner pay, reserves, growth and debt
questions: Why can a profitable business have little cash that its owner can safely withdraw?
How much reinvestment and operating working capital does the business need?
Which daily cash, customer, stock and supplier measures should trigger action?
How do owner pay, borrowing, growth and succession affect transferable earning power?

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

Owners often fund two very different things from one bank account: the work they do and the capital they put at risk. If the owner manages staff every day, their pay for that job is an operating cost. A dividend or draw is a return on ownership. Mixing the two can make a business appear more profitable than it is and can make the owner think a draw is “salary” when it is actually draining working capital.

The first step is to set a reasonable replacement cost for the owner’s work. Ask what duties are performed, how many hours they take, which credentials are required, and what it would cost to hire someone capable of doing them. There may be more than one role: founder sales, purchasing, bookkeeping, repair work, and general management. Do not invent a precise salary from a single online job listing. Document the role and use a range. For a sole proprietor, the bookkeeping or tax treatment may differ from a company’s payroll, so keep tax classification separate from the economic normalization used for analysis.

sections.heading: A reserve belongs to a named risk
sections.text:
“Keep three months of expenses” is a common shortcut. It may be too little for a seasonal importer with long lead times, and too much for a service firm paid in advance with low fixed costs. A reserve should be linked to what could go wrong and how quickly the owner can respond.

List obligations by date: payroll, rent, taxes, key suppliers, loan payments, insurance, and customer deposits that must be refunded if delivery fails. Then identify the risks that could delay receipts: one large buyer, a public-sector payment cycle, FX exposure, weather, a supplier outage, a licensing renewal, or an owner’s illness. The reserve question is not “how many months sounds prudent?” It is “what cash shortfall could the business face before it can change course?”

A useful reserve schedule shows a base case and at least one plausible downside. For example, move a major customer’s expected payment from week 3 to week 7, keep payroll on its actual date, and show the trough. If the business has a committed overdraft, show its limit, conditions, amount already used, expiry date, price, and collateral. Do not count an unapproved facility as cash.

sections.heading: Growth is not always self-funding
sections.text:
A new order can increase profit and worsen cash at the same time. Suppose a fictional wholesaler wins a KSh 900,000 order. The buyer pays after delivery and acceptance in 45 days. The wholesaler must pay KSh 520,000 for stock in two weeks and KSh 80,000 for transport and handling before delivery. The order appears to have a KSh 300,000 gross spread before overhead. But the business needs KSh 600,000 of cash for more than a month before it collects. A deposit, supplier credit, or working-capital facility changes the funding need. None changes the customer’s gross margin by itself.

Before borrowing, write the order’s dates and identify what a lender will actually fund: purchase invoices, a receivable, inventory, or general cash flow. Then check if the facility matures before the buyer is likely to pay. Make a downside case for delayed acceptance, a short delivery, disputed invoice, FX movement, or partial buyer payment. Ask whether the facility is a term loan, revolving credit, overdraft, invoice discounting, or a different contract. Names do not control; the agreement does.

Cash available for debt service should be defined from the actual financing documents. Lenders differ on EBITDA adjustments, taxes, maintenance spend, leases, and one-off items. “DSCR” can mean different things in different contracts. In an article or model, show the chosen formula and source. Do not call a generic ratio the borrower’s covenant without reading the agreement.

sections.heading: What lenders and owners each need to know
sections.text:
A lender asks whether the borrower can repay under the contract and what recovery exists if it cannot. The owner asks whether capital invested produces enough risk-adjusted value and what can be withdrawn without impairing the business. Those questions overlap but are not identical.

Small-business finance research describes how financing sources change as firms grow and accumulate information, track records, and assets that support lending [1]. Classic credit-market research also shows why interest rates alone do not always clear credit demand when lenders have less information about borrower risk [2]. This helps explain why a well-intentioned owner may face documentation requests or a smaller credit limit than expected. The study does not prove that a particular lender has acted fairly or unfairly. The owner’s response is to make the business legible: reconcile bank inflows to invoices, keep statements and tax filings consistent, identify the legal borrower, and maintain an aged receivable schedule. Afrifa’s UK SME study also finds that cash flow changes how the working-capital/performance relationship is modeled, which supports keeping the reserve decision tied to dated cash needs rather than a balance-sheet ratio alone [3].

The owner can plan three different buckets:

 Operating cash: payments needed to deliver contracted work and trade normally.
 Resilience reserve: cash assigned to a stated risk and kept in a liquid, accessible account.
 Potential distribution: the remaining amount after due obligations, scheduled debt payments, and approved reinvestment.

If an owner wants to invest in growth, label it as an investment decision. Show the cash cost, when it might earn a return, what evidence supports demand, and what would make the decision wrong. Then test whether the business survives if the return arrives later or is smaller.

sections.heading: A decision rule that can be explained
sections.text:
Before an owner distribution, ask:

1. Is the business’s historical cash bridge reconciled to statements and invoices?
2. Have we paid or set aside cash for obligations due before the next dependable receipts?
3. Have we funded the replacement and working capital needs of the existing operation?
4. Have we considered signed contracts and the exact loan covenants?
5. Does a plausible delay leave the business above its agreed cash floor?

If the last answer is no, the right decision may be to distribute less even when reported profit is positive. That does not mean the owner’s equity has no value. It means the value and distribution decision have different dates and liquidity tests.

sections.heading: Work the debt decision from use to repayment
sections.text:
Before the business borrows, the owner should be able to point to the purchase, expected benefit and repayment source. For a working-capital line, map the cash cycle: when stock is paid, when it is sold, when the invoice is issued, and when the customer pays. For an asset loan, connect the loan term to the asset’s useful life and the cash it enables. If the use is “general support,” list the actual underlying obligations and decide whether they are temporary timing needs or recurring operating losses.

A borrower-to-lender bridge should define its starting measure. If starting from normalized EBITDA, deduct cash tax, maintenance investment, incremental operating working capital and other senior obligations to estimate pre-financing cash available for debt service. If starting from net income, interest and tax may already be included; do not subtract them again without explaining the adjustment. Add scheduled principal and interest using the signed facility terms. The bank may define DSCR differently, include or exclude certain add-backs, test quarterly or annually, and require minimum cash. Put the covenant definition and test date beside the illustrative ratio before using the model for a real loan.

For the fictional KSh 900,000 order, compare the same customer, supplier and delivery dates under a term loan and a revolver. Assume stock costs KSh 620,000 and delivery plus other variable costs KSh 90,000. The customer pays KSh 1,050,000 sixty days after delivery. Contribution before overhead and financing is KSh 340,000. Suppose a term loan carries 18% annual interest, 2% arrangement fee and six equal monthly principal repayments; the revolver carries 20% interest, a 1% draw fee and a 1% annual fee on undrawn commitment. These are hypothetical terms. The model should calculate draw date, interest days, fees, principal due, cash received and closing debt under each option. Then move customer acceptance or payment by 30 days. If the term loan amortizes before collection, cash may fall below reserve; if the revolver must clean down, the buyer's delay can prevent compliance. Do not compare headline rates alone.

The financing schedule should include required security, personal guarantees, floating or fixed rate, rate resets, unused-line fees, legal charges, covenant tests, borrowing base, clean-down days, renewal date, early repayment fee and default margin where applicable. A quote should be tied to a written offer. The actual contract governs. The workbook can indicate a model breach under selected assumptions; it cannot determine the lender's legal interpretation or waive a covenant.

sections.heading: Decide whether extra equity is better than debt
sections.text:
Debt preserves ownership percentage but adds fixed claims. Equity can absorb uncertainty but dilutes the owner and may require governance rights or preferred returns. Compare the full cash and control effects. If the purchase funds a machine with predictable contracted work, debt may match a durable asset. If it funds product development with uncertain time to revenue, borrowing can create repayment pressure before evidence of demand exists. If the business is already undercapitalized, new equity may protect suppliers and staff while the owner proves whether the model works.

For each funding choice, record cash received net of fees, effective annual cost, principal timing, security, ownership dilution, control rights, repayment source and downside outcome. Include owner equity only when it is committed and available. An informal promise from a relative is not a bankable source until amount, date and terms are agreed. If a lender requires the owner to inject cash first, make that condition explicit in the forecast.

The correct decision may be smaller scope. A firm could lease a vehicle, outsource one route, require a customer deposit, stage equipment purchases, or test demand before hiring full-time. Compare the total cost of those options and who bears residual value and downtime risk. A lease can lower day-one cash need while creating a long payment obligation; it should appear in the same dated schedule as debt.

sections.heading: Protect the business without starving it
sections.text:
Owner distributions, reinvestment and reserve policy compete for the same cash. The owner should agree a rule before year-end, such as paying a fixed monthly amount only while forecast closing cash remains above the reserve under base and downside cases. A year-end sweep can distribute surplus after tax, supplier reconciliations, maintenance approvals and seasonal working capital are confirmed. The rule should not guarantee a draw when invoices or stock needs change.

Use a cash waterfall:

1. Restricted money and customer obligations remain protected.
2. Payroll, tax, safety-critical suppliers and contractually due debt are funded.
3. Maintenance needed to continue current service is funded or explicitly scheduled.
4. The chosen operating reserve and seasonal working capital are preserved.
5. Committed growth investments are tested for incremental return.
6. Remaining cash can be considered for owner distribution or optional expansion.

The order can be adapted to legal requirements and company agreements, but the model should show the trade-offs. If debt covenants prohibit distributions, that condition overrides the discretionary waterfall. If the business has excess cash above a robust reserve, keeping it idle also has a cost; compare debt repayment, maintenance, profitable growth and owner use.

sections.heading: A board-ready growth case
sections.text:
A growth case needs a no-growth reference. Forecast the existing operation first, including replacement capex and normal working capital. Then add only the incremental project: price, unit volume, contribution, new payroll, equipment, lease, launch costs, working-capital build, tax and funding. Do not apply the company’s historic average margin blindly if the new product, buyer or route has different economics.

Use three scenarios. In the base, state expected time to ramp and evidence such as signed orders or repeat customer demand. In the downside, delay opening, reduce volume and assume a customer pays later while the supplier withdraws terms. In the upside, avoid relying on immediate full capacity unless demand is contracted. Show cumulative cash invested, payback date, return on incremental capital and the minimum liquidity point. A project with positive total profit can still fail if cash is needed before the first collection.

Set a stop rule tied to observable milestones: minimum weekly orders, contribution per order, utilization or customer retention by a specific date. Release the next tranche only when evidence arrives. If the test fails, options might include reduce opening hours, change price, renegotiate a lease or stop the next equipment purchase. A stop rule protects the owner from continuing to spend solely because earlier spend is sunk.

sections.heading: Revisit the policy as the business changes
sections.text:
Review reserve and borrowing assumptions when the largest customer changes terms, a supplier shortens credit, the tax calendar changes, the business hires a replacement manager, an asset needs unexpected work or loan rates reset. One annual budget cannot capture these events. Maintain a short debt maturity ladder with amounts due in 30, 90, 180 and 365 days, and begin renewal discussions before the facility expires. If the lender requires seasonal clean-down, identify the exact week the balance must return to zero and whether customer receipts arrive in time.

The final choice is not “borrow or never borrow.” It is whether the financing instrument, payment schedule and fallback fit the asset or cash cycle and the owner's tolerance for risk. If the downside path breaches reserve and there is no committed contingency, reduce the scale or wait. If the project remains cash-positive after realistic delays and maintenance, borrowing can fund a return that exceeds its cost. Record the assumptions and decision date so the owner can revisit them when actual performance replaces the forecast.

sections.heading: A worked reserve and distribution decision
sections.text:
Imagine the business has KSh 2.4 million in unrestricted cash and no other confirmed inflow for four weeks. Payroll is KSh 420,000, rent KSh 160,000, tax remittance KSh 180,000, critical supplier invoices KSh 560,000 and debt service KSh 140,000. A planned machine overhaul requires a KSh 300,000 deposit in week three. Those obligations total KSh 1.76 million, leaving KSh 640,000 before reserve. The owner has set a KSh 450,000 reserve based on a two-week payroll and essential-supplier response window, leaving a theoretical KSh 190,000 above reserve.

Now test the largest buyer paying KSh 500,000 three weeks late. If that receipt was not included in the KSh 2.4 million cash already on hand, the owner must not subtract it from today's cash; instead it delays replenishment and changes the next forecast. Suppose the delay also means an extra KSh 250,000 of stock must be purchased for prepaid orders. The trough becomes KSh 390,000, below the chosen reserve by KSh 60,000. A KSh 190,000 distribution is no longer safe. The owner could defer the payment to themselves, ask for a buyer deposit, negotiate staged supplier delivery or use a committed revolver. The model should show each option’s timing, interest cost and service effect.

This calculation separates three decisions. The workshop may have earned enough annual owner earnings to support a distribution over time. It may have KSh 190,000 of apparent liquidity on the base schedule. But under one credible collection delay and order requirement, the same distribution would breach the reserve. A prudent decision can approve a smaller amount now and revisit after the buyer’s payment clears. The reserve level remains a management choice and should be revisited if payroll, seasonality or facility access changes.

sections.heading: Read a loan request as a transaction, not a slogan
sections.text:
When a lender asks “how much do you need?”, answer with the cash bridge. List the invoice or asset being funded, own contribution, supplier advance, delivery date, customer acceptance date, invoice terms, expected receipt and fallback. If the funding need is general, divide it by use: inventory, payroll, tax arrears, equipment, refinancing or expansion. Some uses may be appropriate for a revolving facility, others for a term loan, and some may indicate a need for equity or restructuring.

A lender can test whether the borrower has a repayment source. The borrower should test whether the repayment schedule matches actual collections and asset life. Compare the debt draw and repayment dates to the 13-week cash forecast, then extend the forecast through the final maturity. Stress a rate reset, fee, delayed customer and shorter supplier terms. Show cash after debt service and after maintenance, not just EBITDA divided by annual interest. If the facility is secured by a vehicle or property, show whether losing that asset would interrupt the very sales forecast used to repay the debt.

Do not borrow solely because a limit is available. A facility with an unused fee may still provide useful resilience, but the owner should know how quickly it can be drawn and what conditions must be met. Conversely, avoiding all debt can cause the business to miss a profitable order even when collections are well supported. Compare expected incremental return with total financing cost and downside loss. The decision note should identify what evidence would cause the owner to cancel the draw.

sections.heading: Put accountability around the policy
sections.text:
Assign the owner or finance lead to update cash weekly, the bookkeeper to reconcile monthly, and the board or co-owners to approve distributions above the agreed cap. If one person controls all cash, statements, supplier terms and records, a trusted backup should be able to verify the balances during absence. Maintain dual authorization for large transfers if practical. Strong access controls protect business continuity as well as against fraud.

Save the policy alongside each forecast. A cash reserve rule is only credible if management can point to why it exists, what obligations it covers, and how it will be reviewed. Record exceptions, who approved them and how the business replenished the reserve. If the owner repeatedly overrides the policy for personal drawings, revisit the amount or the household cash plan rather than pretending the exceptions never happened.

The owner’s pay, the lender’s repayment and the growth project all draw on the same operating cash. Put them in one dated forecast, then assess each against the business’s ability to continue trading, maintain service and meet contracts. That is how an owner can make a practical choice without confusing a promising return with cash already earned.

sections.heading: Decide what each shilling of cash is for
sections.text:
A business owner should separate four decisions that are often mixed together: pay for work performed, repayment of money previously lent by the owner, distribution of accumulated profit, and reinvestment in the company. Use distinct ledger descriptions, approvals and tax treatment. A cash withdrawal is not automatically a dividend, and a dividend is not a substitute for a reasonable salary where the owner works in the business.

Set a distribution calendar, but make the payment conditional on the cash forecast and legal requirements. At each review, ask whether the company has paid or reserved for payroll, taxes, debt service, critical suppliers, committed maintenance and the next working-capital peak. Only then consider discretionary owner distributions. This avoids promising a fixed amount in a month when cash is tied up in a large customer order or seasonal stock build.

A reserve policy should identify the risk it covers, how much cash is assigned, where it is held, who can release it and when the policy is reviewed. Separate an operating buffer for timing mismatches from a specific repair reserve, tax reserve or debt-service reserve. Do not count the same bank balance as backing multiple purposes. For a business with seasonal inflows, show the low point over the full operating cycle; the annual average can hide the month when the company runs short.

sections.heading: Compare growth projects with a common test
sections.text:
An attractive growth idea is not self-funding just because the projected margin is positive. Estimate the initial equipment and setup cost, working capital, hiring and training, launch period, ongoing maintenance, taxes, customer-acquisition cost and time to collect. Identify the minimum volume needed to cover incremental fixed cost and the downside point at which the project consumes cash without a realistic recovery path.

A simple investment page might show three cases:

 Base case: demand supported by signed orders, repeat purchases or a documented pipeline; realistic collection days; full staff and service costs.
 Downside case: slower launch, lower utilization, a price concession, late customer payment, or a longer equipment installation.
 Stop case: the condition that prevents further spending, such as a missed permit, customer cancellation, cost overrun, or failure to reach a milestone by an agreed date.

Ask what the business will stop doing if this project receives cash. Capital has an opportunity cost even when the owner uses retained profits rather than a bank loan. A project that is strategically appealing can still be sequenced later if it would leave no money for current maintenance or payroll.

sections.heading: Borrow for a defined cash gap, with a repayment source
sections.text:
Debt can be sensible when it funds an asset or temporary working-capital need that produces cash before repayment falls due. It is dangerous when a short-term facility is used to cover recurring losses or a permanent mismatch between customer terms and supplier terms. Before borrowing, write down the amount and date of the gap, the use of proceeds, the expected cash source for each repayment, and the consequence if that source arrives late.

Compare the full cost, not only the quoted rate: arrangement and commitment fees, insurance, required balances, security costs, legal charges, early repayment terms, collateral, guarantees, maturity and renewal risk. Compare a term loan matched to an asset's useful cash-generating life with a revolving facility for a genuine short-cycle need. The best structure depends on cash timing and contract terms, not a general claim that one product is always cheaper.

Credit rationing research explains why lenders may limit credit when they cannot distinguish borrower quality or fully observe risk [2]. The practical response is to make the company's own record easier to evaluate: current management accounts, reconciled bank statements, aged receivables, stock evidence, tax status, existing debt schedule, forecast, facility purpose and downside repayment plan. A lender pack should disclose risks and sensitivities, not just present an optimistic case.

sections.heading: Review whether the decision worked
sections.text: For every material distribution, loan or growth decision, record the forecast at approval and compare it with actual results after 30, 90 and 180 days. Track cash generated, margin, collection time, service failures, covenant headroom and the assumptions that were wrong. If the owner repeatedly draws more than normalized free cash, decide whether that reflects a temporary investment phase, a weak cash conversion cycle, an underpriced product, or a business that cannot support the owner's required income. The answer changes whether the next step is improved collections, repricing, cost redesign, a smaller distribution or a planned exit.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Project 1 workbook separates normalized owner earnings before principal, residual cash after scheduled principal and cash after a reserve top-up. Cash13W tests receipt and supplier-payment timing under one Base/Downside selector. Debt and Growth provides an illustrative year-one interest and fee comparison for a term loan, revolving facility and supplier credit, followed by the evidence each decision needs. Evidence Vectors identifies those inputs as a hypothetical borrower case with no offer letter or reported financial year. It is a financing-cost screen, not a full amortization, covenant or debt-capacity model.

articles.title: Buying, selling and succession
questions: Why can a profitable business have little cash that its owner can safely withdraw?
How much reinvestment and operating working capital does the business need?
Which daily cash, customer, stock and supplier measures should trigger action?
How do owner pay, borrowing, growth and succession affect transferable earning power?

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

A buyer asks, “What does the business earn?” The seller replies with what is left in the bank at the end of a good month. Both sides are asking the wrong version of the question.

To estimate what a buyer is acquiring, start with the work, assets, customer relationships, contracts, records, and obligations that transfer. Then ask what it would cost to keep the same operation running after the current owner steps away. A business that earns KSh 2 million before paying the founder for sales, purchasing, hiring, and customer service does not necessarily generate KSh 2 million for a buyer. Some of that amount pays for labor the buyer must replace.

This is why owner normalization and succession planning belong in the same conversation. The buyer needs a replacement-management cost to value the cash flow. The seller needs a succession plan so the business can continue producing that cash flow after the handover.

sections.heading: Adjustments need evidence
sections.text:
A seller may propose “add-backs” for a family vehicle, a one-time legal bill, or an unusually large family salary. An add-back is not automatically valid because the owner labels it one-off. Ask four questions:

 Did the expense appear in the books or cash outflow?
 Was it truly unrelated to future operations?
 Would a new owner incur a replacement cost or a similar expense?
 Can the claimed amount be matched to invoices, payroll, bank records, or a contract?

A one-time store closure cost may be real, but the buyer still needs to assess whether more sites are at risk. A personal expense can be removed from a normalized earnings estimate only if the business will not incur it after sale and the accounting treatment is clear. Unpaid family labor must be priced at a plausible replacement level. An owner’s commercial relationships may also require a transition period rather than an instant earnings multiple.

A simple adjusted earnings schedule should show each change as a line with a description, period, source, proposed adjustment, buyer view, and evidence status. “Owner says” is attribution, not corroboration. The final value should show what happens if disputed adjustments are accepted, partly accepted, or rejected.

sections.heading: Continuity is part of value
sections.text:
A small company can have strong customer demand and still depend on one person’s phone, memory, password, signature, or supplier relationship. If the founder is unavailable for 30 days, can someone else approve payments, access accounting records, contact customers, or collect a receivable? The key-person-risk article already maps role dependency, access, authority, and continuity. A sale process should translate that map into diligence questions.

The transfer plan can be practical: identify who owns the customer relationship; record how orders are priced and approved; document recurring tasks; confirm account and domain access; list licences and contracts; identify who can sign; and set a handover period for the outgoing owner. Build a contact tree and a backup approver. Keep the principal access to company data in company-controlled accounts. These steps help an owner leave without making the whole firm’s operating knowledge leave with them.

Peer-reviewed family-business succession research treats succession as a process with a founder, successor, organization and timing, rather than one signature at closing [1], [2]. Evidence on Italian family firms also found that performance effects varied with successor type and competitive setting in the sample studied [3]. That does not mean family succession fails, or that an outside buyer is always superior. It means owners should evaluate management capability, governance and market conditions, not assume that family ties alone settle the question.

sections.heading: A buyer needs a bridge, not a headline multiple
sections.text:
Suppose a fictional service firm reports KSh 3 million of annual profit. The owner performs work that would cost KSh 1.1–1.5 million to replace. It takes another KSh 250,000 each year to replace computers and maintain essential software. Working capital has been stable, but two customers account for 55% of sales. A buyer might calculate a normalized earnings range after replacement labor and maintenance, then separately adjust for debt, excess cash, customer concentration, working capital delivered at closing, and transaction terms.

There is no universal multiple to plug in. A customer who can cancel next month, a short lease, a licence that cannot transfer, or uncertain stock quality may change the price or the structure of the deal. Deferred consideration, an earn-out or seller financing may allocate some uncertainty. They also create new risks. The contract needs to say what the payment depends on, which financial statements control, who makes decisions during the earn-out, how disputes are resolved, and what happens if a large customer leaves.

For the seller, compare the headline sale price with the cash actually received after debt, transaction costs, taxes, retained obligations and contingent payments. For the buyer, compare purchase price with the amount of capital required after closing. Inventory and receivables are often treated through a working-capital peg or another agreed formula. That mechanism belongs in the transaction documents, not a generic owner-earnings article.

sections.heading: Build the handover backwards
sections.text:
A succession plan can start from the date the owner hopes to step away and work backwards:

1. What must the owner personally stop doing before the business can run without them?
2. Which tasks can be documented, delegated, automated, or covered by a backup?
3. Who can take over customer, supplier and lender relationships?
4. What records will a buyer, family successor or employee successor need to trust the earnings history?
5. What authority will transfer, and when?
6. Which decisions remain with the current owner during transition, and for how long?

The goal is not to remove the owner’s judgment from the business. It is to make the business less fragile when that judgment is unavailable.

A transfer may also change the company’s financing options. Small-business finance research describes how funding sources develop as firms grow and build information and assets that support lending [4]. For an employee buyout, family transfer or outside sale, the parties should therefore test who can borrow, what security or guarantees are required, and whether the post-transfer business can fund the purchase and still meet operating needs. The research does not prescribe a particular transaction structure; it points to financing capacity as a separate diligence question.

sections.heading: Build the same earnings picture for seller, buyer and lender
sections.text:
A seller usually wants the buyer to see the business at its best. A buyer needs a repeatable earnings estimate after the work, assets and cash cycle are properly funded. A lender needs a repayment bridge that survives a weaker year. Put three views side by side rather than arguing over one label.

Start with the filed or bookkeeping figure for operating profit, EBITDA or net income, and identify its period. Reconcile it to bank and tax records when available. List each proposed add-back separately with amount, account, invoice, beneficiary and reason. Accept an adjustment only if the expense is genuinely nonrecurring or personal, the business no longer needs it, and there is no replacement cost. A one-time legal fee may qualify if the dispute has closed; annual company-secretary fees do not. A family member’s salary is not fully an add-back if that person handles procurement or collections. An owner’s vehicle is not free if deliveries depend on it.

Next, calculate the cost of replacing founder duties. Write a task map: customer sales, operational supervision, hiring, quality approvals, bank relationships, regulatory work, procurement and accounting. Estimate hours and qualifications. Some tasks transfer to an existing employee, some require a new manager, and some may disappear if a corporate buyer already has shared services. Make separate owner-operator and corporate-buyer cases. A single generic replacement salary will not fit both.

Then deduct the cash required to keep the earnings level. Estimate maintenance capex from the asset plan; normalize working capital using monthly receivables, inventory and payables over a full seasonal cycle; deduct taxes and interest according to the valuation perspective; and include debt-like claims. Finally, translate enterprise value to equity value without double counting cash, debt, lease liabilities, customer deposits or working-capital adjustments.

sections.heading: An adjustment ledger protects both sides
sections.text:
The ledger should include seller’s claim, buyer’s response, source evidence, accounting treatment, whether it affects historical earnings or forward cash, replacement cost, status and amount accepted. For a KSh 260,000 vehicle expense, the evidence may show KSh 180,000 personal use and KSh 80,000 business delivery. The buyer might add back only the personal portion, then subtract the cost of a replacement delivery vehicle or lease. The net adjustment may be small or zero. This is more credible than accepting or rejecting the entire line.

For a KSh 180,000 legal expense, ask whether the matter is closed, whether related claims remain, and whether the same counsel is retained annually. If the expense resulted from a recurring permit or customer dispute, it may recur. For KSh 120,000 paid to a family member, verify duties and hours; if a new employee would cost KSh 160,000, the expense is not an add-back but perhaps a KSh 40,000 incremental cost. A KSh 90,000 holiday that never appeared in the accounts cannot be added back to earnings. An owner’s personal spending through the business may reduce taxable income but does not increase book profit unless it was booked as an expense.

Every accepted add-back should pass four checks: it is present in the records; it is not already excluded elsewhere; it will not recur under the buyer’s operation; and removing it does not remove necessary revenue-producing work. Keep unresolved adjustments outside the base case until evidence arrives. If they matter to price, use escrow, seller financing or a specific warranty rather than silently embedding them in the multiple.

sections.heading: Normalize working capital by month and by item
sections.text:
A closing balance can be manipulated by timing. The seller can delay supplier payments, accelerate collections, buy unusually large inventory or draw customer deposits just before completion. Compare month-end balances over at least one full operating cycle. If the business is seasonal, use the corresponding month in prior years or a documented monthly normalization rather than a simple year average. Check unusual sales promotions, stock purchases, supplier settlement holidays and one-off customer advances.

Define the working-capital peg in the sale agreement. Specify receivables net of impairment; inventory net of obsolete, damaged and consignment goods; trade payables based on received goods; and any agreed accruals. State whether payroll, tax, customer deposits, deferred revenue, lease liabilities and related-party balances are included or treated as debt-like. Different definitions can move the same KSh 1 million balance between the working-capital adjustment and the debt adjustment, so avoid counting it in both.

Illustration: normalized NWC has averaged KSh 1.4 million, but closing delivered NWC is KSh 1.1 million. The buyer may seek a KSh 300,000 completion adjustment under the agreed formula. But if the shortfall is caused by KSh 300,000 of old disputed invoices, that balance may be worth less than its face value. If it is due to a seasonal inventory dip immediately before peak sales, the buyer may need to fund replacement stock. Show the reason for the gap and the cash it actually takes to restore normal operations.

Supplier arrears require a separate schedule: supplier statement balance, amount due under terms, disputed amount, agreed extension, next delivery and any security or retention of title. A company can show strong working capital because overdue suppliers are large. That is not a benefit delivered to the buyer. The agreement should say who pays those arrears and how any later claim is handled.

sections.heading: Think about price as a range, not a negotiated multiple
sections.text:
Multiples are shorthand for growth, risk, capital needs and transferability. A private company’s value depends on size, customer concentration, management independence, asset quality, recurring revenue, contracts, financing access, tax compliance and evidence quality. Do not copy a public-company multiple and apply it to a small business without considering liquidity, governance and owner dependence.

For a simple range, estimate normalized free cash flow or maintainable owner earnings under low, base and high cases, then apply a valuation method suited to the buyer’s return requirement. A cash-flow model can show the impact of customer loss, margin changes, maintenance needs and working-capital intensity. A multiple method can be a cross-check if comparable transactions are credible and earnings definitions align. Reverse-solve the purchase price to the required return: what growth, margin, salary savings or synergies would the buyer need? If the answer relies on unproven cross-selling or immediate cost cuts, keep those benefits out of the base price.

To move from enterprise value to equity proceeds, identify debt, lease obligations, shareholder loans, unpaid taxes, employee claims, excess or restricted cash, customer deposits and the working-capital true-up. If normalized EBITDA is KSh 2.29 million and a hypothetical 3x–5x range gives enterprise values of KSh 6.87m–11.45m, that is not the seller’s cheque. Subtract debt and debt-like claims; add only excess unrestricted cash; include the completion working-capital adjustment; then account for transaction costs, tax and escrow. The seller should also consider whether deferred consideration or an earn-out is realistically collectible.

sections.heading: Test what the lender can support
sections.text:
A lender needs cash available for debt service after replacement labor, tax, maintenance and required working capital. Build the principal and interest schedule by date. Compare it with the operating cash forecast, not just annual EBITDA. Model a customer paying one month late, the largest contract not renewing, input costs increasing and an asset needing repair. If the business only covers debt under the seller’s full workload and zero maintenance, the price or financing is too high.

A buyer can calculate maximum debt service under a selected minimum coverage assumption, but that assumption is not automatically the bank’s covenant. The lender may define EBITDA add-backs, eligible cash, lease claims and debt service differently. Obtain the actual offer and covenant definition. Include arrangement fees, valuation and legal cost, insurance, collateral and personal guarantees. If the buyer must invest working capital after closing, add that amount to cash required at completion rather than treating it as an operating expense later.

Seller financing can close a valuation gap and signal confidence, but it creates a claim that needs repayment terms, subordination, security, default remedies and tax advice. An earn-out is different: it depends on future results. Define the metric, time period, customer cohort, returns, discounts, owner control and reporting rights. Revenue alone can reward unprofitable sales. Collected contribution or gross profit may be closer to the seller’s influence if the buyer controls overhead and service policy. Document dispute resolution.

sections.heading: A 90-day transition and continuity test
sections.text:
During the first two weeks, confirm bank access, payment approvals, customer and supplier contacts, employee payroll, tax accounts, licenses, leases, insurance, loan covenants, stock ownership and outstanding orders. Reconcile cash and all open invoices. Identify obligations due in the next 30 days and any customer money tied to incomplete delivery. Avoid a large distribution or nonroutine purchase before the first cash close.

From days 15 to 45, shadow the founder on sales quotations, procurement, quality approvals, customer complaints, collections, repairs and regulatory work. Record process steps and transfer credentials lawfully. Identify every duty with no backup. Check whether supplier credit, customer access or a technical permit depends on the founder personally. A company can have good normalized earnings and still be untransferable until those dependencies are addressed.

By day 90, compare actual receipts, contribution, stock ageing and service quality with the diligence model. Verify customer retention and staff continuity. An earn-out should reflect what was agreed and independently observable. Track the cash impact of duplicate staffing, transition support and integration. If the new owner wants to centralize finance or procurement, model the timing and one-time costs before removing staff who hold critical knowledge.

Family succession needs the same discipline. Document who owns shares, who draws salary, who receives distributions, who approves payments and who can sign contracts. Train a successor in the customer and supplier routines while the founder is still available. Agree an emergency transfer plan for illness or death, including bank mandates, key passwords, insurance and authority. Fairness among heirs and operational control may require separate legal and estate planning advice.

sections.heading: Decide with an evidence list
sections.text:
The buyer’s final note can show reported earnings, supported adjustments, replacement labor, normalized maintenance and working capital, financing required, downside debt coverage, equity price range and unresolved evidence. For each open item, state the requested document, custodian, due date and impact on price or contract terms. If the seller will not provide a key customer ledger or loan agreement, reflect that uncertainty in the offer instead of pretending the number is known.

The seller should prepare the same bridge before listing. Clean monthly accounts, reconcile personal expenses, document equipment and maintenance, resolve supplier balances, renew licenses, map customer concentration, train backups and define what cash and working capital will remain at closing. These steps can improve the business even if no sale occurs. A buyer is purchasing future transferable cash generation; clean evidence and reduced founder dependence make that claim more credible.

sections.heading: Separate what is known from what is promised
sections.text:
A sale process often mixes three different kinds of value: cash the business has already produced, cash it may produce if current conditions persist, and value that depends on future work by the buyer or seller. Put each claim in the right column before negotiating.

Verified historical cash can be tied to a bank statement, filed return, customer remittance, payroll record, or supplier invoice. Maintainable earnings require a judgment about whether the historical activity can continue after the sale. Upside depends on a specific action such as adding a branch, winning a contract, raising prices, replacing a machine, or securing a permit. A buyer may pay for upside, but the purchase price should state who bears the execution risk.

For example, suppose a workshop shows normalized annual cash earnings of KSh 6 million after paying a market replacement salary for the founder. The seller says a new service bay can add KSh 2 million. That forecast should not quietly be included in the KSh 6 million base. Ask for installation cost, staff, ramp time, licensing, demand evidence and the cash needed to hold parts. If those items are not funded, the buyer is purchasing a plan, not current earnings. A contingent payment can share risk: the seller receives some proceeds only if documented revenue or gross profit is achieved, with a definition that prevents either side from manipulating timing or shifting costs.

An earn-out can create disputes if the seller is paid on sales while the buyer controls pricing, credit terms, overhead allocation and customer acceptance. Define the metric, accounting policy, reporting access, dispute process, treatment of returns and bad debts, and what happens if the buyer changes the business. A simple cash-at-close price may be preferable when the records are weak or the parties cannot agree on measurement. Complexity does not repair poor evidence.

sections.heading: A buyer's practical diligence sequence
sections.text:
Diligence should follow the way cash moves through the business, not just the order in which folders arrive.

1. Establish the perimeter. Identify the seller, operating company, owners of land and equipment, trading names, subsidiaries, guarantees and related parties. Confirm which contracts, permits, employees, stock, intellectual property and customer data are actually transferable.
2. Tie sales to collections. Sample invoices from order to delivery note, customer statement, bank deposit and ledger. Investigate credit notes issued after year-end, cash sales without sequential receipts, related-party sales, disputed balances, and customers who pay only after the owner calls.
3. Tie costs to delivery. Trace a sample of supplier invoices through purchase order, goods received, stock record and payment. Check whether freight, duties, repairs, owner labour or warranty work is missing from the apparent margin.
4. Rebuild payroll and owner work. List the owner's weekly duties and the employee who can perform them. Use a realistic replacement wage plus employer obligations. A salary add-back without a named replacement plan overstates the buyer's cash.
5. Inspect inventory and equipment. Count stock by SKU, age, condition and last sale. Observe equipment running under normal load; inspect service history, safety certification, spare-parts availability and deferred repairs. Book value is not evidence of usable value.
6. Reconcile obligations. Confirm tax, employee, landlord, lender, supplier, customer-deposit and litigation balances directly where possible. A seller's spreadsheet is a starting schedule, not third-party confirmation.
7. Stress the first year. Build monthly cash needs around seasonality, customer retention, supplier deposits, debt repayment and the transition. A profitable annual forecast can still fail in a month where stock must be paid for before a large customer settles.

Use a materiality threshold to organize work, not to excuse a known control problem. A small unexplained cash difference can signal that the ledger is unreliable; a large balance can be immaterial if independently confirmed and not at risk. Record source, owner, date, test, result and unresolved consequence for each diligence item.

sections.heading: Match the legal price to the economic bridge
sections.text:
Enterprise value is not the cash that reaches the seller. The bridge should state whether the agreed amount assumes cash-free, debt-free delivery, a normal level of working capital, and specified treatment of leases, shareholder loans, unpaid taxes, customer deposits and transaction expenses. Then reconcile that bridge to the completion accounts.

Working capital deserves a seasonal baseline. A business that carries more stock before its busy season may need a higher normal level than a simple twelve-month average suggests. Compare like months across several years, remove unusual one-offs only with evidence, and separately identify old or disputed receivables. A purchase-price adjustment for working capital should not reward the seller for overdue debtors or obsolete stock.

The parties should also write down the measurement rules before closing. Define included accounts, accounting standards, cut-off procedures, stock-count method, reserves for bad debts and obsolete inventory, and access to records. State who prepares the completion accounts, how objections work, and whether an independent accountant decides only the disputed items. Vague wording converts a spreadsheet disagreement into a legal dispute.

sections.heading: A seller's transition plan is part of the asset
sections.text:
A founder may personally remember prices, exceptions, supplier promises and customer preferences that never entered the system. That knowledge is valuable only if it can be transferred. During the diligence period, require the current owner to document recurring work, introduce key customers and suppliers, train successors, transfer passwords and records securely, and explain approvals or informal credit arrangements.

Transition should be measured through operating results, not attendance. Useful milestones include invoice error rate, on-time delivery, customer retention, rework, stock variance, collection days and the percentage of decisions completed without founder intervention. A business that remains dependent on the founder after six months has not completed the transition, even if the handover calendar says it has.

A family successor needs the same clarity. Le Breton-Miller, Miller and Steier describe effective succession as a process involving preparation, relationships, successor development and the transfer of leadership, rather than a single date [2]. In practical terms, let the successor own a real budget, supplier negotiation or customer portfolio before the founder leaves. Agree who can approve spending and hiring. Family harmony is not protected by leaving authority ambiguous.

sections.heading: Closing gates that protect both sides
sections.text:
Before signing an unconditional transfer, answer five questions with evidence:

 Can the buyer operate the business legally on the first day after close?
 Does the buyer have enough liquidity for the first seasonal working-capital peak and known repairs?
 Have material customer, supplier, employee, landlord and lender consents been obtained or clearly conditioned?
 Does the price bridge say how cash, debt, working capital and disputed items are treated?
 Is there a practical plan for the seller to transfer relationships, systems and authority?

If an answer is no, convert it into a closing condition, escrow, holdback, price adjustment or explicit risk allocation. Do not use a vague warranty to substitute for a missing permit or unverified title. A warranty may provide a claim after a loss; it does not keep the doors open while the buyer pursues that claim.

The buyer and seller can then compare scenarios on common assumptions: a normal year, a downside year with slower collections and lost customers, and a transition case with extra management cost. Report cash to the seller separately from the buyer's post-close cash requirement. This avoids the common mistake of treating the headline enterprise value as both the seller's proceeds and the buyer's total investment.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Project 1 workbook provides a Buy Sell and Succession checklist for entity perimeter, title, sales-to-cash tracing, owner duties, asset condition, tax and creditor claims, working-capital baseline, contract transfer and handover milestones. Use it with the Owner Earnings, Maintenance, Working Capital and Debt and Growth schedules to organize diligence. Evidence Vectors identifies which linked schedules are fictional templates and where actual source documents would need to be recorded. The current workbook is an evidence checklist, not a transaction valuation or purchase-price calculator; proposed add-backs still need source documents and a replacement-cost test.

articles.title: Reconstructing owner earnings from public filings
articles.short_title: Reconstructing owner earnings from public filings
questions: How can public filings support a defensible owner-earnings bridge?
What must asset-light and asset-heavy businesses reinvest to preserve productive capacity?
How do banks and insurers determine distributable capital?
Which sector-specific adjustments matter when comparing seven NSE industry profiles?
articles.workbook_name: Project 2 - Listed Companies Owner Earnings and Valuation.xlsx

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

A public company gives us more information than most private businesses, but it does not give us a line called “owner earnings.” We have to build one from the report and keep every analyst judgment visible.

Begin with the filing’s own map. Read the auditor’s opinion, the basis of preparation, the accounting policies and the notes behind profit, working capital, share compensation, leases and capital spending. Record the legal reporting entity, consolidated or parent-only scope, currency, fiscal year, and date the report was published. A group with a Kenyan parent and overseas subsidiaries may report consolidated earnings in a different currency context from the parent’s standalone financial statements.

sections.heading: Reported cash flow first, estimated earning power second
A dated Kenyan example
sections.text:
BAT Kenya’s audited FY2025 report gives a useful starting set of reported facts. Revenue was KES 23,191.945 million; EBIT was KES 7,474.835 million; operating cash flow was KES 6,633.154 million; capital expenditure was KES 301.833 million; and earnings per share was KES 52.46 [3]. These numbers tell us about reported scale, operating profit and cash conversion. They do not, by themselves, establish a maintenance-capital estimate.

The tempting shortcut would be to call the KES 301.833 million of total capital expenditure “maintenance” or to assume it is all growth. Neither conclusion follows from the total. A proper bridge would trace additions to the property, plant and equipment note, compare several years of spending with depreciation, inspect the stated purpose of major projects, identify asset replacements, and check what production or competitive capacity those assets support. If the report does not provide enough detail, the conclusion should read: “maintenance capital is not separately disclosed; a defensible owner-earnings estimate requires a supported range or additional operating records.”

The same applies to the KES 6,633.154 million operating cash flow. It is a reported cash-flow measure for a fiscal period. It is not the amount shareholders can distribute because capital spending, debt obligations, working-capital needs, and future investment still matter. A useful article can show the reported bridge and leave the normalized owner-earnings result unavailable pending maintenance evidence. That is more informative than a precise but invented number.

sections.heading: Make each adjustment traceable
sections.text:
Every analyst adjustment needs a line in a source ledger:

| Field | What to record |
|---|---|
| Filed line | Exact statement/note label and page or table |
| Entity and period | Parent or group, year, currency, reporting date |
| Adjustment | What changes and why |
| Evidence | Filing, management commentary, multi-year record, or external source |
| Status | Filed fact, analyst estimate, hypothesis, or unresolved |
| Sensitivity | How the value changes under a reasonable alternative |

Watch for acquisition effects, discontinued operations, unusual tax benefits, restructuring costs, impairment reversals, capitalized software and development, leases, and share-based compensation. Do not add back a cost just because it is called “non-cash.” Some noncash expenses represent real capital consumed or future dilution. Stock-based compensation, for example, is added back in operating cash flow as a noncash adjustment, while owners can still experience dilution. Use one coherent treatment: keep the expense in earnings, or add it back and separately model the dilution or replacement cost. Do not do both.

sections.heading: Link earnings to value carefully
sections.text:
Ohlson’s peer-reviewed model relates value to earnings, book values and dividends under explicit accounting relationships [4]. It is a useful reminder that valuation depends on future earnings and the capital that supports them. A current owner-earnings estimate can anchor scenarios, but it is not the whole value. Growth requires reinvestment. Returns on invested capital can fade. Risks change the required return. The value of a listed share also depends on how much of the business’s cash generation is available to that equity claim after other claims.

The KCA series and its four final workbooks already show the value of separating screening, financial statements and valuation, portfolio construction, and compounding. The new model should follow that traceable design while adding explicit maintenance-capital ranges, a working-capital maintenance/growth distinction, and a source status for each adjustment.

sections.heading: Create a filing model that another analyst can reproduce
sections.text:
Start by recording the issuer’s legal name, fiscal year-end, filing date, currency, units and consolidation scope. A company may present group earnings in one section and parent-only earnings in another. Do not mix them. Each raw input should point to a statement or note and carry a source ID. Preserve the as-filed value; add any reclassification in a separate column with the reason and formula. A reviewer should be able to recreate every output from that source list.

Build the historical model across at least five years where filings allow. The income statement shows revenue, operating costs, taxes, interest, net income and non-controlling interests. The balance sheet supplies opening and closing receivables, inventory, payables, contract balances, cash, debt, leases, fixed assets and equity. The cash-flow statement gives operating cash, tax and interest paid, capital purchases, asset sales, financing and dividends. Notes explain acquisitions, disposals, stock-based compensation, impairments, leases, commitments and policy changes. A five-year trend is not complete if it ignores a major acquisition that changed the perimeter.

Use reconciliation controls, not visual confidence. Revenue should tie to the filed statement. Group profit should reconcile to parent and non-controlling interests. Opening cash plus reported movement should tie to ending cash. Debt balances should tie to current and noncurrent borrowings in the notes. Changes in assets should reconcile to additions, depreciation, disposals and currency effects. If a tie-out fails, show the variance and do not hide it in “other.”

sections.heading: Move from accounting earnings to a cash estimate
sections.text:
The bridge starts with the claim the analyst wants to value. For equity owners, net income attributable to parent may be a clean starting point, but cash available to equity still reflects capex, working capital, interest and debt repayment. For enterprise value, begin with a pre-financing operating cash measure and later account for debt and lease claims. Keep both approaches consistent. Do not subtract debt from a cash flow after interest and principal were already deducted without explaining the adjustment.

A practical bridge can include reported net income; noncash depreciation and amortization; stock compensation treatment; other material noncash charges; working-capital change; cash capex; tax paid and interest depending on starting point; debt issuance and repayment; acquisitions or disposals; and diluted share count. Then create an analyst owner-earnings estimate that subtracts maintenance spending and additional working capital required to sustain current earning power. Growth investment remains visible but is not mistaken for maintenance. If maintenance cannot be established, show a range and a “not estimable” case.

Noncash charges need different logic. Depreciation is added back to reconcile profit to cash, but replacement spending must be estimated. Impairment is noncash in the period but may indicate weaker future economics. Stock compensation is a real claim on owners. Either leave the expense in earnings and do not add it back, or add it back and model dilution or cash repurchases separately. The model should show both methods side by side if the answer changes materially.

Working capital should be rebuilt from balances, not taken solely from an annual cash-flow line. Calculate year-over-year changes in receivables, inventory, payables, contract assets, accrued expenses and customer advances. Reconcile those movements to cash flow. Acquisitions, foreign exchange, reclassifications and noncash changes can create differences. A rising payable balance can be a temporary source of cash, but if it reflects overdue invoices or supplier distress it is not a durable owner benefit. A customer advance creates cash and a delivery obligation; it is not unrestricted earnings.

sections.heading: Maintenance capex: make the uncertainty measurable
sections.text:
Companies rarely report maintenance capex as a clean number. Build three estimates from evidence. First, inspect asset additions and depreciation by class over several years; this is a starting range, not a conclusion. Second, use the company’s stated renewal plans, engineering reports, operating uptime, useful lives and supplier quotes. Third, compare spending with capacity and output: a large increase in capacity or new factory is growth, while repeated replacement of a worn production line may sustain existing volume. State which method drives low, base and high.

If annual D&A is $1 billion and total capex is $1.4 billion, it does not follow that maintenance is exactly $1 billion and growth $400 million. D&A reflects accounting estimates and past cost; replacement prices and useful lives may differ. Conversely, a year with low capex can mean renewal was deferred. The analyst should check backlogs, repair costs, outages, safety compliance and capitalized software. Record the next evidence needed to narrow the range. A chart that assumes a fixed share of D&A each year may be useful as a sensitivity, but it must remain labeled as an assumption.

Normalized earnings should also handle cycles. Commodity prices, utilization, credit losses, foreign exchange, tax rates and customer ordering can distort a single year. Use several years and identify the economic drivers rather than averaging mechanically. A simple average may combine recession, acquisition, impairment and a different business mix. Create a normalized case with a stated mid-cycle input and stress it against a plausible low case. Use management guidance as an attributed source, not a substitute for independent model logic.

sections.heading: Convert the estimate into a per-share claim
sections.text:
Diluted shares matter because owners own per-share cash, not an abstract corporate total. Track weighted average basic shares, diluted shares, shares issued, options and restricted awards, buybacks, acquisition consideration and treasury shares. Match the share count to the period and earnings numerator. If the issuer reports repurchases, compare the quantity and price with the net change in diluted shares. Repurchases may offset employee awards rather than reduce the share count. Model future dilution and capital spent to offset it.

Then value with a method suited to the claim. An equity cash flow or residual-income model can fit businesses where book capital is central. Enterprise DCF can fit nonfinancial operations if cash flows are before financing and debt/leases are consistently treated. An earnings yield or comparable multiple is a cross-check, not a cure for inconsistent accounting. Use a reverse valuation to determine what growth, margins, capital intensity and terminal economics the market price implies. The key question is whether that path is supported by capacity, customers and reinvestment—not whether the spreadsheet can produce a point value.

Sensitivity should show economically related combinations. A slower growth case may reduce supplier commitments but also utilization and gross margin. A lower sales case may increase receivables days if buyers pay later. A high-rate case can change debt interest and discount rate together. A one-variable table can help identify sensitivity, but a scenario should tell a coherent operating story. Show low/base/high value ranges and the inputs that drive most of the spread.

sections.heading: Write the decision after reviewing the open items
sections.text:
Before acting, summarize the evidence in plain language: what was reported; what the analyst changed; what cannot be estimated; and what the current price appears to require. If valuation depends on an uncertain maintenance range, say how a 20% higher replacement need changes owner earnings and value. If one customer concentration or debt maturity dominates, show the trigger for refreshing the analysis. A reader should know which filing note or next quarter disclosure could change the conclusion.

For a public-market investor, the decision need not be “buy” or “sell.” It can be to wait for the next filing, maintain a smaller position, demand a higher expected return, or treat the issuer as outside the circle of competence. The workbook’s role is to make those trade-offs visible and repeatable. It cannot remove uncertainty, but it can stop accounting presentation, inconsistent units or a hidden assumption from deciding the answer by accident.

sections.heading: Worked bridge: keep the reported year and the normalized year apart
sections.text:
The following example is illustrative, not a restatement of BAT Kenya or any other issuer. Assume a company reports KES 1,000 million of net income, KES 180 million of depreciation and amortization, KES 80 million of share-based compensation, and KES 30 million of gain from selling an old asset. Assume analyst evidence supports KES 260 million of maintenance investment and KES 90 million of additional working capital to sustain the current activity level. A first-pass equity owner-earnings bridge is:

| Line | KES million | Treatment |
|---|---:|---|
| Net income attributable to ordinary shareholders | 1,000 | Filed starting point |
| Add depreciation and amortization | 180 | Noncash expense; replacement cash is estimated below |
| Add share-based compensation | 80 | Only if dilution or replacement cost is modeled separately |
| Remove gain on asset disposal | (30) | Nonrecurring gain included in reported earnings |
| Subtract maintenance investment | (260) | Analyst estimate, supported by asset evidence |
| Subtract incremental working capital | (90) | Growth in cash tied up to sustain the modeled activity |
| Illustrative owner-earnings estimate | 880 | Before any further financing or valuation judgment |

This is not automatically cash available for a dividend. It assumes net income already reflects interest and cash taxes for the period. A working-capital estimate must be consistent with the chosen period and starting method. If the analyst instead begins with operating cash flow, the filed working-capital changes have already affected that line; subtracting them again would double count. The analyst must also explain what happens to the KES 80 million share-based compensation. Leaving it in expenses lowers the result to KES 800 million before other changes; adding it back requires a separate view of future share dilution or repurchases. The correct treatment is the one that values the same economic claim without counting compensation twice.

Suppose the evidence supports maintenance spending from KES 220 million to KES 340 million. The owner-earnings range is KES 920 million to KES 800 million, before other uncertainties. If diluted shares are 100 million, that is KES 9.20 to KES 8.00 per diluted share, subject to the share-compensation treatment. A precise KES 880 million point estimate hides the fact that maintenance evidence is the largest driver. Report the range and the specific asset records that would narrow it.

sections.heading: Reconcile the model to the filed statements before valuing it
sections.text:
A well-built model has three distinct layers. The first is a transcription layer that reproduces the annual report. The second is an analyst layer that adjusts or normalizes filed amounts. The third is a decision layer that converts the estimate into value, expected return and position size. Mixing these layers makes review difficult because an analyst assumption can appear to be a reported fact.

For each statement line, preserve the label used by the issuer and record page or note, reporting entity, unit, period, original currency, exchange rate if converted, and sign convention. Reconcile subtotals to the report. If operating cash flow does not match the audited statement, stop and resolve it before building the valuation. Check parent versus consolidated accounts, continuing operations, restated comparatives, year-end date, and whether amounts are in shillings, thousands or millions. A thousand-fold unit error can make a sophisticated forecast meaningless.

Build a reconciliation from opening cash to closing cash and from opening debt to closing debt. For cash, show operating, investing and financing flows plus foreign-exchange effects. For debt, show new borrowings, repayments, lease additions, foreign exchange, acquisitions, reclassifications and closing balances. Track restricted cash separately. If the annual report's cash definition differs from the analyst's, explain the bridge rather than silently changing the label.

Then use cross-checks that can expose inconsistent assumptions: revenue growth against receivables and inventory growth; margins against product mix and input costs; depreciation against asset additions; cash taxes against the tax note; interest expense against average debt and disclosed rates; dividends and buybacks against the cash-flow statement; and diluted share count against awards, conversions and repurchases. These are not automatic fraud tests. They are prompts to reconcile a surprising result and ask management or source documents for the explanation.

sections.heading: Normalize with a business explanation
sections.text:
Do not average a period without identifying what changed. For a cyclical company, map capacity utilization, selling prices, input costs and inventory through a full cycle where possible. For a bank, focus on credit losses, funding cost and regulatory capital instead of applying an industrial maintenance formula. For an insurer, keep insurance service result, investment result, claims and solvency capital distinct. For an acquisitive company, separate acquired earnings from the cash purchase price, integration expense and incremental shares or debt. If the reporting perimeter changed, comparable growth needs a like-for-like bridge.

A one-off add-back is credible only when the cash or accounting item is identified, the event is nonrecurring in economic substance, and the business will not need a similar expense to keep earning revenue. Repeated “one-time” restructuring costs may be part of the operating model. A tax credit can boost earnings without creating recurring operating performance. An impairment reversal may raise accounting income but not customer cash. The filing note and multi-year record are stronger evidence than an issuer's preferred label.

The dates of evidence matter. A result published after the valuation date cannot be used to claim that an investor could have known it earlier. Keep the fiscal year, report publication date and market-price date as separate fields. This is essential in a backtest and useful in a live investment memo because it reveals when an estimate should have changed.

sections.heading: Make the workbook reviewable by someone who disagrees
sections.text:
A reviewer should be able to change maintenance capex, working-capital intensity, share dilution, discount rate and terminal assumptions without changing the filed inputs. Add a notes field for every analyst assumption: evidence, owner, date entered, rationale, range and next review trigger. A source row should lead to the annual report, page or note; a calculated output should lead to its formula inputs.

Use explicit checks. Balance-sheet assets should equal liabilities and equity where the source statements permit. Cash roll-forward should equal reported ending cash. Debt roll-forward and share count should reconcile or display an explained residual. Units should be consistent in each calculation. Formula cells should never contain manually typed overrides without a separate override label. A range check can flag implausible negative shares, a maintenance estimate above total capex, or an implied value that changes solely because currency units were switched.

Dechow, Kothari and Watts document that accrual earnings and cash flows relate differently across firms and time [1]. The practical model implication is to preserve both measures and explain the divergence, rather than forcing them to agree through a hidden plug. Ohlson's valuation framework also makes accounting earnings and book values part of a structured valuation relationship, not interchangeable with cash or intrinsic value [4]. The analyst should show how the selected method uses each measure and what assumptions remain decisive.

sections.heading: A disciplined output for an investment committee
sections.text:
End the filing analysis with a one-page memo, not just a target price. State the reported facts, analyst adjustments, estimated owner-earnings range, per-share range, major downside mechanism, capital-allocation needs, and the evidence that would change the view. Separate business quality from price: a durable company can be overvalued, and a low multiple can reflect an impaired earnings base.

For BAT Kenya, the published FY2025 figures in the report give revenue, EBIT, operating cash flow, capital expenditure and EPS [3]. Those are a sound starting point, but the article should not manufacture a maintenance split that the report does not disclose. The decision can be explicit: owner earnings remain a range or not estimable until a supported renewal estimate and incremental working-capital requirement are available. That leaves a clear next step—obtain project-level capex, asset-condition and working-capital evidence—instead of disguising uncertainty as precision.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Project 2 workbook includes dated NVIDIA FY2026 filing inputs, a separate owner-earnings bridge, editable assumptions, an asset-heavy issuer screen, bank and insurer context, a seven-issuer NSE evidence matrix, nine profile-specific stress cases, a conditional valuation range, and Sources and Checks. Evidence Vectors carries each populated issuer/regulator measure with its entity, amount/unit, fiscal period, event/year-end date, filing or report date, source ID, retrieval date and workbook locator; scenarios and empty inputs stay separate. Reported facts remain separate from maintenance and working-capital assumptions. The valuation stays unavailable until earnings, growth, discount and terminal rates, diluted shares and a dated price are entered. The detailed cash bridge is NVIDIA-specific; the NSE matrix is a source-led casebook, and Profile Stress uses normalized hypothetical inputs rather than full issuer valuations.

questions: How can public filings support a defensible owner-earnings bridge?
What must asset-light and asset-heavy businesses reinvest to preserve productive capacity?
How do banks and insurers determine distributable capital?
Which sector-specific adjustments matter when comparing seven NSE industry profiles?
