articles.title: NSE cross-sector casebook: seven businesses, seven cash questions
articles.short_title: NSE cross-sector casebook: seven businesses, seven cash questions
questions: How can public filings support a defensible owner-earnings bridge?
What must asset-light and asset-heavy businesses reinvest to preserve productive capacity?
How do banks and insurers determine distributable capital?
Which sector-specific adjustments matter when comparing seven NSE industry profiles?
articles.workbook_name: Project 2 - Listed Companies Owner Earnings and Valuation.xlsx

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

An industrial-company formula can be useful for a Kenyan listed business, but only after we know what its assets and liabilities do. A bank’s customer deposits fund lending. An insurer’s premiums come with future claims. A farm may harvest seasonally and carry biological assets. A utility spends before a plant produces electricity. A telecom network needs continuing capital and spectrum. A manufacturer buys inputs and funds inventory. A property developer may have land, unsold units and customer instalments, but cash tied up in a project can remain unavailable for years.

This casebook uses seven NSE research anchors to ask the same first question in different ways: what cash can the owners ultimately claim after the business funds the operating system that earns it?

| Sector | Research anchor | First cash question | What must not be mistaken for owner earnings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Banking | Equity Group Holdings | After expected loan losses, operating costs and capital retention, how much equity can the bank distribute without constraining safe lending? | Deposits are not spare cash; accounting equity is not identical to eligible regulatory capital. |
| Insurance | Jubilee Holdings | How much profit is earned as insurance service is provided, and how much capital must remain to support claims and solvency? | Premium cash received is not fully distributable; an insurance liability or contractual service margin is not free cash. |
| Energy | KenGen | After plant availability, maintenance, fuel or resource costs, debt and project commitments, what cash remains? | EBITDA omits large renewal needs, debt service and collection timing. |
| Agriculture | Kakuzi | What cash arrives across crop cycles after land, trees, irrigation, labour, packing, cold chain and seasonal inventory are funded? | Accounting movements in biological assets are not necessarily cash harvest proceeds. |
| Telecommunications | Safaricom | After network refresh, spectrum, software, towers, customer acquisition and mobile-money risk, what is recurring equity cash? | Subscriber growth or EBITDA alone does not capture network capex, leases or regulated obligations. |
| Manufacturing | BAT Kenya | After inputs, excise and other obligations, receivables, inventory and replacement investment, what cash is repeatable? | A strong margin is not a maintenance-capex estimate or a future dividend promise. |
| Property | Home Afrika | When are land and units converted into collected cash, and what must be spent to finish contracted developments? | Presales, accounting revenue and unsold land are not interchangeable with cash available to shareholders. |

The examples above are chosen because their operating models differ, not because they have similar valuation multiples. Equity’s 2025 Integrated Report, Jubilee’s 2025 Annual Integrated Report, KenGen’s FY2025 Integrated Report, Kakuzi’s 2025 annual report, BAT Kenya’s 2025 report, Home Afrika’s 2025 reporting, and Safaricom’s reporting catalogue provide dated primary starting points [1]–[7]. Each article calculation should preserve the fiscal period, entity and unit in the source.

sections.heading: Three quick illustrations
Agriculture: profit can lead the cash by a season
sections.text: A grower can record value movements in trees, fruit, or other biological assets before receiving sale proceeds. Harvest volume, grade, export acceptance, prices, packing costs, transport, and buyer-payment timing all affect cash. For Kakuzi, an analyst would compare crop volume and prices with the cash-flow statement, read the biological-assets and bearer-plant notes, then trace investment in plantations and packhouse capacity. The company’s official report record includes its FY2025 annual report and FY2026 half-year publication [4]. The analyst still needs to open the filed reports and link any number used into an evidence ledger.

sections.heading: Telecom: infrastructure must carry the forecast traffic
sections.text: A subscriber count does not tell us whether the network has enough capacity, how often equipment must be refreshed, or what power and lease commitments apply. For Safaricom, follow mobile connectivity and M-PESA separately, then reconcile capital spending, leases, segment results, financing, and cash generation to the group statements. Its reporting catalogue is the primary starting point for dated filings and results [5]. If a service grows faster than the network can carry it, expansion spending may precede revenue. If capex is cut, near-term cash may look better while customer experience or future capacity deteriorates.

sections.heading: Property: deposits can arrive before an earnings story is complete
sections.text: A developer might receive deposits before construction is complete, yet still need cash for contractors, approvals, infrastructure, marketing, debt interest, and handover. A buyer’s instalment is both a receipt and evidence that the seller owes a completed unit or other contractual performance. The model needs project-by-project completion estimates, customer refund rights, and the timing of remaining costs. Home Afrika publishes annual reports and financial publications by reporting year, which supports a dated record rather than reliance on a project headline [7].

sections.heading: Why one multiple is not enough
sections.text:
A price-to-earnings ratio uses equity market value against profit attributable to equity owners. A price-to-book ratio is often useful where a regulated balance sheet is central to earnings. An enterprise-value multiple can work for a nonfinancial operating company when debt and cash are consistently defined. None of those measures makes unlike businesses comparable automatically.

Ohlson’s peer-reviewed valuation framework connects book value, earnings and dividends under an explicit model [8]. Its practical lesson here is not that one formula fits every sector. It is that a valuation depends on future earnings and the assets and capital supporting them. For banks, fair-value information can affect how investors interpret the portfolio and the equity claim [9]. For retailers and manufacturers, working capital absorbs or releases cash, and its economic value depends on expected sales, credit risk and financial constraints [10]. For energy and property firms, replacement and project investment shape the length and scale of future cash generation [11].

Build one method around each issuer’s economics, then use a cross-sector table only to organize the research. For each name, record the question the model can answer and the disclosures it lacks. Do not force a value estimate when the necessary operating or capital information is missing.

sections.heading: A reporting rule for this casebook
sections.text:
A useful NSE comparison table records the report period, publication date, currency and unit; source-file name and page; consolidated or parent scope; reported earnings; cash from operations; capital expenditure; debt and lease claims; shares; dividend declaration and payment date; and unresolved items. Market prices need a separate dated market-source observation. A return calculation should not pair a price from one date with an earnings period from another without labeling the mismatch.

The previous Kenyan Equities and Company Analysis project already has four final workbook roles: screening, statements and valuation, portfolio construction, and compounding. The NSE Dividend Growth workbook separates contributions and income scenarios. Those are helpful companion products, but this casebook’s central task is to make each owner-earnings bridge traceable to its issuer-specific sources and investment needs.

sections.heading: Seven issuer cards: what to calculate from the current reports
Equity Group: earnings growth still has to pass the capital test
sections.text:
Equity Group's FY2025 results report KES 75.5 billion of profit after tax, total assets of KES 1.97 trillion, customer deposits of KES 1.46 trillion and net loans of KES 882.5 billion. The announcement also reports a 1.7% cost of risk and 67.7% NPL coverage, and proposes KES 21.7 billion of dividends, or KES 5.75 per share [12]. The proposed cash dividend is approximately 28.7% of reported group profit after tax. That is a descriptive ratio, not proof of capital headroom.

Build a bank model from average loan and deposit balances, net interest income, fees, credit costs, regional subsidiary contributions, regulatory capital and risk-weighted assets. Separate Equity Bank Kenya from the regional banks and other group activities. Loan growth is not free: it may increase risk-weighted assets and require retained capital. Check whether the strong reported earnings are supported by cashable recurring income, and test a higher credit cost before carrying the proposed payout forward.

sections.heading: Jubilee Holdings: premium and deposit contributions are not earned profit
sections.text:
Jubilee's FY2025 announcement reports gross written premiums and deposit administration contributions of KES 62.4 billion, net profit of KES 5.6 billion and profit before tax of KES 7.2 billion; its H1 2026 update later reports profit before tax of KES 4.4 billion [13]. These are issuer-reported measures for different periods and must not be blended into a single annual run-rate.

Build by insurance line and regulated entity: insurance service result, claims, acquisition expense, reserve development, investment result, reinsurance, IFRS 17 balances, capital and distributions from subsidiaries to the parent. Compare the dividend with after-tax earnings and capital actually available at the paying entity. Ask how much of profit came from underwriting and how much from investment or finance movements. An increase in premiums can mean more future service obligations as well as a larger customer base.

sections.heading: KenGen: profit competes with long-lived plant spending
sections.text:
KenGen's FY2025 integrated report records KES 10.481 billion of profit after tax, KES 17.733 billion of capital investment and KES 30.124 billion of cash and cash equivalents, all in the report's KES-million presentation [3, 14]. Capital investment was about 1.69 times reported profit after tax. This does not mean all investment is maintenance or that none can be deferred; it shows why the dividend cannot be assessed from profit alone.

Trace generation, availability, tariffs, fuel and geothermal costs, receivables from the off-taker, project capex, debt, interest and project commissioning. Separate refurbishment of existing plants from new generation and transmission-related projects. Model delayed payments and project overruns beside generation and debt service. Cash held today may support capital commitments already signed and should not be counted again as an uncommitted shareholder reserve.

sections.heading: Kakuzi: use crop-level cash timing, not one annual profit figure
sections.text:
Kakuzi reported FY2025 revenue of KES 5.369 billion and profit before tax of KES 568 million, versus a KES 167 million pre-tax loss in FY2024; the company also reports that 2025 avocado profit was KES 709 million and macadamia profit KES 365 million [4, 15]. The reported FY2025 turnaround is real as an accounting result, but segment profits are not cash collected and do not add directly to a distributable number after group costs, tax, working capital and renewal.

Build one schedule per crop and operating line. Include planted hectares, tree age, yield, grade, export volume, selling price and currency, harvest timing, packhouse and transport cost, buyer acceptance, collection lag, orchard renewal and biological-asset accounting. The chairman's report describes logistics disruption, pest and disease pressure, lower European prices and a developing route-to-market strategy [15]. These are cash and margin drivers, not background color. Stress a poor-quality shipment and delayed customer remittance, then show whether the dividend is supported from harvest proceeds or from cash accumulated in another season.

sections.heading: Safaricom: split recurring telecom cash from network and market-entry investment
sections.text:
Start with the FY2026 results booklet and the segment and cash-flow notes [5, 16]. Keep Kenya and Ethiopia separate where disclosure allows. Reconcile service revenue, mobile money and data, voice and other income, operating cost, EBITDA, cash from operations, capex, leases, tax and debt. Customer growth is a volume measure; it is not a cash measure until activity is monetized, service costs and partner shares are paid, and customers or agents settle.

For the mature Kenyan business, estimate network renewal and expansion by radio access, core systems, fibre, towers, spectrum, IT and mobile-money systems. For Ethiopia, separate the rollout and customer-acquisition phase from the established operation; currency translation, network investment and startup losses can dominate group trends. Test capex cuts against coverage, capacity, quality and future traffic. A low-capex year could temporarily lift free cash while delaying replacement. Mobile-money float and customer funds are not company cash available for dividends simply because the platform processes large transaction values.

sections.heading: BAT Kenya: taxes, volume pressure and distributions must be reconciled
sections.text:
BAT Kenya's audited FY2025 result reports net revenue of KES 23.192 billion, down 10%; operating profit of KES 7.475 billion; profit before tax of KES 7.671 billion; net cash from operating activities of KES 6.642 billion; and total dividend of KES 70 per share [6, 17]. Its reported 18% growth in pre-tax profit occurred alongside declining net revenue, lower operating cost and a shift in finance result. The investor should separate operating performance from currency or treasury effects and identify whether cost reductions are repeatable without damaging the revenue base.

Rebuild gross sales, excise and VAT, net revenue, operating cost, working capital, tax, capex and cash distributions. Excise and VAT are not operating profit, but their timing and compliance obligations matter to cash. Compare volume, price, product mix and domestic versus export sales; model the effect of continued volume decline and the contribution of alternative products separately. The KES 7.0 billion dividend is higher than KES 5.246 billion of FY2025 profit after tax, so the analysis should ask whether it is supported by retained cash, prior-year earnings or another capital source. The cash-flow statement reports KES 6.642 billion of operating cash before investing and financing, but total owner cash still depends on capital needs and the timing of the payout [17].

sections.heading: Home Afrika: a signed sale or presale is not yet distributable cash
sections.text:
Read Home Afrika's 2025 integrated report, consolidated statements, project schedule and 2026 half-year publication as dated documents [7, 18, 19]. Build a separate cash bridge for each development: opening land and work in progress; completed units; signed reservations and sales; customer deposits collected; remaining construction and infrastructure spend; borrowing and interest; expected handover; refunds or cancellations; and final collection. Determine which entity owns each parcel, project, receivable and debt. A group-level sales headline can hide cash trapped in a subsidiary or a project with a large completion obligation.

For each unit or phase, compare expected net proceeds with cost to complete and the time until cash is unrestricted. Check land title, approvals, contractor claims, security interests, customer rights, service charges and any presale escrow restrictions. An unsold parcel may be valuable but does not automatically fund payroll or a shareholder dividend. Likewise, customer deposits can be a useful financing source but remain linked to delivery and refund obligations. Use the half-year report to see whether promised completion milestones turned into handovers and collections, not just whether reported revenue increased.

sections.heading: Put the companies on one page without forcing a common formula
sections.text:
A cross-sector table should compare the questions, evidence and unresolved risks—not multiply unlike earnings by one shared ratio.

| Issuer | Core calculation | Cash or capital constraint | Primary refresh trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equity Group | Normalized equity earnings less capital needed for loan growth and stress losses | Eligible capital, funding mix and asset quality | Cost of risk, restructurings, buffers, dividend |
| Jubilee | Insurance service and investment earnings after claims and solvency retention | Regulated capital, reserve quality and reinsurance | Claims development, reserve changes, subsidiary solvency |
| KenGen | Cash from existing generation after renewal, debt and committed projects | Plant availability, off-taker collection and construction spend | Outage, receivable delays, cost overrun or project delay |
| Kakuzi | Crop cash after seasonal operations and orchard renewal | Harvest, grade, shipping, weather and working capital | Yield, quality, export acceptance, shipment route |
| Safaricom | Equity cash after network renewal, lease service and market investment | Spectrum, rollout, power, retention and currency | Service monetization, churn, capex intensity, market ramp |
| BAT Kenya | Cash after regulated taxes, working capital and replacement investment | Volume, illicit competition, input and tax timing | Sales decline, margin, cash conversion, payout funding |
| Home Afrika | Cash collected by project after cost to complete and secured obligations | Construction, title, cancellations, debt and liquidity | Handover, collection, approvals, litigation, refinancing |

The first output is therefore not a league table saying which issuer has the most “owner earnings.” It is seven dated bridges with source links and a clear record of what remains unmeasured. Then the analyst can compare valuation and expected return within the right capital structure. A bank may be best evaluated with a residual-income or dividend-capacity model, a developer with project-level net cash realization, and a utility with operating assets and project funding. Ohlson's framework and the peer-reviewed evidence on working capital, bank valuation and replacement capital support careful method selection rather than a single cross-sector shortcut [8–11].

sections.heading: How to use this casebook in an investment meeting
sections.text:
For each company, one participant should present filed facts, a second should challenge the cash bridge, and a third should test the downside scenario. End with a short decision record: what is repeatable, what must be reinvested or retained, which claim ranks ahead of ordinary shareholders, what the share price implies, and which new evidence would change the view.

An analyst should be willing to say “not yet estimable” for a specific component while still completing the rest of the work. For example, Home Afrika's public numbers may support a project cash schedule but not a reliable collection date; Kakuzi's crop cycle may be visible while orchard renewal cost is still poorly split; Safaricom's total capex may be reported while a clean maintenance allocation is not. Name the missing source and its likely impact. The workbook can then preserve a useful range and a research task rather than inventing precision.

sections.heading: A repeatable issuer-review workflow
sections.text:
The casebook can be used as a quarterly research process rather than a one-time comparison. For each issuer, follow the same sequence while allowing the economic bridge to differ:

1. Freeze the information set. Save the report and announcement, publication date, fiscal period, entity scope, currency and unit. Do not mix a later press release with an earlier market-price date in a backtest.
2. Transcribe reported facts. Enter statement and note values with the page number and original label. Reconcile the cash, debt, equity, earnings and share-count roll-forwards where possible.
3. Build the sector bridge. Use retained capital for a bank; claims and solvency for an insurer; asset renewal and projects for a utility; crops and harvest cash for agribusiness; network renewal for telecom; taxes and volume for manufacturing; and project cost-to-complete for property.
4. Mark assumptions and gaps. Label each number as filed, calculated, analyst-estimated, or unresolved. Use a range where evidence supports a range; leave a component unavailable when no evidence supports even a range.
5. Run one joined downside. Choose a plausible operating story and connect it to margin, working capital, capex, funding, capital retention and per-share cash.
6. Write a decision note. State valuation method, current price date, required return or margin of safety, key risk, position size or wait condition, and the next filing or event that could change the estimate.
7. Review the prior call. Compare the last forecast with actual cash, capital, projects, claims, volumes and collections. Record what changed and why.

The sequence creates comparability in source quality and review discipline, not in the underlying company formula. A well-prepared research page can show that the greatest uncertainty is disclosed maintenance spending for one company, credit migration for another, and project collection timing for a third. That difference is itself a useful conclusion.

sections.heading: Common analytical errors across sectors
sections.text:
Several mistakes recur even when the companies are very different. First, analysts compare a calendar year with a fiscal year or parent-only results with consolidated results without noting the mismatch. Second, they treat a press-release measure as if it were an audited cash-flow line. Third, they compare a dividend per share with group net income while omitting payout date, tax, new shares or capital requirements. Fourth, they use EBITDA as a proxy for owners' cash before accounting for debt service, working capital, capex and leases.

A fifth error is to call a one-year increase in cash flow recurring. A favorable movement in receivables, inventory or payables can reverse; an asset disposal can create a large one-off receipt; lower maintenance can defer a bill rather than eliminate it. A sixth error is to use segment profit as though it were distributable. Segment results may not include central cost, tax, financing, minority interests, holding-company obligations or cash restrictions.

A practical response is to build a bridge from the measure most often quoted to the measure relevant to owners. For a bank, bridge reported earnings to retained regulatory capital and payout. For Jubilee, bridge insurance service and investment outcomes to parent cash and subsidiary solvency. For KenGen, bridge profit through plant renewal, projects, working capital and debt. For Kakuzi, bridge biological and crop results to harvest receipts and seasonal funding. For Safaricom, bridge service revenue through network and market investment. For BAT Kenya, bridge operating cash after excise, tax, working capital and dividend. For Home Afrika, bridge project revenue through cost to complete, debt and collected cash.

sections.heading: Research quality and source hierarchy
sections.text:
Peer-reviewed research helps discipline the method, but it should not substitute for issuer facts. Ohlson's model makes clear that earnings and book value matter within explicit valuation assumptions [8]. Barth's work shows that disclosures on financial instruments can be relevant to bank valuation [9]. Kieschnick, Laplante and Moussawi study the relationship between working capital management and shareholder wealth [10]. Livdan and Nezlobin examine how non-geometric depreciation changes investment and replacement-cost analysis [11]. These studies provide frameworks and empirical results in defined samples; none supplies a universal owner-earnings answer for the seven Kenyan companies.

For each claim, prefer an audited report, statutory filing, regulatory return or court record where available. Use a company announcement for the date and terms of a proposal, then check the final filed statement for recognition and cash movement. Use a media report to locate a development or understand context, but identify when the underlying primary document has not been reviewed. A chart or table copied into a presentation should keep the source and exact reporting period.

The peer review should ask whether the source supports the specific sentence, not only whether the source is reputable. If a source says that revenue rose, it does not prove a positive cash conversion. If a report gives capital investment, it does not prove all spending was growth. If a court judgment summarizes an administrator's report, distinguish the summary from an audited statement.

sections.heading: Make the next research action visible
sections.text:
Every workbook row marked unresolved should have a named next action and an estimated decision impact. For example: “Request project-by-project maintenance capex; current base estimate is 20% of total capex and value changes materially if replacement spending is higher”; or “Obtain statutory capital by insurance subsidiary; parent payout model is incomplete without it.” The team should set a due date or an event trigger, not leave the cell as a vague open question.

A comparison across sectors becomes more useful when it reveals where better evidence would change a decision. It should show the owner where cash is earned, where it must stay, when it may become available, and what could prevent it from arriving. The casebook is a guide to those questions, not a contest to rank seven unlike businesses on an artificial common metric.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Project 2 workbook contains a dated evidence matrix for Equity Group, Jubilee, KenGen, Kakuzi, Safaricom, BAT Kenya and Home Afrika. Each row retains its own period, units, measures and source ID; the KenGen capital-investment-to-PAT ratio is calculated from its reported inputs. Evidence Vectors expands populated figures into observation-level records, separates fiscal year-end from publication date (including KenGen's June year-end), fills the missing Equity Group source ID, and leaves Home Afrika's project metrics unpopulated rather than zero. The Profile Stress sheet adds a separate normalized scenario for each of these seven NSE profiles and for NVIDIA and Equinix in the US cases. For example, a crop-yield shock increases seasonal working-capital pressure for Kakuzi, while a customer-collection delay and completion-cost overrun create a funding gap in the fictional Home Afrika profile. Those indices are teaching scenarios, not issuer estimates or a cross-sector ranking. Appendix 04 reproduces all nine assumptions and outputs. The matrix and stress sheet support source selection and issuer-specific questions; neither pretends every issuer already has a complete owner-earnings bridge.

articles.title: The retrospective method
questions: Which warning was visible at the time rather than only after the outcome?
What do Nakumatt and Tuskys records establish about retail cash-cycle stress?
What can Twiga and Copia legal and funding records show, and what remains unknown?
articles.workbook_name: Project 3 - Failure Retrospectives and Warning Systems.xlsx

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

After a company fails, its final crisis can make the ending seem obvious. That feeling is dangerous. The reader now knows which supplier went unpaid, which loan fell due, and which rescue did not arrive. A lender or owner three years earlier did not know those outcomes with certainty.

Fischhoff’s peer-reviewed experiments found that knowledge of an outcome changes how people judge its prior likelihood and how they remember what they knew before [1]. A failure retrospective should therefore keep two timelines: the public information that existed at each decision date, and the later information revealed in administration, court proceedings or liquidation.

sections.heading: Start with the decision date
sections.text:
For every important claim, record:

| Field | Retrospective question |
|---|---|
| Claim | What was said or assumed? |
| Entity | Which legal company, facility, subsidiary or brand does it concern? |
| Information date | When could a decision-maker first have known it? |
| Source date | When was the underlying record created, published or filed? |
| Source class | Audited accounts, contract, court, administrator, company statement, media report, or analyst estimate? |
| Time status | Contemporaneous at the decision date, later disclosed, or unknown? |
| Result | What can this document establish and what can it not establish? |

A leaked presentation may be contemporaneous but unaudited. A court judgment is authoritative about what the court decided and can summarize a party’s submissions, but a party’s claim in a judgment is not automatically a proven fact. An administrator report may give the best available later view of creditors or assets, but it is not what an investor necessarily knew at the earlier date. A media article can help locate a primary document without replacing it.

sections.heading: Rebuild the event sequence before assigning causes
A warning system is a conversation, not a score
Test against false alarms and missed cases
sections.text:
Every warning system produces false alarms and misses. If we only study companies that failed, we will not know which warning signs were common among businesses that recovered. Define the event first: late payment, breach, administration, court liquidation order, insolvency filing, business closure, or owner exit? These are not one outcome. Select a forecast horizon, preserve cases that survived, and disclose the limits of the sample.

A legal process is also not an operating diagnosis. Administration can be used to pursue a rescue or better outcome for creditors; it does not mean liquidation has already occurred. A company under administration may continue operating, restructure or sell assets. A liquidation order is a different legal milestone. State the exact event and source.

sections.heading: The practical retrospective test
sections.text:
For every major alleged cause, ask:

1. What is the strongest primary record for it?
2. Was the record available before the event or only after it?
3. Is it describing cash pressure, accounting performance, contractual default, or a legal outcome?
4. Are there plausible alternative explanations?
5. Would the proposed early warning have been visible to an owner with ordinary records at that time?
6. Did it produce a decision soon enough to matter?

If a claim cannot pass this test, label it as a hypothesis or unresolved question. A good retrospective does not need a villain or a single ratio. It needs to show what was observable, what action could reasonably have followed, and where the evidence runs out.

sections.heading: From an indicator to an owner decision
sections.text:
A useful warning sheet has four parts: the measurement, its trigger, the owner of the response, and the time available to act. “Receivables are rising” is only an observation. A more useful statement is: “The three largest overdue invoices are now KSh 1.8 million, equal to six weeks of payroll; the credit lead will call the buyers today, pause new exposure above the approved limit, and refresh the cash forecast on Friday.” The amounts and thresholds must come from the business’s own records and obligations. The example illustrates the form of a decision, not a universal safe limit.

Separate leading indicators from outcomes. A supplier asking for cash on delivery, a lost credit line, or a new covenant waiver can precede a missed payment. A bounced payment, court petition, or administration appointment is usually a later outcome. A retrospective should ask whether the earlier signal was visible, whether it was recorded, and whether anyone had authority and time to respond. If no one was assigned the decision, a technically accurate dashboard may still have had no practical value.

The forecast itself needs a short, honest horizon. A weekly cash schedule can list opening unrestricted cash, confirmed customer receipts, committed purchases, wages, rent, taxes, debt service and a minimum operating reserve. Put uncertain receipts in a separate column with a probability or evidence note; do not quietly treat a sales promise as cash. Run a base case and one or two adverse cases, such as a key customer paying two weeks late or a supplier withdrawing terms. The point is not to predict the exact failure date. It is to find which assumption would force a decision first.

After each review, preserve the forecast version and the actual result. Compare the amount and date of expected receipts and payments with what happened. This reveals whether repeated errors came from late customer data, optimistic sales assumptions, unrecorded obligations, or a genuinely unpredictable event. A warning system should improve its inputs and ownership as well as its thresholds.

sections.heading: What a retrospective can fairly conclude
sections.text:
A sound account distinguishes a mechanism from proof of causation. If a retailer has a large overdue supplier balance, that can indicate a cash squeeze and can threaten replenishment. To claim that the arrears caused closure, however, we would need evidence about timing, the supplier’s response, other financing, store economics and plausible alternatives. When documents show sequence but not the counterfactual, write “consistent with” or “may have contributed,” then say what evidence would decide the issue.

This restraint does not make the analysis timid. It helps owners act on claims they can verify: cash dates, inventory ageing, customer concentration, contract renewals, debt maturities and who controls payment access. It also makes cases comparable. A company with an administration order, one with a missed loan payment and one that closed without a formal filing should not be counted as identical failures merely because a news article used the word “collapsed.”

sections.heading: Build the case file so someone else can reproduce the timeline
sections.text:
A retrospective becomes practical when it can be rebuilt from records rather than memory. Start a case register with one row per legal entity, trading name, facility or material business unit. Record registration number if available, ownership, trading period, jurisdiction, administrator or liquidator, court case number, and whether the entity continued trading. Add a relationship map that distinguishes parent, subsidiary, shareholder, lender, supplier, brand and asset owner. A shared name or director does not prove that two companies had the same cash or liability.

Then create an evidence ledger. Each item should include source title, publisher or custodian, source date, date it became public, period covered, entity, page or paragraph, evidence type, exact claim supported, limitations, and a link or file path. Preserve a short excerpt or factual note rather than copying pages of text. A judgment may establish that the court made an order on a date and may summarize a report. It does not automatically independently verify every allegation quoted from a party. A press release can show what management claimed at the time. A later administrator report may show what records were available after control changed. Those sources answer different questions.

Use four confidence labels:

 Established by primary record: the document directly states the fact, such as a court order date or an audited balance.
 Attributed statement: a named person or report made the claim, but the underlying evidence is not independently available.
 Analyst reconstruction: a value is calculated from stated inputs using a visible method.
 Open question: the available record does not support a conclusion.

These labels prevent a neat narrative from flattening different evidence into one voice. They also help later researchers identify the missing page or file that would upgrade a tentative claim.

sections.heading: Keep a reporting vector, not a headline number
sections.text:
A row containing “KES5.2bn, 2021” is not enough to plot a trend or compare it with a later balance. The amount needs a reporting vector: the legal entity; the measure; amount and unit; period or date the measure covers; date of the underlying event; date the record was prepared; date the record became public; source and page; and status as a filed fact, attributed claim, calculation or estimate. Add the retrieval date so a later researcher can identify which version was checked. Store “not stated” in a missing field. Do not borrow a date from another column to make a blank look complete.

The Nakumatt court record shows why. A ruling delivered on 11 March 2021 summarized an administrator update prepared on 1 February 2021. The administrator was reported to have raised KSh5,218,737,409; more than KSh3.5bn had been paid to creditors, including KSh766,641,309 to landlords [8]. Those are three distinct measurements. The landlord payments sit inside the creditor-payment description, so adding them would double count. The court summary does not provide a transaction-level schedule, the full period covered by “raised,” or individual receipt and payment dates. The report date cannot be treated as the date that all the money was raised or paid.

In the ledger, write the first amount as an administrator-reported cumulative figure with its coverage period marked unknown. Record the second as a lower bound, not an exact KSh3.5bn. Record the landlord amount as an included component, not a fourth cash flow. Give each a source locator and a separate date the court made the summary public. A chart should either show these as dated report observations—with a label that the underlying period is unknown—or keep them out of a transaction-timing series. It should never place the full amount on 1 February merely because that is the report date.

This simple discipline is useful for investor rounds, debt facilities, court claims and operating results alike. A financing announcement, signed agreement, close, drawdown and bank receipt are separate states. A judgment can repeat a petitioner's claim without converting it into an admitted liability. A reported annual figure has a financial period that may end months before publication. The Evidence Vectors sheet in the workbook is designed to keep those dates and evidence states visible; the article uses its rows only for the claim each source can actually support.

sections.heading: Rebuild cash pressure month by month where the record permits
sections.text:
Annual accounts are often too coarse to show the order in which a business ran out of options. If monthly management accounts or bank statements are available, calculate unrestricted cash by week or month, collections, payroll, critical supplier payments, statutory obligations, debt service and owner injections. Reconcile opening to closing bank cash and identify restricted, pledged or client money. If only annual figures exist, do not invent monthly runway; show the broad annual trend and identify the missing data.

A private-company runway should be based on an operating cash forecast, not a headline cash balance divided by recent monthly burn. A cash balance may include customer deposits, restricted funds, borrowed money or proceeds from an asset sale. Burn can change with seasonality, launch spending, a large stock purchase, collections and creditor terms. Reconstruct the period's movement first. Then calculate how much cash remained after obligations already due and after committed spending.

For each period, separate operating receipts from financing. New equity, debt, grants, owner advances, supplier credit and asset-sale proceeds are different sources with different claims. A new round can extend runway without improving gross margin or contribution. A facility can delay default while increasing future repayment pressure. A supplier extension can preserve cash now while leaving an overdue payable. The article should say what the financing achieved and what risk it moved forward.

When only balance-sheet snapshots are available, estimate a broad range and state the assumptions. The lower bound might include confirmed cash and known immediate obligations; the upper bound might include uncollected receivables only to the degree supported by subsequent receipts and exclude disputed claims. Do not label the result “runway” without a time horizon and a burn rate consistent with the cash scope.

sections.heading: Separate early warnings from late outcomes
sections.text:
An owner can use a warning system only if the indicator arrives early enough for an action. Classify each indicator as leading, coincident or lagging. A weekly fall in minimum forecast cash may be leading. A supplier reducing terms can be an early signal or a routine renegotiation. A returned payment is a serious event but may already be late. A court petition or administration appointment usually belongs in the event chronology, not the early-warning dashboard.

For each signal, test the operational chain:

1. What changed in the underlying evidence?
2. Who received the information and on what date?
3. Who had authority to act?
4. What realistic action was available then?
5. How long would that action take to affect cash?
6. Did the business have enough time and capacity to carry it out?

This chain matters because dashboards do not rescue companies by themselves. A sales manager may know that a major account is disputing invoices but lack authority to stop new credit. A founder may know a loan is coming due but wait because the lender gave a verbal assurance. A board may receive a forecast after an irreversible order has been placed. The retrospective should test the organization around the indicator, not only the indicator.

sections.heading: A practical example: a cash warning that was actionable
sections.text:
Imagine a fictional food distributor, Coastal Supply Ltd. At the end of March, it has KSh 6.0 million of unrestricted bank cash, KSh 12.0 million of invoices due from customers over the next month, payroll of KSh 2.4 million, supplier commitments of KSh 5.0 million, tax of KSh 0.8 million, and debt service of KSh 1.2 million. The 13-week forecast shows a minimum balance of KSh 0.3 million in week five. One customer owes KSh 4.0 million, has disputed delivery of two orders and historically pays 30 to 45 days late.

The warning is not simply that cash is “low.” It is that the forecast relies on a specific disputed KSh 4.0 million receipt before supplier and payroll payments fall due. The owner can ask the customer to confirm accepted delivery, send proof of delivery, collect the undisputed portion, negotiate a partial payment plan, pause further credit above an approved exposure limit, and discuss a staged supplier payment before the due date. The company can also defer a discretionary equipment purchase if doing so does not create a safety or reliability risk.

At the next review, compare each action with cash outcome and customer contribution. If the customer pays the undisputed amount but disputes the rest, update future credit terms and the cash forecast. If the supplier accepts a documented schedule without penalty or lost supply, record that. If the company freezes all customer orders and loses a profitable reliable account, the warning response has protected cash at too high a cost. A practical system evaluates decisions by their effects on cash, gross contribution, service, legal obligations and relationships.

The fictional example illustrates response design only; it is not a factual account of a Kenyan company or a universal threshold. A real case should use the source ledger to show when the owner knew the dispute, whether the cash forecast existed, and what alternatives were contractually and operationally available.

sections.heading: Test whether the warning would have survived a false-alarm review
sections.text:
After a failure, an analyst can easily identify many signals that looked ominous in hindsight. The challenge is to ask whether the same measure would have produced too many false alarms among businesses that survived. Use both failed and continuing companies where the data allow. Preserve the cases that recovered, refinanced or changed strategy. Record firms that faced late customers, supplier pressure or high leverage but did not fail. This lets the researcher distinguish a risk factor from a deterministic cause.

Define the unit of analysis and outcome before counting cases. A company can miss a payment but remain in business; an entity can enter administration while stores continue operating; a brand can disappear while the legal company is still under a process; a founder can sell the business without insolvency. Do not combine these into one “failure” label without explaining the choice.

If the sample is small, avoid fitting a complex statistical model. Use a case table and document the observable pattern. If the researcher does estimate a threshold, report the number of cases, time period, data missingness, look-ahead bias, false positive rate and missed-case rate. Shumway's hazard-model approach is relevant because distress risk changes over time and covariates can vary [2]. Campbell, Hilscher and Szilagyi use public-market and accounting signals in a different sample and separate distress from returns [3]. These are methodological reference points, not plug-in coefficients for local private firms.

sections.heading: From retrospective findings to an operating control
sections.text:
The final product should translate each credible warning into a control that a living business can use. A control needs a measure, source, frequency, threshold, response owner, action, deadline and escalation path. For instance, “largest overdue receivable exceeds the amount the 13-week forecast can absorb” can trigger a same-day collection review, credit approval pause for additional exposure, and customer escalation. The threshold derives from actual liquidity and contractual terms rather than a generic industry ratio.

Match the action to the warning type. A collection problem may require document repair or customer contact. A margin problem may require SKU-level contribution analysis and repricing. Inventory ageing may call for a clearance or purchasing hold, but not if the inventory is a critical spare or a confirmed seasonal product. Refinancing risk needs a lender pack months before maturity. Governance and key-person risk may require dual bank access, succession documentation or board escalation.

Record the decision and review date. If an exception is overridden, write who approved it, why, what evidence supports it, when it expires and what would reverse the decision. A control that can be overridden silently is not a reliable warning system.

sections.heading: A fair retrospective has a useful ending
sections.text:
Close each case with four statements:

 What the public record establishes: dates, orders, filed balances, named appointments or disclosed payments.
 What the record suggests but does not prove: mechanisms consistent with stress, such as rising overdue creditors or cash-consuming growth.
 What remains unknown: monthly cash, contract terms, inventory realizability, owner withdrawals, related-party exposure or lender negotiations.
 What a similar owner can do now: forecast low cash, age receivables and stock, schedule maturities, document decision rights and test alternate actions.

The value is in giving an owner a practical early action while preserving the limits of the evidence. This approach avoids both hindsight certainty and vague caution: it says what could have been measured, what decision might have followed, and what outcome should be tracked to learn whether the intervention worked.

sections.heading: Preserve the analyst's own decision record
sections.text:
A complete retrospective also records what the analyst recommended, what evidence was missing, how confident the estimate was, and what later event would have changed the view. This allows a team to distinguish a weak operating signal from a reasonable judgment made with incomplete information. The purpose is to improve the next cash forecast and response, not to reward hindsight for predicting an outcome that was unknowable at the time.

A retrospective should also state the decision boundary. A credible warning may justify calling a customer, pausing a new commitment or seeking advice without proving that insolvency was inevitable. The article should distinguish an operating intervention from a legal conclusion, then note when the evidence became sufficient to escalate.

The strongest output is a dated record that says what was knowable, when the response could still help, and what later evidence changed the interpretation. That record lets an owner act promptly without turning a warning into a verdict.

The review closes with a specific update condition: name the filing, cash report, court document or operating measure that would change the current view, and schedule when to check it. That keeps the retrospective useful after publication.

The outcome note should also say who will check the next record and by what date. A signal that no one owns can be obvious in hindsight and useless in the moment.

A future update should preserve the earlier data cut while adding new administrator reports, judgments or recoveries as later evidence. This makes the chronology auditable instead of rewriting the past with information learned afterward.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Project 3 workbook includes a legal-entity register, decision-date timeline, evidence ledger, funding-raised register, fictional 13-week cash and CCC case, warnings and actions, and Sources and Checks. Evidence Vectors separates underlying event date, source-record date and public judgment/report date, while identifying whether an entry is a legal fact, administrator/creditor claim, secondary report, calculation, scenario or gap. It separates court-recorded claims from analyst sums and secondary reporting. The cash model is a teaching example, not historical company cash flow, and the warning sheet asks for a company-specific trigger, owner, action and response time rather than a universal failure score.

sections.heading: Technical appendices
sections.text:
The worked calculations and source boundaries below extend this article's examples. They keep assumptions and unresolved inputs visible so readers can reproduce the steps without mistaking an illustration for an issuer or sector estimate.

- Appendix 01 - A reproducible retrospective and warning test
- Appendix 02 - Court-record evidence, entity boundaries and open claims

articles.title: Nakumatt and Tuskys: two retail distress records
articles.short_title: Nakumatt and Tuskys: two retail distress records
questions: Which warning was visible at the time rather than only after the outcome?
What do Nakumatt and Tuskys records establish about retail cash-cycle stress?
What can Twiga and Copia legal and funding records show, and what remains unknown?

sections.heading: Opening
sections.text:
Revised practical article; source details and figures are dated to their cited filing or event, with current evidence reviewed through 24 September 2026.

Nakumatt and Tuskys are often discussed together as Kenyan supermarket failures. They are useful cases for asking what went wrong in a cash-intensive retail model, but their court records do not tell one interchangeable story. Each had its own legal company, creditor list, financing, operating history, and process. A retrospective that treats both as one event loses the facts that matter to an owner or lender.

The first step is to identify the legal entity behind each brand:

 Nakumatt Holdings Limited was placed under administration by a High Court order on 22 January 2018, according to the court’s 2021 ruling [1].
 Tusker Mattresses Limited operated the supermarket chain using the Tuskys name, according to the High Court judgment of 31 May 2023 [2]. That judgment issued an interim liquidation order and appointed a provisional liquidator.

Administration and liquidation are different legal stages. Administration can be used to pursue a rescue or a better outcome for creditors. Liquidation involves winding up the company under the applicable process. One company’s status cannot be inferred from the other’s.

sections.heading: What the Nakumatt court record says
sections.text:
In March 2021, the High Court considered the administrator’s update report dated 1 February 2021. The judgment states that the administrator reported having raised KSh 5,218,737,409 and paid more than KSh 3.5 billion to creditors, including KSh 766,641,309 to landlords [1]. It then summarizes the administrator’s belief that Nakumatt had no property that might allow a distribution to creditors, while debts and legal cases remained to be managed. The court extended the administration to allow the administrator to carry out tasks in the report and disapplied parts of the statutory process.

This is an important distinction. The court’s summary of the administrator’s report is evidence of what the report stated. It is not a complete audited cash-flow history for the retailer. The judgment does not tell us what the business’s average cash conversion cycle was in each pre-administration year, what every asset sold for, or the final recovery received by each creditor. Nor does the reference to “no property” mean that all legal claims had ended. The court allowed administration to continue because matters remained to be managed.

For an owner, the practical question is what records would have shown the pressure before the court process: store-by-store contribution after rent and logistics, inventory ageing and shrinkage, supplier days, rent arrears, customer/supplier settlement timing, borrowing maturity, and uncommitted cash. The case materials reviewed here do not provide a complete contemporaneous data set for each of those measures. The article should not invent one.

sections.heading: What the Tuskys judgment says
sections.text:
The May 2023 judgment consolidated three creditor petitions. The petitioners stated that Tuskys owed them KSh 248,220,797.38, KSh 11,284,096.50, and KSh 30,892,518.92 respectively [2]. Those are amounts claimed by the petitioning creditors, not automatically the total amount ultimately owed to every creditor. The court considered the company’s response and the period in which it had been given an opportunity to restructure. The judge concluded that the company had failed to demonstrate a viable prospect of maintaining solvency, allowed the petitions, issued an interim liquidation order, and appointed a provisional liquidator.

The judgment is a strong source for that legal outcome and the positions placed before the court. It should not be used to state an exact recovery for all suppliers or workers. A later 2025 ruling in the insolvency matter records the interim liquidator seeking additional time to engage a forensic auditor and complete the statement of affairs [3]. A request in court is not the same thing as the final result of an audit or a completed liquidation. Any article published later should check for subsequent court orders and the liquidator’s latest report.

sections.heading: The working-capital questions retail owners can use
The retrospective boundary
sections.text:
The public court records establish significant distress, creditor claims, and different legal outcomes. They do not let us confidently attribute each company’s decline to one cause, calculate its last normalized owner earnings, or estimate what shareholders would have recovered without the insolvency file and full statements of affairs. Company history, store closures, family ownership or debt headlines can suggest questions. They are not a substitute for audited accounts, contemporaneous management records and administrator reports.

A warning model could preserve the timing of changes rather than classify each retailer from one isolated year; hazard models are one approach used in public-company distress research [6]. That literature does not supply a ready-made threshold for Kenyan supermarkets. A rigorous next stage would request or locate the relevant audited statements, administrator reports, creditor statements, insolvency orders, and any liquidator statement of affairs. Then an analyst could build a timeline using only contemporaneous information up to each warning date and compare it with what the later record revealed. Until those records are compiled, the right finding is bounded: these retail companies entered severe distress; the court records support particular dated legal and creditor facts; detailed pre-failure cash-flow causation remains unresolved.

sections.heading: How to turn the cases into a testable retail review
sections.text:
A board or lender reviewing a supermarket should put the operating statements next to the cash calendar. Start with sales by store and category, then subtract landed product cost, promotions, shrinkage, payment costs, delivery and store-level payroll. Rent, central distribution and head-office costs need an explicit allocation rule. A store can report positive gross profit and still consume cash after rent, utilities, security and logistics. Conversely, a new store may be temporarily cash-negative while reaching a viable sales base; the records should show whether the ramp was planned and funded.

For inventory, compare purchase receipts with point-of-sale sell-through, age stock by product and store, and mark damaged, expired or slow-moving items separately. For payables, reconcile supplier statements to the ledger and contract terms; an unpaid invoice is not automatically an agreed extension. For rent, list arrears and the next contractual dates by location. Then combine the figures in a weekly forecast that includes payroll, tax, debt payments and realistic supplier settlement dates. These records would help test a cash-cycle explanation. They cannot be imputed to Nakumatt or Tuskys without their underlying data.

Consider a clearly hypothetical store: it earns KSh 10 million in monthly sales, but its gross margin falls by two percentage points while rent and payroll remain fixed. The first response should not be “cut inventory” in the abstract. Management would check whether the margin decline comes from discounts, category mix, supplier cost, waste or pricing; then estimate the cash effect of each action. A blanket stock cut could worsen availability and sales. The useful warning is the bridge between a measured change, its likely cause, and the option that preserves positive contribution.

sections.heading: A dated evidence ledger for the public cases
sections.text:
The next researcher can make the court-record work reproducible with one row per assertion. Record the quoted statement, the named speaker, legal company, document date, court or administrator status, and whether the amount is a claim, an estimate, a payment, or an adjudicated liability. Keep a separate “known by decision date” view. Nakumatt’s 2021 ruling summarizes a 2021 administrator update; that is valuable evidence of the later process, but not a substitute for a 2016 or 2017 management forecast. The Tuskys petition amounts belong to the petitioners’ assertions as summarized in a 2023 judgment; they should not be added and labelled as all company debt.

A strong later version could connect those ledger rows to audited statements, lease schedules, borrowing documents, inventory records, administrator reports and the liquidator’s statement of affairs. It could then test competing explanations: weak store economics, working-capital stress, financing constraints, governance, or some combination. Until those documents are located, the responsible result is an evidence-bounded comparison of two legal proceedings, not a ranking of which retailer failed “worse.”

sections.heading: Compare the records without turning them into one story
sections.text:
Nakumatt and Tuskys help an owner study two parts of retail distress: the operating cash cycle and the legal process that follows when obligations cannot be met. The materials currently cited show different formal proceedings and different windows into the companies. Nakumatt entered administration in January 2018; the 2021 ruling later summarized an administrator update, creditor payments and tasks that remained [1]. Tusker Mattresses faced consolidated creditor petitions and a 2023 interim liquidation order; a 2025 ruling later recorded the interim liquidator's request for time to engage a forensic auditor and complete the statement of affairs [2, 3].

The distinction changes what a reader can safely infer. A court record may identify the entity, procedural stage, dates, creditor claims and directions. It may not provide a clean history of every store's economics or all claims admitted. A later request for forensic work suggests that the financial reconstruction was still in progress at that point; it does not tell us what the final report concluded. A retrospective should update the status when a later court order or liquidator report becomes available, while keeping earlier statements in their original date context.

The two records should therefore be kept in separate case folders. Do not combine petition amounts, administrator receipts, store counts, assets or creditor recoveries unless each source establishes that they cover comparable scopes. Do not treat the same brand, supplier or landlord as proof that the legal estates are the same. If a creditor traded with both companies, record each contract and claim against the correct entity.

sections.heading: Reconstruct the retail engine from transactions
sections.text:
Retail operates on thin timing margins. The store collects quickly from many shoppers but pays a series of suppliers, landlords, employees and logistics providers. The gap can provide low-cost operating finance when the supplier terms are agreed and sustainable. It can become a source of distress when stock turns slow, invoices are disputed, terms are shortened or overdue amounts accumulate.

For a retailer with adequate records, calculate an approximate cash conversion cycle:

 Inventory days: average inventory divided by cost of goods sold, multiplied by the period's days.
 Receivable days: average trade receivables divided by credit sales, multiplied by the period's days.
 Payable days: average trade payables divided by purchases on credit, multiplied by the period's days.
 Cash conversion cycle: inventory days plus receivable days less payable days.

The ratios are only diagnostic. Use the same entity, period and accounting basis. If credit sales or supplier purchases are not disclosed, explain the proxy. A supermarket with substantial till sales may have a very low receivable balance, while a wholesaler can have a long customer collection cycle. Trade payables must be compared with credit purchases, not automatically with cost of sales, especially when inventory and purchases are changing quickly.

Imagine, purely as an operating example, a retailer that sells KSh 20 million each week, incurs KSh 17 million of weekly product cost, holds KSh 68 million of average stock and owes suppliers KSh 51 million for purchases on 30-day terms. Inventory is about four weeks of cost and payables are about three weeks of cost. Even before rent, payroll, taxes, shrinkage and other obligations, roughly one week of product cost is tied up in the cycle. If slow lines rise by KSh 10 million, supplier terms fall from 30 to 14 days, and rent is due before the weekend's receipts settle, the liquidity gap can widen sharply without an immediate decline in reported annual revenue.

The example is not a claim about Nakumatt or Tuskys. It shows why a yearly profit number is not enough to reconstruct a retailer's cash position. For each month, an analyst would want daily or weekly cash receipts, supplier due dates, inventory receipts and sales, store-level contribution, rent schedule, payroll and borrowing. Where those records are absent from the public file, the article should present the measurement design and state that case-specific attribution remains unknown.

sections.heading: Distinguish profitable sales from cash-consuming growth
sections.text:
A retailer can grow sales by adding stores, extending credit to wholesale customers, widening the assortment or discounting to increase basket size. Each choice changes cash needs. A new location creates deposits, fit-out, opening inventory, staff and rent before reaching a stable volume. A promotion can lift sales and still destroy contribution if discount, handling and shrinkage exceed the incremental margin. More SKU variety can improve customer choice but increase slow stock and replenishment complexity.

A store-level contribution report should start with net sales after discounts and returns, then subtract landed product cost, direct store payroll, payment fees, packaging, delivery, shrinkage, utilities and rent. Show central distribution and head-office allocation separately so that the reader can see the allocation rule. Then compare the store's contribution with opening costs, refurbishment and working-capital requirements. If a location is consistently negative, decide whether it is in a funded ramp period, strategically necessary, or structurally uneconomic. Avoid allowing a profitable flagship to conceal chronic losses at another site.

Category analysis should follow margin and cash turn together. A fast-selling item with a small contribution can still be valuable if it brings customers who buy higher-margin products; a high-margin product may be poor cash if it sits for months or spoils. Track gross contribution per shelf or unit of inventory, markdowns, write-offs, returns, promotions, stock-outs and supplier rebates. Verify that rebates are earned, collectible and not already netted against purchase cost.

sections.heading: Map supplier arrears and landlord exposure precisely
sections.text:
A payable schedule should separate current invoices, invoices within agreed terms, disputed amounts, overdue invoices, supplier advances and balances under a signed rescheduling agreement. Reconcile supplier statements to the general ledger and obtain confirmations for the largest balances. A payment delay is not automatically an agreed extension. If the business has exceeded terms, identify which suppliers have stopped deliveries or changed from credit to cash on delivery.

For landlords, list location, legal lessor, rent due date, arrears, deposit, service charges, renewal, break rights, guarantee and any court or termination notice. Store closure may reduce future cash burn but trigger lease claims, employee costs, stock transfers and customer disruption. Compare the cost of closing with the cash contribution and exit obligations of continuing. A retailer that delays rent may preserve immediate liquidity while weakening its ability to keep the sites essential to its sales network.

The accounts payable and lease files also matter to a failure retrospective because they reveal the order of events. If a supplier first requested payment, later stopped deliveries and only then filed a claim, each date belongs in the timeline. If a landlord petition states an amount, record it as a claim until there is an adjudicated or agreed balance. Never turn an aggregate creditor claim into an exact measure of the company's total obligations without evidence.

sections.heading: Use a weekly rescue review before a legal crisis
sections.text:
An owner or board facing a cash squeeze should meet weekly with finance, merchandising, operations and collections. The first page is a 13-week cash forecast with unrestricted opening cash and named receipts by expected date. The second page lists stock by ageing and criticality, suppliers whose terms changed, rent or tax obligations due, debt maturities and orders that require a deposit. The meeting then decides which spending can be stopped, which collections need escalation, which suppliers require a transparent schedule, and what financing or restructuring conversation must begin.

Every action should be tested for its effect on total economics:

 Will a purchasing freeze prevent stock-out of high-contribution items?
 Will a promotion convert slow inventory into cash after discount, fees and returns?
 Does a supplier extension have written consent and preserve supply?
 Does a location closure save rent and payroll after exit and relocation costs?
 Does a new loan finance a defined recovery or only postpone recurring losses?
 Does new equity or an owner injection fund a viable operation or meet old arrears without a turnaround plan?

The board should establish approval limits and a named person who can update the forecast. If the same owner controls sales, purchasing, supplier setup and payment, add independent review of bank reconciliations, supplier master changes and large disbursements. Weak cash controls can hide error and fraud as well as ordinary timing problems.

sections.heading: What the case evidence can and cannot teach
sections.text:
The court materials in this article establish dated legal findings and attributed financial claims; they do not provide the monthly transactional records needed for a complete operating model [1–3]. Peer-reviewed studies of working capital and SME profitability support examining receivable, inventory and payable policies, but their samples and settings do not identify the cause of either Kenyan retailer's distress [4, 5]. Shumway's hazard model shows why distress analysis should consider timing and changing variables rather than classify a company from one annual ratio [6]. The practical lesson is to build a time-aware reconstruction from primary records before deciding whether growth, governance, credit, supplier terms or store economics was decisive.

A useful conclusion can be both bounded and practical: the legal records show that two major supermarket entities reached formal distress processes; their cash-cycle drivers are testable; and the cited public materials do not yet establish a full pre-distress monthly cause-and-effect story. A retailer can use the dashboard, cash forecast, entity map and source ledger now. A researcher can update the historical account when the official statement of affairs or a later court order becomes available.

sections.heading: A more useful cash comparison than a final-year headline
sections.text:
A disciplined retailer analysis would compare at least three levels of evidence. First, store and category contribution explains whether sales covered direct product, service and location costs. Second, the group cash bridge explains whether the business funded stock, rent, staff, tax and debt on time. Third, the insolvency record explains what the administrator or liquidator later reported about assets, claims, payments and remaining tasks. A strong result at one level does not answer the other two.

A final-year profit can include noncash valuation movements or accruals, while a final-year cash receipt can come from new debt, sale proceeds or a temporary supplier stretch. A retailer with a negative operating contribution cannot be rescued indefinitely by delaying invoices. But an unpaid supplier balance alone does not tell us whether the stores could have been viable with new equity, a sale, fewer locations or better purchasing terms. The retrospective needs both an operating and financing counterfactual.

A case table can make that boundary plain:

| Question | Evidence that would answer it | What the public judgments cited here establish |
|---|---|---|
| Were stores contributing after rent and direct costs? | Store-level management accounts and lease schedules | Not available in the cited rulings |
| How large and old was inventory? | Stock ledger, counts, write-offs and administrator valuation | Not a complete SKU or age profile |
| What was owed to creditors? | Verified statement of affairs, admitted claims and security | Particular claims and administrator-reported payments, not a universal final balance |
| What cash arrived from asset or store disposals? | Bank records and administrator realization statement | Some administrator-reported collections for Nakumatt; not a full disposition ledger |
| What could owners have changed earlier? | Contemporaneous forecasts, board records, contracts and supplier terms | Not established by the court summaries alone |

The table helps a reader distinguish a limitation of public evidence from a claim that the records do not exist. A further research step is to obtain or locate the administrator's update reports, liquidation statements, audited accounts and formal creditor schedules, then match each to the correct proceeding.

sections.text: The Project 3 workbook keeps Nakumatt Holdings and Tusker Mattresses separate in Case Register and Timeline. Evidence Ledger preserves what the court records as administrator-reported receipts, creditor payments and petition claims; the three Tuskys petition amounts sum to KSh290,397,412.80, but they are claims in the consolidated petitions, not a complete verified creditor total. Evidence Vectors distinguishes Nakumatt's administrator update date (1 February 2021) from the later judgment date (11 March 2021), records the unknown Tuskys claim-balance date, and flags that KSh3.5bn in creditor payments is a lower bound. Retail Review is a fictional store example also used here: KSh10m monthly sales, 28% gross margin, KSh7.2m cost of goods, KSh1.8m direct payroll and KSh1.2m rent/utilities yield negative KSh200,000 contribution before other costs. Its KSh2.5m average stock less KSh2.2m payables leaves KSh300,000 of modeled stock funding. Neither result reconstructs Nakumatt's or Tuskys's historical accounts.

articles.title: Twiga and Copia: funding, legal entities and what the record can show
articles.short_title: Twiga and Copia: funding, legal entities and what the record can show
questions: Which warning was visible at the time rather than only after the outcome?
What do Nakumatt and Tuskys records establish about retail cash-cycle stress?
What can Twiga and Copia legal and funding records show, and what remains unknown?
