articles.title: What kind of money was raised?
articles.short_title: What kind of money was raised?
questions: What do the headline total, funding breadth and concentration each measure?
How do equity, debt and asset-linked funding change what a business must earn or repay?
What happened after funding, and what evidence is needed to establish investor recoveries or losses?
articles.workbook_name: Startup Funding Market and Outcomes Workbook.xlsx

sections.heading: Debt is not automatically bad capital, and equity is not automatically patient capital
sections.text:
Suppose two Kenyan companies each announce that they raised KSh 500 million. The headline makes them look comparable. One may have sold new shares to fund product experiments with no fixed repayment date. The other may have taken a secured, dollar-linked facility to finance equipment that pays for itself through customer instalments. A third possibility is that a lender announced a commitment that the company has not fully drawn. Those are three different events, with different cash claims and different risks.

That is why the debt-versus-equity discussion matters. The 2025 tracker data cited in Part 1 say Kenya’s funding included $582 million of debt and $383 million of equity, with debt close to 60% of the published amount [1]. The annual summary describes large energy companies as key drivers. The mix tells us something about the instruments recorded in that dataset. It does not tell us which firms received which terms, how much was disbursed, whether the debt financed assets or operating losses, or which capital was best for the borrower.

The practical question is not “Is debt worse than equity?” It is: Does the instrument match the asset, cash-flow timing, currency and uncertainty it is financing? If a founder cannot answer that with dates and a downside case, the company may be accepting capital that makes next quarter’s cash problem worse.

sections.heading: First translate the label into a contract
sections.text:
“Debt” can mean a bank loan, overdraft, invoice facility, equipment lease, asset-backed securitization, convertible note, venture loan or supplier credit. They do not have the same repayment source or seniority. “Equity” can mean ordinary shares, preferred shares, a convertible instrument that later becomes shares, or a fund investment made through a holding company. Grants may be restricted to a specified programme, milestone or recipient. The word in a press release is only the starting point.

For each transaction, write down eight things:

1. Who provides the capital and who legally receives it? A parent and an operating subsidiary may be different borrowers.
2. What is the legal instrument? Read the signed agreement, not just a press release label.
3. What amount is available, and when? Separate announced, committed, signed, closed, drawn and cleared cash.
4. What does it cost? Include interest, fees, arrangement costs, warrants, currency hedges, default charges and any preferred return.
5. What claims does the financier have? Identify security, guarantees, seniority, covenants, information rights and voting control.
6. What activity is funded? Inventory, equipment, customer receivables, research, payroll, expansion, refinancing or a combination.
7. What cash flow or next event repays it? Name the receipts, sale, refinance, grant milestone or future equity round.
8. What happens if that source arrives late or not at all? Map default, dilution, restructuring, asset seizure, waiver, extension or shutdown options.

A single transaction can combine several instruments. A company may draw a secured line, issue preferred shares and receive a grant during the same quarter. Add them into one “funding raised” headline only after recording the amount, date and status separately. Otherwise readers cannot tell which cash remains available and what claims follow it.

sections.heading: Debt can fund an asset. It can also borrow from a future that never arrives
sections.text:
Debt is useful when the borrower can forecast cash receipts well enough to service principal and interest under a conservative case. Asset finance may fund solar equipment, a vehicle fleet, inventory with contracted buyers or invoices from creditworthy customers. The lender may look primarily at the asset, receivable pool, customer collection history, sponsor support and enforceability of contracts.

That structure is different from an early-stage software venture raising equity to test a product that has not yet found repeatable demand. The latter may have valuable intangible assets but no predictable monthly cash. A scheduled repayment can force a premature sale, aggressive customer collections or spending cuts that undermine the experiment. Equity can absorb more variation, but it dilutes founders and investors and may introduce governance rights or a preferred return.

The Africa: The Big Deal data show why debt labels need more detail: the 2025 Kenyan total was heavily shaped by energy and asset-financing activity [1]. A facility connected to energy equipment could be economically sound and repayable even when it is not the type of venture capital often imagined in startup discussions. Conversely, a large facility can create concentrated risk if the company’s customer payments, imported equipment and debt service are denominated in different currencies.

Public transaction announcements can illustrate structure without giving every term. Sun King has disclosed debt and securitization arrangements involving development-finance and commercial partners [2]. A disclosed transaction can show that a capital market exists for a particular asset pool. It does not reveal the rate, repayment waterfall or remaining cash position of every company described as “solar finance.” To estimate those, we need the original agreement or a detailed issuer disclosure.

sections.heading: A worked debt case: check the first payment before celebrating the round
sections.text:
Assume an equipment distributor borrows KSh 100 million for 24 months at 18% nominal annual interest. It repays equal principal each month. This is an invented example; it is not a current Kenyan facility offer. Equal monthly principal is KSh 100m ÷ 24, or approximately KSh 4.167m. If interest is charged monthly at 1.5% of opening principal, first-month interest is KSh 1.5m and first-month total debt service is about KSh 5.667m.

| Month | Opening principal (KSh m) | Principal due (KSh m) | Interest at 1.5% (KSh m) | Scheduled service (KSh m) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 100.000 | 4.167 | 1.500 | 5.667 |
| 2 | 95.833 | 4.167 | 1.438 | 5.604 |
| 3 | 91.667 | 4.167 | 1.375 | 5.542 |
| 12 | 54.167 | 4.167 | 0.813 | 4.979 |
| 24 | 4.167 | 4.167 | 0.063 | 4.229 |

Across the 24 months, the simple model produces approximately KSh 18.75m of interest and KSh 118.75m total principal plus interest, before fees, taxes, legal costs, arrears charges or hedging. The calculation assumes the lender uses a 1.5% monthly rate on a declining balance and that the borrower pays on time. A real contract may use another day-count convention, a flat rate, fees, a grace period, balloon repayment or different payment dates.

Suppose the financed portfolio generates KSh 6.2m of monthly cash available for debt service after necessary operating cost, tax, maintenance, collection cost and working-capital need. First-month coverage is 6.2 ÷ 5.667 = 1.09 times. If collections are 20% below plan, available cash falls to KSh 4.96m, and coverage becomes 4.96 ÷ 5.667 = 0.88 times; the monthly shortfall is about KSh 707,000. The measure is illustrative, not a recommended covenant. A lender’s agreement defines its own DSCR, permitted add-backs and test periods.

The borrower should now ask: do customers actually pay before the loan due date? Are the receivables enforceable? Will the portfolio require replacement equipment or servicing? Are taxes and collection losses included? Does the debt currency match the customer cash currency? Is there a reserve for late payments? The financing may be viable if the debt tenor matches asset receipts and the stress is manageable. It may be dangerous if the investor relies on the next equity round to cover every scheduled payment.

sections.heading: Equity buys a different kind of time, at a price
sections.text:
Equity does not require scheduled principal repayment, which can give an uncertain business room to test demand. But it is not free. The investor receives ownership, voting or information rights, and often contractual protections that affect future financing and a sale. A preferred-share class may have priority over ordinary shares in a sale or liquidation. A founder may be diluted in future rounds, option-pool expansions or conversions.

A basic dilution calculation keeps the pre-money and post-money values distinct. If an investor puts KSh 30m into a company at a KSh 120m pre-money valuation, post-money valuation is KSh 150m. The new investor owns 30 ÷ 150 = 20% on the simplified fully diluted basis. Existing holders collectively fall to 80%, before any option-pool increase, earlier convertible conversion, liquidation preference or later round. This arithmetic does not say whether KSh 120m is fair; it shows what the stated price implies.

A founder should read the whole term sheet: class and seniority of shares; liquidation preference and participation; anti-dilution; board and observer rights; protective provisions; founder vesting; option pool and who bears its creation; information rights; reserved matters; pro-rata rights; transfer restrictions; exit and drag/tag rights; and conditions precedent. “We raised $10m” does not tell the reader whether the company sold 10% or 40%, whether the investor has a guaranteed multiple on exit, or how much money is left after a secondary sale or debt repayment.

Equity is often described as “patient,” but the fund behind it has its own life, return target, governance model and follow-on capacity. A fund may encourage a rapid growth path because its portfolio is built around outcomes where a small number of very large exits drive returns. That can fit a scalable business with improving unit contribution. It can conflict with a slower route to profitability or a company whose investors cannot provide the next round. The founder should ask who will fund the next milestone and what evidence that decision will require.

sections.heading: Convertible notes, SAFEs and “we will decide later”
sections.text:
A convertible instrument can postpone setting a valuation, but it does not remove the economic terms. Review the principal, interest, maturity date, valuation cap, discount, conversion trigger, qualified-financing threshold, repayment or extension options, most-favoured-nation clause and treatment at a sale or shutdown. Model several conversion prices with the existing option pool and earlier notes included. A low cap combined with a discount can give an investor a larger share than a founder expects from the headline cheque.

A SAFE or similar future-equity contract may not accrue ordinary interest or have a maturity in the way a conventional note does, but it still creates a future claim on ownership. Kenyan legal treatment, tax and foreign-law governing provisions should be reviewed by qualified counsel. Never label a convertible as plain equity before conversion or plain debt without checking repayment rights and local enforceability.

A company may also have several bridge instruments outstanding. If every investor expects the next round to convert them, one delayed equity close can create a maturity wall or negotiation over waivers. The cash forecast should list actual due dates and legal claim priority, not just a single “funding balance.”

sections.heading: Grants and blended finance have restrictions and reporting obligations
sections.text:
A grant can fund a public-benefit pilot, customer affordability programme, research milestone or market entry where a purely commercial investor would not yet fund the activity. It usually does not give the grantor ordinary ownership. But grants often restrict eligible costs, require matching funds, set delivery milestones, allow audits and require repayment or clawback if conditions are not met. An award announcement does not equal unrestricted cash.

Blended finance can combine grants, concessional debt, commercial loans, guarantees and equity to share risks. That can bring a new service to customers or make a capital asset financeable. The analytical question is whether each tranche has a clear purpose and whether the business can continue after a subsidy ends. Count the grant on the date it is received and usable. Do not include a pending reimbursement in current cash unless the claim is accepted and payment timing is supported.

For founders, keep a grant register with agreement date, amount, currency, eligible budget, disbursement milestones, matching requirement, reporting date and restricted balance. If a grant pays for a pilot but salaries or customer acquisition continue afterward, include the post-grant cash requirement in the base plan. A successful pilot is not the same as a funded operating model.

sections.heading: Asset finance, securitization and receivables funding
sections.text:
Asset finance uses an identifiable asset or pool of cash flows to structure the repayment. A company may borrow against equipment, lease vehicles or sell/pledge future receivables through a securitization. The facility may sit at a special-purpose vehicle rather than the brand customers recognize. The investor, servicer, originator and legal borrower can be different entities.

A receivables facility should be tested against the pool's quality and the cash waterfall: eligible invoice rules; customer concentrations; payment delays; dilution from returns or disputes; first-loss reserve; servicing fees; overcollateralization; collection account control; recourse; and conditions that stop new borrowing. If customer collections fall below the assumed loss rate, the borrowing base may shrink just as the company needs more working capital.

Asset-backed finance can be more suitable than ordinary venture equity for a mature receivable pool. It can also leave the operating company with less flexible cash and a new set of covenants. A founder should build three schedules: assets originated or sold; collections by customer cohort; and facility draws and repayments. Do not infer the rate or risk-sharing terms from a transaction headline.

sections.heading: Match currency and tenor to cash receipts
sections.text:
Currency mismatch is a real financing cost even when the interest rate looks low. If a company earns shillings but owes dollars, a shilling depreciation can increase the shilling value of principal and interest. If revenue is in dollars but payroll and suppliers are in shillings, that mismatch may work differently. Record the currency of each significant revenue stream, input cost, debt, lease, customer installment and bank balance.

Tenor matters as much as rate. A 12-month facility financing an asset that pays back over three years creates refinancing risk. A five-year facility for inventory that turns in 60 days may be unnecessarily expensive. Map scheduled repayments to the cash-conversion cycle and useful life; model first payment, grace-period end, balloon and covenant test dates. Put the downside cash trough beside the repayment schedule.

A simple currency stress can be framed without forecasting exchange rates: recalculate debt service under a 10%, 20% or 30% adverse movement, using the actual exchange rate at the model date and clearly labeling the shock as a scenario. If the company has a natural hedge or a forward contract, document notional, tenor, collateral, rollover and counterparty limits. The shock is a resilience check, not a prediction.

sections.heading: What the research says—and what it does not say about Kenya
sections.text:
Robb and Robinson examine capital-structure choices among new US firms using the Kauffman Firm Survey and show that external debt, especially business debt, was more prominent in startup finance than a venture-capital-only story would imply [4]. Cole and Sokolyk find that in their US startup sample, firms using business debt at startup were more likely to survive and have higher revenue three years later than all-equity firms, while personal debt did not show the same pattern [5]. Those are observational results in defined datasets. More creditworthy firms may be more likely to obtain business loans, so the estimates should not be read as proof that debt causes survival or that the same results hold in Kenya.

Berger and Udell describe how small-business financing changes across firm growth stages and how private debt and equity markets serve different information and risk profiles [3]. De Rassenfosse and Fischer study venture-debt lenders and report the importance of venture backing and intellectual property in lender decisions in their US lender survey [6]. These studies are helpful for framing a due-diligence conversation. They do not establish terms available to Kenyan borrowers or the repayment performance of African solar portfolios.

A funding article should therefore use peer-reviewed research to explain possible mechanisms, then use contracts and cash records to analyze named transactions. The local deal tracker describes transaction amounts and instruments; it does not substitute for a borrower’s loan agreement, bank statement or audited financials.

sections.heading: A practical capital-fit scorecard
sections.text:
A founder and investor can review each financing offer with six tests:

| Test | Green evidence | Question that should stop the decision |
|---|---|---|
| Use | Specific asset, milestone or receivable pool | Is the stated use actually allowed under the agreement? |
| Repayment or return | Named cash source or milestone | Does repayment depend on a new round the borrower cannot control? |
| Currency | Revenue and obligation aligned or hedged | Who absorbs a material FX move? |
| Tenor | Due dates match customer collections or asset life | Does the first repayment arrive before cash generation? |
| Downside | Cash forecast includes slower collection, lower sales and cost overrun | Who funds the shortfall and by what date? |
| Control and claims | Ownership, security, preference and governance understood | Can the contract remove operating flexibility needed to recover? |

If two or more answers are unknown, the next action is not necessarily to reject the offer. It is to request the agreement, model, legal-entity map and repayment schedule before accepting it. If the provider will not disclose a material term, record that limitation rather than assuming the most favorable version.

sections.heading: Compare instruments with the same capital need
sections.text:
To see why debt and equity should not be ranked by a single “confidence” label, hold the cash need constant. Imagine the equipment distributor needs KSh 100m for a two-year portfolio. Under the invented debt terms above, scheduled repayment totals about KSh 118.75m over two years, assuming the company pays on time and incurs no extra fees. The lender has no ordinary ownership in the upside, but may have security and default rights. Under a simple equity alternative, the company could issue 20% for KSh 100m at a KSh 400m pre-money valuation, producing KSh 500m post-money. If the company later sold for KSh 1bn and no other dilution, preference or transaction cost existed, that shareholding would correspond to KSh 200m of gross value; if the business failed, equity could be worthless.

Those numbers are not comparable returns. Debt receives a contracted claim and is exposed to default and recovery; equity receives a residual claim and is exposed to dilution, valuation and exit timing. The debt also requires cash on specific dates; the equity may require governance concessions and future rounds. A founder comparing the two should model company value and cash under several outcomes, not compare the interest percentage with the projected exit multiple as if both were certain.

A useful financing decision asks whether the funded activity can produce a return that exceeds the full financing cost after operating risk, taxes, downtime, losses, collection costs, currency changes and working capital. If the project generates cash after the first debt payment but not before it, the long-run return may be positive while the company still defaults in month one. Equity can bridge that timing gap, but if the enterprise has little chance of reaching the next milestone, new shares may simply postpone a necessary decision. The right mix is specific to the asset and forecast.

sections.heading: Capital needs change as the business learns
sections.text:
At idea stage, the founder may be financing research, incorporation and a prototype. At pilot stage, the company pays for customer tests and early delivery before repeat economics are known. At scale, it may finance inventory, receivables, hiring, infrastructure and expansion. At each stage, the uncertainty and cash cycle change. A line of credit that is useful after recurring invoices exist may be unsuitable before any customer contract has been delivered.

This does not mean startups must follow a fixed sequence from grant to angel to venture capital to debt. A profitable trading business may use customer deposits and trade credit from the beginning. A climate hardware company may need equipment finance when it has signed offtake. A deep-technology venture may require equity for a long research cycle. A platform with fast growth but slow collections may need working capital even after it has raised a major equity round. The funding source should follow the cost and risk being financed, not a fundraising chart in a pitch deck.

For each planned raise, the board should distinguish four needs: cash to keep the current service reliable; cash to fund growth that has positive incremental contribution; cash to cover losses while a product or market is tested; and cash to refinance or settle old claims. Those uses should not be hidden under “working capital.” If equity is paying old debt, say so. If a new facility is financing inventory required by a signed contract, identify the invoice and collection schedule. If the company is funding an unproven market test, decide in advance what evidence ends the test.

sections.heading: The questions to ask when a company announces a round
sections.text:
When reading a funding announcement, use it as a prompt for seven concrete follow-ups:

- Is the amount the headline size, the signed commitment, the cash drawn or the cash cleared in the operating bank account?
- Does the named investor provide all the money or participate in a syndicate with conditions?
- Is the legal borrower or share issuer the same entity that employs staff, sells to customers and owns the financed asset?
- Does the capital add new cash to the company, refinance an older lender or purchase shares from an existing investor?
- What is the exact currency, disbursement calendar and restriction on use?
- What monthly cash obligation, ownership dilution, liquidation preference or reporting duty follows?
- Which customer, asset, grant milestone, refinance or later round repays or justifies the capital?

The answers will often be private. In that case, the responsible article can state what the announcement identifies and what remains unavailable. A source gap does not mean the instrument is bad; it means the reader cannot judge its fit yet. The company can improve its own capital planning by building this transaction ledger before the next announcement, because the same fields help reconcile a board forecast, a bank covenant and a future investor's due diligence.

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Startup Funding Market and Outcomes workbook contains the worked schedules discussed here. Instrument Guide separates equity, loans, asset finance, receivables finance, convertibles, grants, supplier credit and customer advances. Debt Service schedules a hypothetical KSh100m, 24-month equal-principal loan at 18%: principal totals KSh100m, base interest KSh18.75m and scheduled repayment KSh118.75m before fees. Its combined stress raises the rate to 23% and cuts monthly CFADS from KSh6.2m to KSh4.96m; first-month stressed DSCR falls to about 0.82. Equity Dilution reproduces KSh30m at KSh120m pre-money as 20% ownership and the separate KSh100m/KSh400m pre-money illustration. Deal Ledger remains blank until a named transaction's legal recipient, instrument, timing and receipt are evidenced. Appendix 02 reproduces the formulas and tells the reader why debt service and equity value are not equivalent returns.

articles.title: What happened after the raise?
questions: What do the headline total, funding breadth and concentration each measure?
How do equity, debt and asset-linked funding change what a business must earn or repay?
What happened after funding, and what evidence is needed to establish investor recoveries or losses?

sections.heading: Follow the company, the cash and the legal claim separately
sections.text:
A social post says 13 Kenyan startups “collapsed after raising” a combined Sh93 billion. The sentence feels conclusive: large funding, failed companies, money gone. But it puts three questions into one label. Which legal entity received the financing? What happened to each business and its operating companies? What money, if any, did investors or creditors recover? Without those answers, the total is not a failure rate or an investor-loss figure.

The screenshot’s 13 amounts do add to KSh 93.31 billion, which rounds to Sh93 billion [1]. The five largest items add to KSh 75.7 billion, or about 81.1% of that selected list. That calculation is useful for understanding the list’s internal concentration. It does not verify the amounts, establish a national funding share or prove a loss. The post supplies no underlying deal ledger, transaction status, currency-conversion dates, legal recipients or source methods beyond “MoneyAcademyKE.”

This article gives the list a more practical treatment. It separates financing events from operating outcomes, gives each legal entity its own dated status, and shows what records would be needed to estimate recovery. It also explains why a company can raise a large amount and still run out of cash—and why an adverse outcome does not prove that every earlier investment decision was irrational.

sections.heading: “Raised” has several possible meanings
sections.text:
A funding story can refer to an amount announced in a press release, a signed term sheet, a committed facility, a closed transaction, cash drawn, or funds that cleared into the company’s bank account. Those stages can be months apart. A credit facility may have a maximum commitment but permit drawings only against eligible assets. A multi-tranche equity round may close in stages. A grant may be awarded subject to milestones. A public amount may include capital invested in subsidiaries, assets acquired in a transaction or a refinancing that pays an older creditor.

For each company, record the financial event in a transaction ledger rather than one cumulative headline:

| Field | Why it changes the conclusion |
|---|---|
| Investor, lender or grantor | Identifies who supplied the capital and whether it was related-party support |
| Legal recipient and borrower | Separates a brand from the entity that owns the cash, asset or obligation |
| Instrument and priority | Distinguishes common/preferred equity, loan, convertible, grant, lease, supplier credit and customer advance |
| Announcement, signing, close and cash dates | Prevents an announced commitment from becoming a false cash receipt |
| Amount and original currency | Preserves the transaction before any conversion or rounding |
| Drawdown and repayment | Shows how much debt was used and how much principal was returned |
| Security, guarantees and maturity | Identifies claims ahead of shareholders and possible founder exposure |
| Use of proceeds and restrictions | Distinguishes new operations, asset purchases, refinancing and secondary share sales |
| Source and verification level | Separates filed or signed evidence from company statements, reporting and social claims |

When totals are converted to Kenyan shillings, keep the original currency and the exchange rate/date beside the converted value. Translating a US-dollar round at today’s exchange rate can be a valid illustration of current scale. It is not the amount of cash received in Kenya at the time. If a US-dollar figure was announced but paid in several tranches, use the cash receipt dates and rates for the cash-flow record.

sections.heading: “Collapsed” is not one company status
sections.text:
A company may continue selling after a funding round ends. It may close one country operation while trading elsewhere, restructure debt, sell assets, merge with a competitor, enter administration, be liquidated, or cease operations without a formal insolvency process. These outcomes matter differently to employees, customers, lenders, investors and suppliers. They should not be collapsed into a single “failed” category.

Use a status table with exact company names and dates. Keep at least two fields: operating status and legal process. “Trading” is an operating status. “Under administration” is a legal process. A company can trade during administration; an entity can cease activity without liquidation. The legal status of a parent does not automatically determine the status of every subsidiary, and a brand can outlive the original corporate entity.

A source can also be accurate but too broad for a company-level claim. Financial Sector Deepening Kenya (FSD Kenya) reported in 2024 that several prominent firms, including Sendy, Swvl, WeFarm, Copia Global, iProcure and Gro Intelligence, had either closed, entered administration or exited Kenya; it separately described MarketForce, Twiga Foods and Wasoko as facing cash shortages, downsizing, restructuring or pursuing mergers [2]. That groups several outcomes together. It does not tell us which exact status applies to each company at every date. The report is valuable context, but company-level assertions still need dated primary records.

sections.heading: What can be said about the 13-company list today?
sections.text:
The table below records the screenshot’s claimed amounts as leads. It deliberately does not treat them as verified funding received. The outcomes are bounded by the public materials identified in the source capture and verification ledger.

| Company as displayed | Screenshot amount | Current public-evidence treatment |
|---|---:|---|
| Twiga Foods | Sh24.10bn | September 2026 reporting names GT Flow Limited and Templar Field Limited as separately under administration; official notices and the claimed funding aggregate still need direct verification [8] |
| Copia | Sh16.00bn | Kenya Gazette notice appoints administrators to Copia Kenya Limited in May 2024; the amount and investor recovery are unreconciled [3] |
| Gro Intelligence | Sh15.30bn | Included in FSD Kenya’s group of firms that closed, entered administration or exited Kenya; the report does not assign the exact category here [2] |
| Koko Networks | Sh13.00bn | Amount and entity-level outcome remain unverified in the supplied evidence bundle |
| Mobius Motors | Sh7.30bn | Amount and dated legal/operating outcome require primary company and transaction records |
| MarketForce | Sh5.50bn | FSD Kenya describes MarketForce among companies that downsized, restructured or pursued mergers; exact entity, date and result need verification [2] |
| WeFarm | Sh4.20bn | Included in FSD Kenya’s combined closed/administration/exit group; exact outcome is not allocated there [2] |
| Sendy | Sh3.20bn | Included in FSD Kenya’s combined closed/administration/exit group; the legal entity and recovery records remain open [2] |
| iProcure | Sh2.20bn | Included in FSD Kenya’s combined closed/administration/exit group; exact process and claim perimeter need verification [2] |
| Lipa Later | Sh2.20bn | Funding amount, legal borrower and dated outcome remain unresolved in the source bundle |
| Kune Foods | Sh0.13bn | Funding amount and current legal/operating status require primary verification |
| Zumi | Sh0.13bn | Funding amount and company outcome need transaction-level and entity-level sources |
| Notify Logistics | Sh0.05bn | Funding amount, recipient and outcome remain unverified |

The amount column is in KSh billions and comes from a screenshot, not audited filings. The table does not claim that the listed firm itself received every shilling: an investor may have funded a parent, foreign holding company, project vehicle or separate operating subsidiary. It also does not imply that the company still owes all financing or that an investor recovered nothing.

The distinction is visible in the Twiga example. The September reports cited in the research materials refer to GT Flow Limited (formerly Twiga Foods One Limited) and Templar Field Limited (formerly Twiga Foods Limited) as separate companies. One report describes an administration effective in August 2026; another describes a September board appointment. The underlying Gazette notice and administrator communication have not both been directly verified in this package [8]. The responsible wording is attribution to the report, with an open primary-source check. Even if the appointments are confirmed, they do not by themselves establish that every entity using the Twiga name entered administration or that all investor claims are unrecoverable.

Copia provides a stronger primary-record example. The Kenya Gazette of 31 May 2024 states that administrators were appointed to Copia Kenya Limited [3]. A ruling delivered on 23 April 2026 is available here only as a secondary reproduction; it reports that the court granted a two-month extension to the administrators, although they had sought six months [4]. I did not locate the ruling on Kenya Law during this check. Treat the term extension as a dated, secondary-reported court outcome, not proof of Copia's status after that order or of any creditor's final recovery. The Gazette appointment identifies an entity and process; it does not tell us the company's pre-administration cash economics or final creditor waterfall.

sections.heading: Recalculate what the screenshot actually proves
sections.text:
The 13 listed amounts sum to Sh93.31bn. The top five entries—Twiga, Copia, Gro Intelligence, Koko Networks and Mobius—sum to Sh75.70bn. The ratio is:

Sh75.70bn ÷ Sh93.31bn = 81.13%.

That proves only the arithmetic relationship among the 13 displayed claims. It says nothing about national venture funding because the list is selected around firms described as collapsed, mixes outcomes, covers more than one financing period and uses an unverified currency conversion. It is a sample chosen after adverse events, not a complete list of all funded startups. A high concentration among the largest failed firms may be interesting, but it cannot estimate the probability that a funded Kenyan startup fails.

FSD Kenya listed dollar-denominated funding claims for nine companies in a 2024 discussion: Twiga $195m, Wasoko $144m, Gro Intelligence $125m, Copia Global $120m, Swvl $100m, MarketForce $42.5m, WeFarm $32m, Sendy $26.5m and iProcure $17.2m [2]. These amounts sum to $802.2m. FSD describes the firms collectively as having raised over $800m and cites several commercial databases and media sources. That arithmetic is a check of FSD’s displayed entries, not a second audit. It differs in companies, currencies, source date and classification from the screenshot’s Sh93.31bn list; the two should not be converted and compared without original round schedules and common FX dates.

The task is not to find a single “correct” cumulative number by averaging lists. It is to build an event-level record and show the range of transactions confirmed, attributed or unresolved. If the list includes a loan that was refinanced, count the original loan and refinancing as separate financing events but do not treat both as new cash available for operations. If it includes a secondary share purchase, distinguish the seller’s proceeds from capital injected into the company. If a facility was never drawn, do not add its full committed amount to cash received.

sections.heading: Raised capital is not the same as investor loss
sections.text:
A company can raise KSh 1bn in equity, spend part on product and payroll, return some assets, sell a subsidiary, raise a later round and eventually enter administration. An equity investor’s realized result depends on the amount actually paid in, any distributions or secondary-sale proceeds, final share value and transaction costs. A creditor’s result depends on allowed claims, priority, security, costs of the process and distributions from the borrower’s estate. The national funding amount is neither result.

For an investor, a simple realized equity measure is:

Realized cash loss = cash invested − cash distributions − net proceeds received on share sales or liquidation.

This is not a complete investment return. It ignores timing, follow-on contributions, taxes, fees, FX and unrealized value. For an annualized return, use dated cash flows and a clearly defined valuation date. If the company remains under administration, the shareholder value may be unresolved rather than zero.

For a creditor, a simple recovery ratio could be:

Recovery rate = cash distributions received ÷ allowed claim amount.

The numerator should identify whether it is principal, interest, collateral proceeds or a compromise. The denominator should distinguish secured and unsecured claims and state the date. A petition amount is not automatically an allowed claim; a court judgment may record what a party asserted without finally adjudicating every amount. A company’s “raised” sum cannot be substituted for the creditor denominator.

The Nakumatt court record gives a useful example of source status. A 2021 ruling summarizes an administrator report stating that KSh 5,218,737,409 had been raised and more than KSh 3.5bn paid to creditors, including KSh 766,641,309 to landlords [5]. The “raised” amount is what the administrator reportedly stated about the process, not a full audited annual cash-flow series. The landlord amount is included within the reported creditor payments; adding it again would double count. These are valuable case facts, but not a final recovery rate for every claimant.

The Tuskys judgment offers another arithmetic test. Three petitioners stated claims of KSh 248,220,797.38, KSh 11,284,096.50 and KSh 30,892,518.92 [6]. Their sum is KSh 290,397,412.80. It remains the sum of three petitioners’ claims, not total company debt or final creditor loss. The later ruling identifies Tusker Mattresses Limited as in liquidation and discusses a liquidator’s request for time to conduct a forensic audit and file a statement of affairs [7]. That request is not the completed audit result.

sections.heading: A raise can extend runway without fixing unit economics
sections.text:
Funding can pay payroll, marketing, inventory or debt service for a period. Whether that extends a viable business depends on contribution, collection timing and the cost of serving customers. Take a fictional delivery route: it invoices KSh 100,000 of sales, spends KSh 66,000 on goods, KSh 14,000 on delivery and handling, and KSh 8,000 on customer support and payment costs. Contribution is KSh 12,000 before hub rent, central staff, financing, vehicle replacement, tax and growth spending.

If customer cash arrives 45 days after delivery but suppliers require payment in 15 days, the route can show positive contribution while consuming working capital. More orders may improve route density and reduce cost per delivery; more orders can also deepen the cash gap if customers pay late or new inventory must be purchased in advance. Equity can finance that experiment without a fixed monthly repayment, but only if management sets a test period and stop criteria. A receivables facility could finance accepted invoices, but only if the terms and customer quality support the borrowing base. Neither instrument creates contribution by itself.

An investor reviewing a company after a raise should trace the “sources and uses” schedule: opening cash; cash received by date; restricted proceeds; operating receipts; inventory and supplier payments; payroll and customer acquisition; capex; debt service; and closing unrestricted cash. Then ask which metrics changed after the financing: gross contribution per order, returns, retention, collections, service quality, staff productivity and cash required per unit of growth. If all that is available is a fundraising headline and an administration notice, the right conclusion is that the operating bridge remains unknown.

sections.heading: What peer-reviewed research adds to the retrospective
sections.text:
Venture-capital funding cycles can affect both the quantity and the type of ventures funded. Janeway, Nanda and Rhodes-Kropf review research on VC booms and busts, including evidence that capital supply, sector concentration and investor incentives can affect the kinds of firms selected and the terms offered [9]. Nanda and Rhodes-Kropf’s study of investment cycles finds that firms initially financed in more active periods were more likely to go bankrupt but successful firms also had stronger innovation and exit outcomes [10]. The sample is US venture-backed companies. It does not prove that a Kenyan funding boom caused any company in this list to fail. It does caution against using either funding abundance or funding scarcity as a direct measure of company quality.

Shumway’s hazard-model research demonstrates why financial distress is a time-to-event problem rather than a single ratio observed once [11]. Fischhoff’s work on hindsight bias is relevant when analysts revisit a company after a public administration or closure [12]. Once an outcome is known, earlier expansion, hiring or fundraising decisions can look more obviously reckless than they did to people acting with partial information at the time. A fair analysis saves the information set by date, then separately adds later records.

The work of the case study is not to excuse management or investor choices. It is to identify the mechanism supported by evidence: a missed customer collection, an asset financed longer than the loan tenor, an unprofitable customer cohort, a failed refinancing, supplier arrears, a loss of distribution access or a governance decision. If the record cannot discriminate among causes, write what it establishes and name the missing document.

sections.heading: Build a company outcome file in five passes
sections.text:
Pass 1: Map the legal entities. List parent, holding company, operating subsidiaries, asset-owning entities and trade names. Record company numbers and former names. Draw the ownership relationships only where a filing, registry record, contract or administrator notice supports them. Do not infer that shared branding means shared liabilities.

Pass 2: Reconcile funding. Add one row per transaction with announcement, close and cash dates, original currency, legal recipient, instrument, security, amount drawn and source. Separate a company's own shares sold from secondary sales; separate cash equity from loan commitments; flag later refinancing.

Pass 3: Build the operating timeline. Record what was public or known to management at each decision date: product launches, customer terms, route openings, hiring, shutdowns, leadership changes, missed payments, fundraising, acquisition, court filing and administrator appointment. Use exact dates and identify who could access the information.

Pass 4: Trace cash and unit economics. If available, link customer orders to delivered sales, cash collections, direct cost, returns, delivery cost, working-capital investment, capex and debt service. Calculate contribution by cohort or unit. Keep company-level cash history blank if records are absent; do not fill it with a fictional example and label it as history.

Pass 5: Classify the outcome and recovery. Date the trading status, legal status, asset sale or merger separately. Estimate creditor recoveries only from administrator distributions or confirmed payments. Estimate equity outcomes only from distributions, secondary proceeds or a supportable remaining valuation. If unresolved, retain “unknown.”

sections.heading: A decision record for the next founder and investor
sections.text:
For founders, the lesson is to connect every raise to a milestone and a cash plan. Before signing, test what happens if the next round is delayed six months, if a top customer pays late, if inventory turns more slowly, or if the currency moves against the company. Name the action for each trigger and the person accountable. Record any personal guarantees, liens or security granted by affiliates.

For investors, record the financing thesis before the outcome is known. What evidence supported the customer opportunity? What was the expected capital need to reach a durable margin? Which assumptions were uncertain? What would count as a successful adjustment, a failed hypothesis or a new funding need? A later failure does not alone show that the original investment was irrational. A contemporaneous investment memo makes that test possible.

For journalists, ecosystem teams and policymakers, do not add all “raised” values for a selected group and call the result losses. Separate financing instrument, entity, outcome, time period, national market and source. If the data are incomplete, state which records could change the conclusion. Readers can handle an unresolved finding when the next research step is concrete.

sections.heading: What the 13-company screenshot currently supports
sections.text:
The screenshot supports two limited facts: it displayed 13 named brands with claimed amounts, and those amounts arithmetically total KSh 93.31bn. The five largest displayed claims form about 81.1% of that selected list. FSD Kenya’s 2024 report supplies a later public snapshot of several companies’ financing and broad operating/legal outcomes, while court and Gazette materials give more precise entity and legal-process records for Copia, Nakumatt and Tuskys. September 2026 reporting adds a new, still-to-be-verified administration status for two Twiga-related legal entities.

The research does not yet support the claim that every listed startup “collapsed,” that each amount reached the named Kenyan operating company, or that investors lost KSh 93bn. It also cannot reconstruct each company’s owner earnings or declare one cause of distress. The useful next output is a verified ledger and matched workbook, not a stronger adjective.

sections.heading: Do not turn a selected list into a startup failure rate
sections.text:
The screenshot begins with companies already described as collapsed. It is therefore a case list selected on an outcome. To estimate a failure rate, start with a defined population: for example, every Kenya-tagged venture that received a source-defined first equity or debt transaction in 2020, then observe each for five years. The researcher would need a denominator of all qualifying recipients, including firms that continue trading, were acquired, changed business model, stopped operating or remain unresolved. If companies are included only after a reported closure, the sample cannot tell us the share of all funded ventures that closed.

The outcome also needs a fixed definition and horizon. “Closed operations in Kenya” is different from “liquidated legal entity”; “administration” is a legal procedure, not necessarily a terminal operating state. An acquisition can preserve employees and products while ending the original shareholders' investment. A voluntary pivot can close one business line without ending the parent company. Code each dimension separately and allow more than one event date. State whether the event is first legal filing, cessation of trading, asset sale, acquisition or final dissolution.

Follow-up periods differ. A company funded in 2025 has had less time to fail than one funded in 2018. If the analysis counts only companies whose outcomes are already known, it will overrepresent older cohorts. Survival or hazard methods can handle unequal observation time when dates and event definitions are reliable, but they cannot fix missing companies or inconsistent source coverage. Shumway's public-company bankruptcy study treats failure as a time-dependent outcome; it does not supply a Kenyan startup base rate [11].

An evidence-quality column should accompany the outcome code. A court judgment can verify that an order was issued, and may summarize a creditor's statement. It does not independently establish every allegation in that statement. A company release can verify what management announced, not the ultimate cash recovery. A media report can date an event and point to a Gazette notice. A screenshot can preserve the wording of a claim. Those source types can all be useful, but their uses differ.

A practical case register can record one row per dated event with: legal entity; former name; country operation; event date; public date; source; source passage; event category; operational status; legal status; evidence level; and follow-up record needed. Keep the earlier status in history rather than overwriting it when a later event arrives. This lets a reviewer answer both “What is the status now?” and “What could a lender or supplier have known then?”

sections.heading: Workbook map
sections.text: The Startup Funding Market and Outcomes workbook has a Company Outcomes sheet that places each screenshot amount beside its current evidence note, but does not label every company a failure. Deal Ledger separates announcement, closing, drawdown and cash receipt and stays blank until evidence supports a transaction. Sources and Checks records the Gazette, court and tracker sources and flags where the company or funding entity still needs reconciliation. There is no recovery total because investor-level recoveries have not been established, and the selected 13-company list is not a cohort from which a failure rate can be estimated. Appendix 03 provides the full claim-by-claim register and the next evidence request for each case.
